en: Geologists classify faults partly by dip, the angle the fault plane makes with the horizontal, from steep near-vertical cracks to low-angle slides.
verify_reason: Dip is angle from horizontal; classification by dip is correct.

en: If the slip is mostly up or down the sloping plane, the fault is dip-slip; if the slip is mostly sideways, it is strike-slip.
verify_reason: Dip-slip is up/down; strike-slip is sideways.

en: A thrust fault is a reverse fault with a gentle dip, so hanging-wall rocks ride up a low-angle plane instead of a steep one.
verify_reason: Thrust faults are low-angle reverse faults.

en: On a dipping fault, you name the slip by what the hanging wall did: down for normal, up for reverse, matching the angle of the plane.
verify_reason: Hanging wall down normal, up reverse.

en: Humans are placed in Class Mammalia because, like other mammals, they have mammary glands that can produce milk for young.
verify_reason: Mammary glands are defining mammalian trait.

en: Humans are mammals because they grow hair, the same body covering that, as fur, helps classify dogs, cats, and bats in Mammalia.
verify_reason: Hair/fur is a mammal trait.

en: The three tiny middle-ear bones are a mammal trait; humans have them, which is one anatomical reason we belong in Class Mammalia.
verify_reason: Three middle-ear bones are mammal trait.

en: Humans keep a steady warm body temperature using metabolism, an endotherm trait shared with other mammals and used in classification.
verify_reason: Endothermy is shared mammalian trait.

en: Humans give birth to live young that develop inside the mother, matching the typical mammalian pattern used to place us in Class Mammalia.
verify_reason: Live birth is typical mammalian pattern.

en: A muscular diaphragm that powers breathing is another mammal feature humans share, supporting the Class Mammalia placement.
verify_reason: Diaphragm is a mammal feature.

en: Skin with sweat glands and mammary glands is part of the mammal package; humans have both, so we are not reptiles or birds.
verify_reason: Sweat and mammary glands are mammal features.

en: A four-chambered heart that keeps oxygen-rich blood separate is typical of mammals; humans have that heart plan, matching Class Mammalia.
verify_reason: Four-chambered heart typical of mammals.

en: Mammals have a lower jaw made of one bone on each side; humans show that jaw plan, another reason we are classified as mammals.
verify_reason: Mammals have one lower jaw bone per side; humans share this.

en: Talking and using tools do not put humans in Mammalia; the class is about shared body traits such as hair, milk, and ear bones.
verify_reason: Mammal class is based on body traits, not talking or tools.

en: Humans are primates because our eyes face forward with overlapping vision, a primate trait that helps judge distance.
verify_reason: Forward eyes with overlapping vision are a primate trait.

en: Humans have grasping hands with a mobile thumb, a primate trait used to hold branches or tools and to place us in Order Primates.
verify_reason: Grasping hands with mobile thumb are primate features.

en: Flat nails instead of sharp claws on the fingers and toes are a primate feature humans share with monkeys and apes.
verify_reason: Flat nails are a shared primate feature.

en: Primates have large brains relative to body size; humans fit that pattern, which is one reason we are placed in Order Primates.
verify_reason: Large brain relative to body size fits primates.

en: Many primates learn by watching others; humans do this intensely, a behavioral trait that fits Order Primates along with the body traits.
verify_reason: Social learning is common in primates, including humans.

en: A well-developed collarbone and flexible shoulder help primates climb or reach; humans keep that skeleton plan even if we walk on two legs.
verify_reason: Collarbone and flexible shoulder are primate skeletal traits.

en: Classification stacks: humans are mammals because of milk and hair, and primates because of forward eyes and grasping hands, not one label alone.
verify_reason: Classification uses stacked mammal and primate traits.

en: Humans are not classed with fish or reptiles because those groups lack hair, mammary glands, and the mammal ear-bone set.
verify_reason: Fish and reptiles lack defining mammal traits.

en: Apes are primates too; humans sit inside that order with them, which is why we share nails, forward eyes, and a large brain.
verify_reason: Apes and humans share primate traits.

en: Monkeys belong to Order Primates as well; humans are classified there for the same primate body plan, not because people are monkeys.
verify_reason: Monkeys are primates; humans share the primate body plan.

en: Binocular vision, seeing one scene with both eyes at once, is a primate trait humans have and a reason for the Order Primates placement.
verify_reason: Accurate for grade 5; binocular vision is a primate trait.

en: An opposable thumb that can touch the other fingers is a primate grasping trait; humans use it, which supports the primate classification.
verify_reason: Accurate; opposable thumbs support primate grasping traits.

en: Primates emphasize the neocortex, a brain region for complex sensing and social life; humans show that primate pattern in extreme form.
verify_reason: Accurate; primates have large neocortex for complex behavior.

en: A shorter snout and more emphasis on vision than smell is typical of primates; the human face follows that primate pattern.
verify_reason: Accurate; primates favor vision over smell with shorter snouts.

en: Humans typically have two mammary glands, still the mammal milk organs that place us in Mammalia even though litter size is usually one.
verify_reason: Accurate; mammary glands define mammals, humans have two.

en: Humans are placental mammals: the young are nourished through a placenta before birth, a mammal subgroup that still sits inside Class Mammalia.
verify_reason: Accurate; humans are placental mammals within Mammalia.

en: Different tooth types in one mouth, incisors through molars, are typical of mammals; humans have that set, matching Class Mammalia.
verify_reason: Accurate; different tooth types are typical of mammals.

en: Mammalia is a wide class that also holds whales and cows; Primates is the narrower order that groups humans with other forward-eyed, grasping relatives.
verify_reason: Accurate; Mammalia is broader, Primates is narrower.

en: Language, clothes, and cities do not define the biological class or order; those are culture, while Mammalia and Primates are body-plan groups.
verify_reason: Accurate; culture does not define biological classification.

en: In the ranked system, Class Mammalia sits above Order Primates; humans belong to both, like an address with a city and a street.
verify_reason: Accurate; class ranks above order.

en: Walking upright is a human specialty, not the trait that puts us in Mammalia or Primates; those groups are defined by older shared characters.
verify_reason: Accurate; bipedalism is not a Mammalia or Primates trait.

en: Tarsiers are primates but not monkeys; humans share the order with them because of primate eyes and hands, even though the faces look different.
verify_reason: Accurate; tarsiers are primates but not monkeys.

en: Feeding young on milk after birth is the everyday mammal clue; humans do this, which is why Class Mammalia includes us.
verify_reason: Mammals feed young milk; humans do, so this is correct.

en: Two of the mammal middle-ear bones came from jaw bones in earlier animals; humans have that mammal ear, a classification character for Mammalia.
verify_reason: Mammal middle-ear bones evolved from jaw bones; true for humans.

en: Fingerprints help grip, but they are not the main reason for Order Primates; forward eyes, nails, and grasping hands are the standard characters.
verify_reason: Primate traits are forward eyes, nails, grasping hands; fingerprints not main.

en: A class table can list mammal traits on the left and primate traits on the right, then tick which ones humans show, which is all of the standard ones.
verify_reason: Humans show standard mammal and primate traits; table idea works.

en: Whales have milk and hair traces so they are mammals, but they lack grasping hands and forward primate eyes, so they are not in Order Primates.
verify_reason: Whales are mammals but lack primate hand and eye traits.

en: Lemurs are primates of Madagascar; humans share the order with them because of the primate body plan, even though lemur faces look very different.
verify_reason: Lemurs are primates; humans share the order with them.

en: A complete explanation uses because: humans are mammals because of hair and milk, and primates because of forward eyes, nails, and grasping hands.
verify_reason: Correctly links mammal and primate traits using because.

en: Humans belong to Class Mammalia for mammal body traits and to Order Primates for primate eyes, hands, and nails, two nested reasons, not a single nickname.
verify_reason: Correctly states two nested classification reasons for humans.

en: A simple proportion to remember is about seven tenths water to three tenths land, so water, not land, makes up most of Earth's face.
verify_reason: Earth's surface is about seven-tenths water, three-tenths land.

en: The Southern Hemisphere has even more of its surface as ocean than the Northern Hemisphere, which holds most of the planet's land.
verify_reason: Southern Hemisphere has more ocean; most land is northern.

en: On an equal-area world map the blue ocean still clearly outweighs the land, a visual check that water covers most of Earth's surface.
verify_reason: Equal-area maps show ocean covering more surface than land.

en: If Earth's surface were ten equal tiles, about three would be land and about seven would be water, so land is the smaller share.
verify_reason: About three of ten tiles land, seven water; land smaller.

en: Start with the DOST website or its attached agencies, then write the page title and date so your typhoon-support notes can be checked later.
verify_reason: Good practice for verifiable notes.

en: PAGASA is a DOST-attached agency, so its typhoon bulletins are an official source for how authorities warn communities before landfall.
verify_reason: PAGASA is DOST-attached and issues official warnings.

en: The NDRRMC site lists how national and local offices share tasks after a typhoon, a reliable place to see who supports which community need.
verify_reason: NDRRMC coordinates disaster response roles.

en: The Office of Civil Defense runs operations centers that collect situation reports, a support system you can identify on official civil-defense pages.
verify_reason: OCD runs operations centers and situation reports.

en: DSWD pages describe family food packs and other relief goods prepositioned for typhoon-hit towns, an example of material support after a storm.
verify_reason: DSWD provides food packs and relief goods.

en: City and municipal websites often post which schools or halls are evacuation centers, local authority support you should copy from that official page.
verify_reason: LGUs post evacuation center locations.

en: When you gather typhoon-support facts, prefer pages ending in gov.ph so you are reading the authority itself, not a copied rumor.
verify_reason: Official gov.ph domains are authoritative.

en: Copy the URL of the DOST, PAGASA, or NDRRMC page you used, because a support claim without a link is hard for classmates to verify.
verify_reason: URLs let classmates verify claims.

en: Authority support starts before landfall: official wind signals and rainfall warnings help communities move early, which you can document from PAGASA.
verify_reason: PAGASA warnings enable early action.

en: NDRRMC and local DRRM pages identify search-and-rescue groups sent to flooded or isolated barangays, a life-saving form of typhoon support.
verify_reason: NDRRMC/local DRRM identify search-and-rescue teams.

en: DILG circulars on official sites tell local governments to prepare evacuation and curfew rules, showing how national authorities back towns during typhoons.
verify_reason: DILG issues local disaster preparedness circulars.

en: DepEd or LGU pages that announce class suspension are a form of support: they keep students off flooded roads, and you can cite the dated notice.
verify_reason: DepEd/LGU announcements are official, dated, and safety-related.

en: DOH situation reports can list medical teams and clean-water advice for typhoon-hit areas, health support that belongs in a sourced class report.
verify_reason: DOH reports include health teams and water advice.

en: Always record the date on a typhoon bulletin, because support instructions change as the storm moves, and an old page can mislead a community.
verify_reason: Bulletins change; dates prevent using outdated guidance.

en: Official agency pages publish hotlines for rescue and relief; copying those numbers from gov.ph is gathering support information the competency asks for.
verify_reason: Official hotlines are verifiable support information.

en: A Facebook screenshot is not enough; match the claim to a PAGASA or NDRRMC page before you treat it as how authorities are supporting people.
verify_reason: Verify social media claims against official agency pages.

en: DSWD and OCD reports often say goods were prepositioned in regional warehouses before landfall, support that happens while the weather is still building.
verify_reason: DSWD/OCD pre-position goods before landfall.

en: Official disaster reports may list AFP or PNP help with rescue and security in typhoon zones, national-force support you should attribute to that report.
verify_reason: AFP/PNP assistance appears in official reports.

en: After the strongest winds, authorities keep evacuation shelters open while flooding lasts, a support step described in many LGU and NDRRMC updates.
verify_reason: Shelters stay open during flooding per official updates.

en: Older DOST hazard-map projects such as Project NOAH remain a secondary source for flood-prone places that need extra typhoon support planning.
verify_reason: Project NOAH archives remain useful hazard-map sources.

en: Authorities support flood-prone towns with rainfall warnings even when the wind signal is still low, a distinction you can see on PAGASA's warning pages.
verify_reason: PAGASA rainfall warnings can precede high wind signals.

en: When foreign aid arrives, NDRRMC pages often record how it is coordinated, so the official channel for outside support is still a government site.
verify_reason: NDRRMC coordinates and records foreign aid.

en: A clear report names each agency's job: PAGASA warns, DSWD feeds and shelters, OCD coordinates, LGUs evacuate, all documented on their sites.
verify_reason: Agencies have distinct documented disaster roles.

en: NDRRMC numbered situation reports list affected families and assistance already delivered, a dated official source for support after the typhoon.
verify_reason: NDRRMC reports are dated official sources with affected families and aid.

en: The Philippine Red Cross website describes volunteer rescue and blood services that work with government during typhoons, a partner you can cite beside NDRRMC.
verify_reason: Red Cross provides rescue and blood services alongside government.

en: Authorities often support communities with drinking water and hygiene kits when floods contaminate wells, details that appear in DOH or DSWD updates.
verify_reason: DOH and DSWD updates often include water and hygiene aid.

en: DOE or electric-coop bulletins can list which towns have power back, infrastructure support after a typhoon that you should date and source.
verify_reason: DOE and electric co-ops list towns with restored power.

en: If you cannot find a hotline on an official page, leave it blank; inventing a number is not gathering information and can send people to the wrong help.
verify_reason: Inventing hotlines misleads people needing real help.

en: Regional OCD or DRRM office pages show how support is organized closer to the affected provinces, not only from a Manila headline.
verify_reason: Regional OCD and DRRM pages show local support organization.

en: DA updates may describe seeds or assistance for farmers whose fields were flooded or wind-damaged, livelihood support after the weather eases.
verify_reason: DA updates may list seeds and aid for damaged farms.

en: Some DSWD or UNICEF-partner notes describe child-friendly spaces in evacuation centers, a support service you can record from a named humanitarian page.
verify_reason: DSWD and UNICEF partners describe child-friendly spaces in shelters.

topic: list what you still cannot find
en: End the investigation by listing questions the websites did not answer, because honest gathering includes gaps in how support was described.
verify_reason: Listing gaps is honest information gathering.

en: Barangay DRRM committees, described in DILG or LGU pages, are the nearest official support for warning neighbors and opening a local shelter.
verify_reason: Barangay DRRM committees are nearest local official support.

en: If an official DSWD or LGU page lists emergency cash aid after a named typhoon, cite that page rather than a forwarded text message.

en: DepEd memos on official sites often allow schools to serve as evacuation shelters, a support use of public buildings during and after typhoons.
verify_reason: DepEd policies allow schools as evacuation centers.

en: Look on NDRRMC or DSWD pages for notes on assisting persons with disabilities in evacuation, a support detail easy to miss if you only skim headlines.
verify_reason: NDRRMC and DSWD include disability-inclusive evacuation guidance.

en: Some OCD reports mention backup radios or satellite links for cut-off towns, communications support when typhoons take down ordinary towers.
verify_reason: OCD reports mention backup radios or satellite links.

en: Keep a folder per storm with dated printouts from DOST-PAGASA and NDRRMC, so your class can see how official support changed through the event.
verify_reason: Dated PAGASA and NDRRMC printouts track official updates.

en: DPWH notices can describe clearing blocked drainage after a typhoon, infrastructure support that is still part of how authorities help communities recover.
verify_reason: DPWH clears drainage as post-typhoon infrastructure support.

en: PHIVOLCS pages are for earthquakes and volcanoes; for typhoon support, stay on PAGASA, NDRRMC, and DSWD so the gathered help matches the hazard.
verify_reason: PHIVOLCS covers earthquakes/volcanoes; use typhoon agencies for typhoons.

en: Some official warnings are issued in Filipino and English; gathering both versions can show how authorities try to reach more households.

en: Post-disaster NDRRMC reports that count houses repaired or families served are still support information, not only the hours while the wind was strongest.

en: Authorities use rainfall, wind, and surge forecasts together to decide who should move, a science-based support process documented on PAGASA and NDRRMC sites.
verify_reason: Forecasts guide evacuation decisions.

en: Official situation reports sometimes list accredited volunteer groups, so you can name partners without treating an unsourced chat as government policy.
verify_reason: Situation reports list accredited volunteer groups.

en: DA or LGU pages may advise moving animals out of flood plains before a typhoon, livelihood support that sits beside human evacuation orders.
verify_reason: DA/LGU pages advise moving livestock from flood plains.

en: Authorities also support communities by announcing when it is safer to return; gather that all-clear from the same official channels, not from a guess.
verify_reason: Official all-clear should come from authorities, not guesses.

en: Other reliable sites include WMO summaries and academic hazard papers, but local support actions should still be confirmed on Philippine government pages.
verify_reason: WMO and academic sources are reliable; local actions need government confirmation.

en: Match the local PAGASA name of the cyclone on the support page, so you do not mix relief numbers from two different storms.

en: Official pages frame evacuation as protection, a way authorities support people in mapped danger zones rather than as a punishment for staying.
verify_reason: Evacuation is protective support, not punishment.

en: The competency is about typhoon-affected communities, so a DOST scholarship page is the wrong source even though it is an official DOST website.
verify_reason: Scholarship page is off-topic for typhoon community support.

en: A strong class packet cites at least three official pages, such as PAGASA, NDRRMC, and DSWD, then says what support each one documents.
verify_reason: Three official sources document different support roles.

en: DPWH or local engineering pages that post passable roads after a typhoon help families and relief trucks, a logistics support you can date and quote.
verify_reason: DPWH road updates aid logistics; date and quote them.

en: DOH or DSWD pages may mention psychosocial support in evacuation centers; if you include it, quote the named page and do not give medical advice yourself.

en: A poster can show screenshots of official homepages with the dates, plus one sentence each on warning, rescue, and relief as the three support layers.

en: Copy casualty or damage numbers only as printed on the NDRRMC sitrep, and say 'according to that report,' because unofficial counts are often wrong.
verify_reason: Use NDRRMC sitrep numbers and attribute them.

en: Authorities support communities through recovery months with housing and livelihood programs, which later official reports still document after the headlines fade.

en: Better forecasts from DOST-PAGASA are themselves a form of support: earlier, clearer warnings give families more hours to move and to pack.
verify_reason: Better forecasts give earlier warnings and more preparation time.

en: Some LGU pages list which office stays open as an emergency operations center, a practical support detail students can gather from the city site.
verify_reason: Accurate; LGU pages often list emergency operations center details.

en: Before the season, NDRRMC and PAGASA sites post preparedness checklists, support that happens even when no named cyclone exists yet.
verify_reason: NDRRMC and PAGASA do post preparedness checklists before season.

en: Quote one official sentence about support, then paraphrase in your own words, so the gathered fact stays tied to the agency and still reads as yours.
verify_reason: Good research practice; quote and paraphrase accurately.

en: A complete answer names more than warnings: it also identifies relief, rescue, shelter, and recovery actions found on official websites.
verify_reason: Complete support includes relief, rescue, shelter, recovery.

en: Gathering here means opening DOST and other reliable sites, naming the authority, and recording how that office actually helps typhoon-hit communities.
verify_reason: Accurate task definition for gathering official support info.

en: Tidal energy needs a useful difference between high tide and low tide, the range secondary sources measure before anyone builds a plant.
verify_reason: Tidal range is high-low difference; correct.

en: A tidal barrage is built across a suitable estuary so the height difference drives turbines as the basin fills and empties.
verify_reason: Barrage across estuary uses height difference; correct.

en: Where a narrow channel speeds the tide, underwater turbines can harvest the current without a full barrage wall across a bay.
verify_reason: Tidal stream turbines in narrow channels; correct.

en: Secondary energy studies look for large tidal range or fast tidal streams, because a pretty beach with small tides cannot power a plant.
verify_reason: Large range or fast streams needed; correct.

en: Tide times can be predicted years ahead from astronomy, so tidal energy is regular in a way wind energy is not, a point energy agencies often stress.
verify_reason: Tides are astronomically predictable; correct.

topic: twice a day in many places
en: Many coasts have two highs and two lows each day, so a well-sited plant can generate on a repeating daily schedule of tidal difference.
verify_reason: Many coasts have semidiurnal tides; correct.

en: A tidal lagoon uses a walled basin beside the coast so the same rise-and-fall difference turns turbines without closing an entire river mouth.
verify_reason: Tidal lagoon uses walled basin; correct.

en: When you name a site as promising, cite a DOE, IRENA, or peer-reviewed resource map rather than a tourism blog about a pretty strait.
verify_reason: Good source guidance for research.

en: Secondary sources also warn that barrages can change mudflats and fish movement, so a good site must have both energy and an accepted environmental plan.
verify_reason: True; barrages can affect habitats and fish.

en: Even a strong tide is useless for electricity if there is no grid connection; energy studies list both the water resource and the nearby power lines.
verify_reason: True; power needs grid access.

en: South Korea's Sihwa tidal power plant is a documented barrage-style site that secondary sources use as a working example of exploiting tidal difference.
verify_reason: True; Sihwa is a real barrage plant.

topic: La Rance as a documented plant
en: France's La Rance plant has generated electricity from tidal difference for decades, a classic secondary-source example of a barrage across an estuary.
verify_reason: True; La Rance is a classic example.

en: Tidal-stream turbines need enough depth to stay submerged at low tide, a site filter that resource maps use besides current speed.
verify_reason: True; turbines need low-tide clearance.

en: Busy shipping channels may have fast tides but are poor plant sites if turbines would block ships, a conflict energy papers routinely discuss.
verify_reason: True; shipping conflicts matter.

en: Spring tides, when Sun and Moon align, make a larger tidal difference and thus more potential energy than neap tides in the same place.
verify_reason: True; aligned Sun and Moon increase range.

en: Neap tides have a smaller high-to-low difference, so a plant's output is not the same every day even though the schedule stays predictable.
verify_reason: True; neap tides reduce output.

en: DOE and academic papers have screened Philippine straits for tidal-stream potential; cite those studies instead of guessing from a ferry ride.
verify_reason: True; studies exist, better than guessing.

en: Some barrage designs generate on both the flood and the ebb, using the difference in both directions to make more of the daily tidal cycle.
verify_reason: True; some designs generate both directions.

en: A few designs pump extra water into the basin at high tide to enlarge the difference later, a method described in engineering reviews of tidal plants.
verify_reason: Pumping at high tide can increase head.

en: A storm surge is weather piled water, not the regular astronomical tide; sources for tidal energy must use tide tables, not typhoon water levels.
verify_reason: Storm surge is weather-driven, not astronomical tide.

en: The Moon's gravity, with the Sun's, makes the tidal difference; secondary physics pages are the right source for why the water keeps rising and falling.
verify_reason: Moon and Sun gravity cause tides.

en: Before claiming a bay can make power, sources measure months of tide-gauge data; one afternoon of watching the shore is not a resource study.
verify_reason: Long-term tide data is needed.

en: Energy agencies also report high construction cost for barrages, so a suitable tide is necessary but not enough if the project cannot be paid for.
verify_reason: Barrages are costly; tide alone isn't enough.

en: Modern source papers discuss fish passages and turbine slowdowns as ways to exploit tides while reducing harm to migrating animals.
verify_reason: Fish passages and slower turbines reduce harm.

en: Small island grids might use a modest tidal-stream unit if measurements show a reliable current, a situation different from a giant estuary barrage.
verify_reason: Small tidal-stream units suit reliable currents.

en: Because tides shift later each day, sources discuss whether generation times match evening demand, a siting question besides the size of the difference.
verify_reason: Tides shift daily, affecting demand match.

en: Barrage basins can trap sediment, shrinking the useful water difference over years, a long-term issue secondary environmental reviews flag.
verify_reason: Sediment can reduce basin capacity over time.

topic: look up a tide table first
en: A class investigation can start with a published tide table for a bay, then ask whether the listed high-low gap is large enough to interest an energy study.
verify_reason: Tide tables help check high-low gap.

en: Tidal energy is called renewable in textbooks because the Earth-Moon orbit keeps making the difference, unlike a coal pile that can run out.
verify_reason: Earth-Moon orbit continually drives tides.

en: Some coastal energy papers compare tidal sites with offshore wind; your task is still to identify the tidal-difference cases, not to switch topics to wind.
verify_reason: Some papers compare tidal and wind; task focus is tidal.

en: When you copy a site from a paper, write the typical tidal range in meters and the mean current speed, the two numbers that justify exploiting the difference.
verify_reason: Tidal range and current speed are key site numbers.

en: The Bay of Fundy is often cited for an unusually large tidal range, a world example of a place where the difference is large enough to study for power.
verify_reason: Bay of Fundy has large tidal range.

en: A few technology reviews describe tethered tidal kites that fly in a current, another proposed way to exploit tidal-stream difference in deep channels.
verify_reason: Tidal kites are real proposed devices.

en: National energy papers also mention permits for using a waterway, so a scientifically good tide still needs legal clearance to be exploited.
verify_reason: Permits are needed for waterway use.

en: Secondary siting guides call for consulting fishing communities, because a turbine field can change the very channel people already use.
verify_reason: Consulting fishing communities is advised.

en: A proper study measures both spring and neap cycles so the smallest useful difference is known, not only the most dramatic high tide of the month.
verify_reason: Spring and neap measurements show minimum range.

en: Some tidal-stream designs use vertical-axis turbines that work with reversing current, matching a tide that flows two ways each day.
verify_reason: Vertical-axis turbines suit reversing tidal currents.

en: Other designs look like underwater wind turbines facing the current; sources still classify them as tidal-stream devices, not wind machines.
verify_reason: Underwater wind-like turbines are tidal-stream devices.

topic: head is another word for difference
en: Engineering sources call the high-to-low water gap the tidal head; a larger head means more potential energy per cubic meter of water.
verify_reason: Tidal head is water-level gap; larger means more energy.

en: If the listed tidal head is only a few tens of centimeters, secondary sources usually drop the site, because turbines need a more useful difference.
verify_reason: Accurate; small tidal head is not useful for turbines.

en: One month of tide data can miss seasonal changes; energy papers prefer multi-year gauges before they call a difference exploitable.
verify_reason: Accurate; long-term data captures seasonal tide changes.

en: A class can use a government energy outlook, a peer-reviewed siting paper, and a tide table, three secondary sources that together identify a possible site type.
verify_reason: Accurate; these are appropriate secondary sources.

topic: do not promise a local plant
en: Identifying a situation where tides could be used is not the same as promising a plant in your hometown; keep the claim as large as the source.
verify_reason: Accurate; claim should match source evidence.

en: Some older barrages generate mainly on the ebb, releasing stored high water through turbines when the sea outside has already fallen.
verify_reason: Accurate; ebb generation uses falling tide.

en: Other schemes generate as the tide floods into a basin, another documented way of using the incoming height difference.
verify_reason: Accurate; flood generation uses incoming tide.

en: Marine energy reviews mention rust and biofouling on turbines, practical limits on exploiting a good tide that physics alone does not show.
verify_reason: Accurate; rust and biofouling limit real turbines.

en: Papers on tidal-stream farms discuss spacing turbines so the wake of one does not steal the current difference from the next.
verify_reason: Accurate; wakes reduce current for nearby turbines.

en: A global tidal-energy atlas is a secondary source for spotting where the difference is large; local studies then check whether that spot can actually be built.
verify_reason: Accurate; atlas finds sites, local studies confirm.

en: The competency asks for situations where the tidal difference could be exploited, meaning converted to useful electricity, not merely watched from a pier.
verify_reason: Accurate; exploitable means converted to electricity.

en: Sources group sites into closed-basin barrages or lagoons versus open-stream turbines, two different situations for using the same tidal rise and fall.
verify_reason: Accurate; barrages and stream turbines are two types.

en: Unlike solar power, a tidal difference still arrives at night, a reason secondary energy comparisons list tides as a complementary renewable.
verify_reason: Accurate; tides occur at night unlike solar.

en: A typhoon swell is not the tidal resource; exploiting tidal difference means using the regular astronomical cycle, which sources separate from storm waves.
verify_reason: Tidal power uses regular astronomical tides, not storm swells.

topic: quote the range in about meters
en: If a paper says a mean range of about five meters, copy it as 'about five meters' and name the paper; do not invent a more dramatic number.
verify_reason: Accurate guidance about citing sources honestly.

en: A complete identification names a site type that is both physically suitable and discussed as acceptable in the sources, not only a huge tide on a map.
verify_reason: Correct; requires physical and source-based suitability.

en: In one sentence: secondary sources look for large, regular high-to-low water differences in estuaries or fast channels, then ask if turbines can safely use them.
verify_reason: Accurate summary of tidal site selection.

en: Mechanical energy is the kinetic plus potential energy that is still available to do work, such as lifting, turning, or speeding something up.
verify_reason: Correct; mechanical energy is kinetic plus potential.

en: To state an object's mechanical energy you add the energy of its motion to the energy stored by its position or shape, not only one of those parts.
verify_reason: Correct; mechanical energy includes both parts.

topic: both can be zero or not
en: A still object high on a shelf has mechanical energy from potential alone, while a sliding object on the floor can have mechanical energy from kinetic alone.
verify_reason: Correct; potential or kinetic can act alone.

en: To discuss a shower's regular timing, check a current astronomy almanac or PAGASA skywatch page rather than a random social-media date.
verify_reason: Accurate advice to use reliable astronomy sources.

en: A shower is named for the constellation that holds its radiant, and that name stays the same year after year as the stream is crossed again.
verify_reason: Correct; showers are named by radiant constellation.

en: Many annual showers come from a parent comet whose orbit still sheds dust, so Earth meets that dust on a schedule set by both orbits.
verify_reason: Correct; many showers come from comet dust.

en: The Geminids are a regular December shower whose parent is an asteroid-like body, showing that not every annual stream is from a classic comet.
verify_reason: Correct; Geminids parent is asteroid-like.

en: The Quadrantid meteor shower is a regular early-January event, another calendar marker listed in yearly meteor-shower tables.
verify_reason: Correct; Quadrantids occur in early January.

en: A shower has a peak night and a wider season; reliable tables list both, so 'regular' does not mean only a single hour each year.
verify_reason: Peak night and wider season are both listed.

en: The International Meteor Organization publishes yearly calendars of expected showers, a secondary source students can cite for regular dates.
verify_reason: IMO yearly calendars are citable secondary sources.

en: Random sporadic meteors can appear any night, but a shower is the regular, clustered burst when Earth hits a known dust stream.
verify_reason: Sporadics differ from regular shower bursts.

en: Earth's year-long trip around the Sun is the clock: the same stretch of orbit is where a given shower's dust is waiting each year.
verify_reason: Earth's orbit timing makes showers repeat yearly.

en: The shower still occurs on schedule even if a bright Moon hides many meteors, so regularity is about the stream, not about how many you personally see.
verify_reason: Moonlight affects visibility, not shower timing.

en: The Lyrids are a regular April shower tied to comet Thatcher, listed on annual sky calendars along with the better-known Perseids.
verify_reason: Lyrids are April shower from comet Thatcher.

en: The Orionids return each October from dust of comet Halley, a regular shower whose parent comet is famous from other years as well.
verify_reason: Orionids are October Halley debris.

en: The Eta Aquariids are a regular May shower also linked to comet Halley, showing one comet trail can make more than one annual meeting.
verify_reason: Halley's orbit yields two annual showers.

en: Secondary sources often list a zenithal hourly rate for the peak; that number describes a typical regular year, not a guarantee for your backyard.
verify_reason: ZHR is idealized peak rate, not local guarantee.

en: Many annual showers are visible from the Philippines, though some northern radiants sit lower; a local astronomy club table is a useful source.
verify_reason: Philippines sees many showers; local tables help.

en: A meteor storm is a rare extra-dense year, not the usual regular shower; textbooks separate those outliers from the ordinary annual return.
verify_reason: Storms are rare outliers, not regular showers.

topic: cite the year of the table
en: When you copy a peak date, write the year of the table, because leap years and orbital drift can shift the listed night by a day.
verify_reason: Peak dates shift; cite table year.

en: Some streams are centuries old, yet Earth still crosses them on a yearly rhythm, which is why the shower is called regular even if the comet is faint now.
verify_reason: Accurate; old streams can still cause yearly showers.

en: The meteors do not come from the stars of Perseus or Gemini; those names only mark the sky direction of a regular, nearby dust crossing.
verify_reason: Correct; constellation names only mark radiant direction.

en: Many annual showers are better after midnight because that side of Earth then faces into the dust stream, a regular geometric reason in the sources.
verify_reason: Correct; after midnight Earth faces into dust stream.

en: The Ursids are a quieter regular shower near late December, often listed beside the Geminids on the same yearly meteor calendar.
verify_reason: Accurate; Ursids peak near late December.

en: A reliable discussion uses observatory dates, not a story that showers are random wishes; regularity is an orbital fact you can look up.
verify_reason: Correct; reliable sources use predictable orbital dates.

en: How many nights a shower lasts depends on how wide the dust stream is, which is why some regular showers are short and others last weeks.
verify_reason: Correct; stream width affects shower duration.

en: Yearly tables also list typical meteor speed for each shower, another regular property of that stream, not a new surprise each August.
verify_reason: Accurate; meteor speed is a regular listed property.

en: Photographers plan the same showers on the same weeks each year, practical evidence that the occurrence is regular enough to schedule.
verify_reason: Correct; predictable dates allow planned photography.

en: Listing both Orionids and Eta Aquariids from Halley is a way secondary sources show that one parent orbit can give two regular Earth crossings.
verify_reason: Correct; Halley's orbit yields two annual showers.

en: In one sentence: meteor showers occur regularly because Earth's orbit keeps meeting known dust trails at repeatable times you can look up.
verify_reason: Accurate; Earth's orbit repeats dust-trail crossings.

en: Secondary sources group mutations as beneficial, harmful, or neutral depending on whether they help, hurt, or barely change an organism's survival.
verify_reason: Correct; mutations are beneficial, harmful, or neutral.

en: Many sources say most DNA changes are neutral, meaning the protein or the organism works about as before, with no clear help or harm.
verify_reason: Accurate; most DNA changes are neutral.

en: A well-studied beneficial mutation lets some adults keep digesting milk sugar, an example textbooks cite from human population genetics.
verify_reason: Lactase persistence is a real textbook beneficial mutation example.

en: A mutation that lets a bacterium survive an antibiotic is beneficial for that microbe but harmful for a sick person, so effect depends on whose survival you mean.
verify_reason: Beneficial for bacterium, harmful for patient; context matters.

en: Harmful mutations can change a protein's shape so a cell process fails, which secondary biology pages use as the usual disease example without naming a scare list.
verify_reason: Harmful mutations can alter protein shape and disrupt cell processes.

en: A rare mutation in a human immune receptor can reduce HIV infection risk, a beneficial example sources discuss, not a reason to seek infection.
verify_reason: CCR5 mutation can reduce HIV infection risk; factual.

en: A mutation that blocks chlorophyll is harmful for a green plant because it can no longer harvest sunlight well, a plant example of a damaging change.
verify_reason: Chlorophyll loss harms photosynthesis, so plant is damaged.

en: A color mutation may hide a moth on dark bark but expose it on pale bark, showing that beneficial versus harmful depends on the environment.
verify_reason: Moth color advantage depends on bark background.

en: If a DNA letter changes but the same amino acid is still coded, sources often call the mutation silent or neutral for the protein.
verify_reason: Same amino acid means protein often unchanged.

topic: not always in the body you feel
en: A mutation in one skin cell is not the same as a mutation in an egg or sperm; sources separate those when they discuss effects on offspring.
verify_reason: Somatic versus germline mutations affect offspring differently.

en: Harmful mutations that disable the brakes on cell division can contribute to cancer, a serious effect sources describe without saying every mutation causes it.
verify_reason: Mutations disabling cell-division brakes can lead to cancer.

en: Mutations that switch a needed gene off are often harmful, which is why sources treat many knock-out changes as damaging unless the gene was unused.
verify_reason: Needed gene loss is often harmful; unused gene may be neutral.

en: A mutation that gives a new activity can be beneficial, harmful, or both, so secondary sources refuse a single label without naming the trait.
verify_reason: New activity can help, harm, or both depending on trait.

en: RNA viruses mutate quickly; some changes help the virus spread and are harmful to hosts, an example of benefit and harm at two levels.
verify_reason: RNA viruses mutate fast; spread helps virus, harms host.

en: Some fruit mutations that stop seeds can be useful to farmers and eaters even if they would be harmful for the plant in the wild.
verify_reason: Seedless fruits help people but hurt wild plant reproduction.

en: If one website calls every mutation dangerous, check a textbook: the three-way split into help, harm, and no effect is the consensus view.
verify_reason: Textbooks agree mutations can help, harm, or do nothing.

en: Population-genetics sources say many neutral mutations spread by chance, not because they help, which is why 'no effect' still matters in evolution.
verify_reason: Neutral mutations can spread by chance in evolution.

topic: sickle cell already known skip restating
en: Do not stop at one famous blood example; sources also list plant, microbe, and silent DNA cases when they explain the three effect types.
verify_reason: Sources give plant, microbe, and silent DNA examples too.

en: Ultraviolet light can damage DNA and raise mutation rate; whether each change helps, hurts, or does nothing is a separate later question.
verify_reason: UV damages DNA; effects of each change vary.

en: Cells proofread DNA copies, so many mistakes never become mutations; sources mention this when they explain why not every copying error is harmful.
verify_reason: Proofreading catches many DNA copying mistakes before mutation.

en: Lab sources show bacteria gaining a mutation that lets them eat a new sugar, a beneficial change for those cells in that dish.
verify_reason: Bacteria can gain beneficial mutations for new food.

en: A harmful mutation can hide if one good copy of the gene still works, so sources warn that 'no effect now' is not always 'never harmful'.
verify_reason: A working gene copy can mask a harmful recessive mutation.

en: Much DNA does not code for protein; many letter changes there are scored neutral unless a control switch was hit, a distinction textbooks make.
verify_reason: Noncoding DNA changes are often neutral unless regulatory regions affected.

en: Whole-genome duplications in plants can be beneficial by making bigger fruits or new species, a large mutation sources treat as sometimes helpful.
verify_reason: Polyploidy can enlarge organs and create new plant species.

en: Class facts may name disease as a harmful effect, but they should not tell anyone they are ill; that judgment belongs to a clinician and a sourced test.
verify_reason: Correct; medical diagnosis needs clinicians and tests.

en: Neutral does not mean 'nothing happened in the DNA'; it means the change did not clearly help or hurt the organism's function or survival.
verify_reason: Neutral means no clear help/hurt, not no DNA change.

en: Human-gene databases list many harmful variants, so they can bias a report unless you also sample sources that discuss neutral and beneficial cases.
verify_reason: Databases overrepresent harmful variants; need balanced sources.

en: Plant breeders sometimes keep beneficial mutations for yield or disease resistance, then write those examples in agricultural science sources.
verify_reason: Breeders do select beneficial mutations for crops.

en: Sources note that many harmful mutations in early embryos never become a born organism, so the surviving population is already filtered.
verify_reason: Many harmful embryo mutations are lost before birth.

en: A class chart with beneficial, harmful, and neutral columns, each with a cited example, matches the competency better than a single scary story.
verify_reason: Chart with cited examples is appropriate for learning.

en: Some inherited color-vision changes are treated as harmful for certain tasks and nearly neutral for others, a reminder to name the job when labeling an effect.
verify_reason: Color-vision effects depend on task; context matters.

en: Changes in already-broken genes are often scored neutral because those sequences were not making a needed protein anyway.
verify_reason: Broken genes often don't affect function, so neutral.

en: Beneficial means better survival or reproduction in a stated setting, not 'good' in a moral sense, a wording secondary biology sources keep careful.
verify_reason: Beneficial means survival/reproduction, not moral good.

en: Oxygen sits in group 16 of the periodic table, so it has six valence electrons, the ones in its outer shell.
verify_reason: Correct; group 16 means six valence electrons.

en: To find oxygen's valence electrons, find oxygen on the table and read its main-group number: group 16 means six outer electrons.
verify_reason: Correct; main-group number gives outer electron count.

en: On older tables oxygen is in group VIA; the Roman six is the same count: oxygen has six valence electrons.
verify_reason: Correct; older group VIA also means six.

en: For groups 13 to 18, subtract ten from the group number: oxygen is group 16, and 16 minus 10 is six valence electrons.
verify_reason: Correct for groups 13 to 18.

en: Oxygen is in period 2, so its valence shell is the second shell, which holds those six outer electrons.
verify_reason: Correct; period 2 means second shell is valence shell.

en: Oxygen's atomic number is eight: two electrons fill the inner shell, leaving six as valence electrons in the outer shell.
verify_reason: Correct; oxygen has 2 inner and 6 outer electrons.

en: A simple shell pattern for oxygen is two, then six; the six is the valence count you also get from its column on the table.
verify_reason: Correct; shell pattern 2,6 matches group count.

en: Six valence electrons means oxygen is two short of a full set of eight, which is why it often forms two bonds.
verify_reason: Correct; oxygen often forms two bonds.

en: Sulfur sits under oxygen in the same group, so sulfur also has six valence electrons; the column, not the row, gives that number.
verify_reason: Correct; same group gives sulfur six valence electrons.

en: Do not give oxygen eight valence electrons; eight belongs to neon in group 18, two columns to the right of oxygen.
verify_reason: Correct; neon has eight valence electrons.

en: Fluorine sits one column right of oxygen, so fluorine has seven valence electrons, while oxygen in group 16 has six.
verify_reason: Correct; fluorine has seven valence electrons.

en: Nitrogen sits one column left of oxygen, so nitrogen has five valence electrons; stepping right to oxygen adds one, making six.
verify_reason: Correct; nitrogen has five valence electrons.

en: Carbon in group 14 has four valence electrons; oxygen is two groups farther right, so oxygen has six.
verify_reason: Correct group-to-valence comparison.

en: Oxygen heads the chalcogen family, group 16, whose members share six valence electrons even though their atoms get heavier down the column.
verify_reason: Group 16 elements have six valence electrons.

en: You do not have to list all eight electrons every time: oxygen's box on the table already tells you the outer count is six.
verify_reason: Group number gives oxygen's six outer electrons.

en: Oxygen is in the p-block with four p electrons plus two s electrons in the outer shell, totaling six valence electrons.
verify_reason: Oxygen has 2s2 2p4, totaling six valence electrons.

en: Valence electrons are the outer-shell electrons that do the bonding; for oxygen those outer electrons number six, from group 16.
verify_reason: Valence electrons are outer-shell bonding electrons.

en: Oxygen's two inner electrons are not valence electrons; only the six in the outer shell, shown by its group, count as valence.
verify_reason: Only outer-shell electrons count as valence.

en: When oxygen gains two electrons to fill its valence shell, it becomes O-two-minus, because six plus two makes eight.
verify_reason: Oxygen gains two electrons to form O2-.

en: In a water molecule oxygen makes two bonds, matching a need for two more electrons to finish a set of eight around six valence electrons.
verify_reason: Oxygen needs two electrons, so forms two bonds.

en: On the table, find the symbol O, then look at the top of that column: the group label is how you name oxygen's six valence electrons.
verify_reason: Group 16 label indicates six valence electrons.

topic: do not use period as valence
en: Oxygen's period number is 2, which is not its valence count; the period is the shell, and the group gives the six valence electrons.
verify_reason: Period gives shell, group gives valence count.

en: Selenium, farther down oxygen's column, still has six valence electrons; changing period does not change that group-16 outer count.
verify_reason: Same group means same valence electron count.

en: Tellurium is another group-16 element under oxygen, so it too has six valence electrons even though the atom is much heavier.
verify_reason: Group 16 elements share six valence electrons.

en: Oxygen is not a noble gas, so its outer shell is not full; six valence electrons leave two empty places in an octet.
verify_reason: Oxygen has six valence electrons and needs two for an octet.

en: A full outer shell for oxygen would be eight electrons; starting from six valence electrons, oxygen is two away from that octet.
verify_reason: Oxygen has six valence electrons, two short of eight.

en: Do not confuse group 16 with the transition metals of group 6; oxygen is a main-group nonmetal with six valence electrons.
verify_reason: Group 16 is main-group nonmetals, not group 6 transition metals.

en: Oxygen's box is on the right side of the table, in the p-block, where group 16 elements show six valence electrons.
verify_reason: Oxygen is in p-block group 16 with six valence electrons.

en: Helium in group 18 has a full first shell of two, but oxygen's valence shell is the second shell with six electrons, not two.
verify_reason: Helium has two valence electrons; oxygen has six in second shell.

en: In an oxygen molecule each atom still has six valence electrons; they share pairs so both can look like they have eight.
verify_reason: Each oxygen contributes six valence electrons and shares to reach eight.

en: A double bond in O-two uses four shared electrons, which fits two oxygen atoms that each started with six valence electrons.
verify_reason: O2 double bond shares four electrons total.

en: If a classmate says oxygen has eight valence electrons, check the group header: eight would be group 18, not oxygen's group 16.
verify_reason: Group 18 has eight valence electrons, group 16 has six.

en: The number you write for oxygen's valence electrons is six, not eight; eight is the atomic number, which counts all electrons.
verify_reason: Oxygen has six valence electrons; atomic number eight counts all electrons.

en: When you draw oxygen, count the dots: if you drew eight dots you used neon's group, not oxygen's six valence electrons.
verify_reason: Oxygen dot structure has six dots, neon has eight.

en: Nitrogen, oxygen, and fluorine share period 2 but not the same valence count: five, six, and seven as you move right.
verify_reason: Nitrogen, oxygen, fluorine have five, six, seven valence electrons.

en: Left-side metals often have one, two, or three valence electrons; oxygen on the right is a nonmetal with six.
verify_reason: Main-group metals have 1–3; oxygen group 16 has six.

en: Some textbooks title group 16 the oxygen family; that heading is a reminder that oxygen's valence electron number is six.
verify_reason: Group 16 is oxygen family; six valence electrons.

en: Use a printed periodic table, find O, read the group, then write 'oxygen has six valence electrons' as the answer the competency asks.
verify_reason: Periodic table group 16 gives oxygen six valence electrons.

en: The outer configuration 2s-two 2p-four adds to six electrons, matching oxygen's group-16 place on the periodic table.
verify_reason: 2s2 2p4 totals six valence electrons.

en: Knowing oxygen has six valence electrons from the table helps you predict it often needs two more electrons in compounds.
verify_reason: Oxygen needs two electrons to complete octet.

topic: do not count protons as valence
en: Oxygen has eight protons, but protons are not valence electrons; the table's group, not the proton count, gives the six outer electrons.
verify_reason: Protons aren't valence electrons; group gives six.

en: Oxygen-16 has mass number 16, which is not the valence count; mass number is protons plus neutrons, while group 16 gives six valence electrons.
verify_reason: Mass number 16 is protons plus neutrons, not valence.

en: Oxygen-16 and oxygen-18 have the same six valence electrons, because isotopes share the group and the electron count, not the neutron count.
verify_reason: Isotopes differ in neutrons, not valence electrons.

en: A classroom check is 'sixteen means six' for oxygen: group 16, six valence electrons, after you subtract ten from the IUPAC group number.
verify_reason: Group 16 minus ten gives six valence electrons.

en: The nearest noble gas after oxygen is neon, with eight valence electrons; oxygen has not reached that shell, so it has six, not eight.
verify_reason: Neon has eight valence electrons; oxygen has six.

en: Hydrogen is not in oxygen's group, so you cannot copy hydrogen's one valence electron onto oxygen; oxygen's own column says six.
verify_reason: Hydrogen's group differs; oxygen's group gives six.

en: Silicon under carbon has four valence electrons; the analog for oxygen's six is sulfur under oxygen, not silicon.
verify_reason: Silicon is below carbon; sulfur is below oxygen.

en: The period-2 sequence boron, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen has three, four, five, then six valence electrons, matching their group numbers minus ten.
verify_reason: Valence counts and group-number pattern are correct.

en: Whether oxygen is a single atom in a problem or O-two gas, its place on the table still says six valence electrons per oxygen atom.
verify_reason: Each oxygen atom still has six valence electrons.

topic: do not use group 8 old iron
en: Some old tables numbered iron in group VIII; that is not oxygen's column and must not be used to guess oxygen's six valence electrons.
verify_reason: Old group VIII was iron's column, not oxygen's.

en: Place six electron dots around O, usually as two pairs and two singles, matching six valence electrons from group 16.
verify_reason: Oxygen Lewis dot shows six electrons correctly.

en: Oxygen's six valence electrons are often drawn as two lone pairs plus two unpaired electrons, the unpaired ones ready to form bonds.
verify_reason: Two lone pairs and two unpaired electrons is correct.

en: The bent shape of water comes from oxygen keeping two lone pairs from those six valence electrons while making two bonds to hydrogen.
verify_reason: Two lone pairs on oxygen explain water's bent shape.

en: In carbon dioxide, oxygen atoms still start with six valence electrons each; they share with carbon so each oxygen is surrounded by eight.
verify_reason: Each oxygen shares to reach eight electrons.

en: The competency asks you to identify a number: based on oxygen's periodic-table position, that number of valence electrons is six.
verify_reason: Oxygen has six valence electrons.

en: A complete answer can say: oxygen is group 16, main-group valence is six, so oxygen has six valence electrons.
verify_reason: Group 16 gives six valence electrons.

en: Even polonium, near the bottom of group 16, is still counted as having six valence electrons from that same column as oxygen.
verify_reason: Group 16 elements have six valence electrons.

en: Superheavy group-16 elements are not classroom samples, but they sit in oxygen's column, the column that means six valence electrons.
verify_reason: Group 16 has six valence electrons; superheavy members are not classroom samples.

topic: color of box does not matter
en: Whether a table colors oxygen as a nonmetal or a gas, the valence count still comes from the group, which is six.
verify_reason: Color coding doesn't affect group valence count.

en: Oxygen gas at room temperature does not change the valence number; a gas, liquid, or solid of the element still has six valence electrons per atom.
verify_reason: State of matter doesn't change valence electrons per atom.

en: A common oxidation number of minus two for oxygen matches gaining two electrons to finish an octet that started with six valence electrons.
verify_reason: Oxygen commonly gains two electrons, matching -2 oxidation state.

topic: plus two is not typical oxygen
en: Oxygen almost never has a plus-six valence story like some sulfur compounds; the table still says six outer electrons, usually used to gain two.
verify_reason: Oxygen rarely has positive oxidation states; six outer electrons usually gain two.

en: Scan the p-block until you see the column that starts with oxygen at the top: that whole column is six valence electrons.
verify_reason: Group 16 column starts with oxygen; all have six valence electrons.

en: Oxygen is the lightest element in its group, but being first does not change the valence count; the group still means six.
verify_reason: Being lightest doesn't change group valence count.

en: Magnesium in group 2 has two valence electrons; oxygen in group 16 has six, so MgO can form when two and six make a full transfer picture.
verify_reason: Mg loses two, O gains two; MgO forms.

en: Sodium has one valence electron from group 1; it does not match oxygen, which has six from group 16.
verify_reason: Sodium has one valence electron; oxygen has six.

en: Aluminum has three valence electrons from group 13; two aluminum atoms can pair with three oxygen atoms that each have six valence electrons.
verify_reason: Two Al atoms and three O atoms balance charges in Al2O3.

topic: do not read atomic mass as six
en: Oxygen's atomic mass is about 16, which is not the valence number; ignore the mass in the box when the question asks for valence electrons.
verify_reason: Atomic mass about 16 isn't valence count; ignore it.

en: An element box shows atomic number, symbol, and mass; none of those is the valence count except as a clue that eight electrons include six outer ones.
verify_reason: Atomic number 8 clues two inner and six outer electrons.

en: Atomic number 8 tells you there are eight electrons in a neutral oxygen atom; the table's group then splits them as two inner and six valence.
verify_reason: Correct.

en: Even when you later talk about oxide ions, you still start from the table: oxygen atoms begin with six valence electrons.
verify_reason: Correct.

en: A worksheet can use three steps: locate O, read group 16, report six valence electrons, which is exactly the skill this competency names.
verify_reason: Correct.

en: Check a neighbor element: if your table reading gives fluorine seven and nitrogen five, then oxygen between them must be six.
verify_reason: Correct.

topic: no need to memorize a rhyme only
en: A rhyme can help, but the reliable method is the table position: oxygen's group is the reason the valence number is six.
verify_reason: Correct.

topic: gases on the right still six
en: Many colored tables mark oxygen as a gas on the right; that color codes physical state, while the group still codes six valence electrons.
verify_reason: Correct.

en: If you draw two rings around an oxygen nucleus, put two electrons on the inner ring and six on the outer ring to match group 16.
verify_reason: Correct.

en: On a shell drawing the outer ring is the valence shell; for oxygen that outer ring should show six electrons, not eight.
verify_reason: Correct.

en: The competency says 'based on its position' because the periodic table is the tool: you read six from oxygen's group, not from a random memory.
verify_reason: Correct.

en: Classroom wall charts often print 16 above oxygen's column; that printed 16 is your cue to write six valence electrons for oxygen.
verify_reason: Correct.

en: Students sometimes copy carbon's four valence electrons onto every period-2 element; oxygen is not carbon, and its group gives six.
verify_reason: Correct.

en: Another common error is giving every right-side element eight electrons; neon has eight, oxygen two boxes left has six.
verify_reason: Correct.

en: Phosphorus in group 15 has five valence electrons; it is next to sulfur, not a model for oxygen, which sits above sulfur with six.
verify_reason: Correct; phosphorus and oxygen valence counts match periodic table.

en: Chlorine in group 17 has seven valence electrons; oxygen is not a halogen, so do not give it seven, give it six.
verify_reason: Correct; chlorine has seven, oxygen six valence electrons.

en: In one sentence: oxygen is in group 16, so a neutral oxygen atom has six valence electrons according to the periodic table.
verify_reason: Correct; group 16 gives oxygen six valence electrons.

en: Later bonding lessons use this number: six valence electrons is why oxygen so often makes two bonds or becomes a two-minus ion.
verify_reason: Correct; six valence electrons explains oxygen's two bonds.

en: A trustworthy source for this fact is the periodic table itself: oxygen's position in group 16 identifies six valence electrons.
verify_reason: Correct; periodic table group shows valence electrons.

en: Modern plate motion is measured with GNSS networks that record a station's position over years, then convert the tiny shifts into a velocity.
verify_reason: Correct; GNSS positions over years yield velocities.

en: Scientists compare continuous GNSS stations that run every day with campaign surveys that reoccupy a mark for a few days each year.
verify_reason: Correct; continuous and campaign GNSS methods are compared.

en: Very-long-baseline interferometry times radio signals from distant quasars at far-apart dishes to detect how those dishes, and their plates, have moved.
verify_reason: Correct; VLBI uses quasar signal timing to detect motion.

en: Satellite laser ranging times a laser pulse to a reflector satellite and back, a space-geodesy process that helps track plate-scale displacements.
verify_reason: Correct; SLR measures plate-scale displacement.

en: Where plates meet under the ocean, scientists use seafloor geodesy such as acoustic ranging to benchmarks on the bottom, not only land GPS.
verify_reason: Correct; seafloor geodesy uses acoustic benchmarks.

en: PHIVOLCS and partner networks run GNSS stations across the Philippines to detect how fast local crust is displacing along faults and trenches.
verify_reason: Correct; PHIVOLCS runs GNSS for crustal deformation.

en: NAMRIA maintains geodetic control marks whose repeated GNSS occupations help measure national-scale displacement of the islands.
verify_reason: Correct; NAMRIA control marks support displacement measurements.

en: A single GPS reading is not a plate velocity; scientists need a time series long enough that seasonal wiggles do not hide the slow displacement.
verify_reason: Single readings cannot isolate slow plate motion.

en: Displacement is reported in a global reference frame so a station's motion is compared with a stable model of Earth's rotation and the other plates.
verify_reason: Global reference frame enables consistent plate comparisons.

en: With many stations, scientists compute strain, how a region stretches or shortens, a process that goes beyond one point's displacement.
verify_reason: Strain uses many stations to show regional deformation.

en: Older bathymetry compared with new multibeam maps, tied to GPS, can show how a seafloor feature has been displaced over decades.
verify_reason: Repeat bathymetry with GPS can reveal seafloor displacement.

en: Engineers install corner reflectors so InSAR can measure a known point's displacement even in a vegetated Philippine landscape.
verify_reason: Corner reflectors provide stable InSAR targets in vegetation.

en: Modern papers combine GNSS point velocities with InSAR maps so both the exact station motion and the spatial pattern of displacement are measured.
verify_reason: Combining GNSS and InSAR gives point and spatial motion.

en: A seismograph records shaking in seconds; it is not the process used to measure the slow centimeter-per-year displacement of a whole plate.
verify_reason: Seismographs record shaking, not slow plate motion.

en: A campaign GPS survey returns to the same benchmark years later; the difference in coordinates is the measured displacement of that mark.
verify_reason: Reoccupying benchmarks measures coordinate change over years.

en: Published plate velocities include uncertainty; a modern process reports both the displacement rate and how large the measurement error is.
verify_reason: Velocity estimates include measurement uncertainty.

en: The competency asks you to name processes such as GNSS, InSAR, VLBI, or seafloor acoustics, not only to say that plates move slowly.
verify_reason: Competency requires naming geodetic techniques, not just motion.

en: To predict the archipelago in 50 million years, first measure today's plate velocity from GNSS, then assume it stays roughly similar unless models say otherwise.
verify_reason: Measure current velocity, then project with models.

en: A first sketch multiplies current speed by 50 million years, converting centimeters per year into kilometers of future displacement.
verify_reason: Multiplying rate by time gives future displacement.

en: Use a published plate-motion model, not a freehand guess, so the Philippine Sea plate and neighboring plates have consistent velocities.
verify_reason: Published models give consistent plate velocities.

en: The archipelago's future shape depends on more than one plate, so the method is to apply each nearby plate's velocity, not only one number.
verify_reason: Multiple plates affect the Philippines' future shape.

en: Where crust dives into a trench it can be removed, so a fair prediction notes that some seafloor may disappear instead of simply sliding sideways.
verify_reason: Subduction recycles crust at trenches.

en: State the uncertainty: plate speed and direction can change over millions of years, so the 50-million-year sketch is a model, not a promise.
verify_reason: Plate motion changes; model is not certain.

en: Some methods step the map forward in smaller intervals, redrawing trenches as they move, instead of one giant jump of 50 million years.
verify_reason: Stepping redraws moving trenches more accurately.

en: Treat island groups as blocks that can rotate as well as slide, because a velocity at Manila may not equal a velocity at Davao.
verify_reason: Island blocks can rotate and slide differently.

en: Unless a cited model states a distance, write 'about the same direction at today's rate' rather than inventing a kilometer figure for 50 million years.
verify_reason: Avoid made-up distances; state rate-based direction.

en: Check published reconstructions of the last 50 million years; if the method worked backward, using it forward is at least consistent with that tool.
verify_reason: Past reconstructions check forward-model consistency.

en: Classroom methods can use a plate-velocity calculator: enter today's vector, choose 50 million years, and plot the predicted point.
verify_reason: Calculator plots constant-rate prediction.

en: Predict both position and shape: blocks may spread or squeeze, so the outline of the archipelago can change even if the center only translates.
verify_reason: Shape and position both change.

en: Include the Philippine Trench as a boundary that can consume seafloor, a method step so the future map is not just the islands sliding as a rigid sticker.
verify_reason: Philippine Trench consumes seafloor, not rigid sliding.

en: Use different velocities for the Palawan side and the Pacific-trench side if GNSS shows they are not one rigid block.
verify_reason: GNSS can show different block motions; using separate velocities is correct.

en: Write a map key that lists assumptions: constant velocity, rigid blocks or not, and which plate model you used for the 50-million-year sketch.
verify_reason: Listing assumptions and plate model is good scientific practice.

en: Convert units carefully: about two centimeters per year times 50 million years is about 1,000 kilometers if that rate truly stayed constant.
verify_reason: 2 cm/yr × 50 Myr = 1,000 km.

en: Coastlines will erode and grow, so the method predicts tectonic position of crustal blocks, not the exact beach outline of today's map.
verify_reason: Coastlines change; crustal block positions are what is predicted.

en: Compare your sketch with a published Cenozoic reconstruction; large disagreement means a method step, such as the chosen velocity, needs checking.
verify_reason: Comparing with published reconstructions checks method errors.

en: Advanced methods rotate a plate about an Euler pole instead of sliding it in a straight line, a better geometric prediction for 50 million years.
verify_reason: Euler pole rotation is more accurate on a sphere.

en: If a nearby ridge makes new seafloor, the method should add area on that side rather than only moving today's pieces like furniture.
verify_reason: Seafloor spreading adds area; must include new crust.

en: If blocks collide, the prediction of shape should allow shortening and mountains, not just a translated copy of today's archipelago.
verify_reason: Collisions shorten crust and build mountains.

en: A method demo uses foam blocks on paper arrows: move each block 50 scaled steps and photograph the new arrangement as the predicted map.
verify_reason: Foam-block demo is a valid classroom model.

en: Always write 'in 50 million years' on the sketch so no one reads it as next century; the method is geologic, not a weather forecast.
verify_reason: Labeling time span prevents misinterpretation.

en: The 'current velocity' in the competency is the GNSS-measured rate, so the method starts with those published millimeters-to-centimeters per year.
verify_reason: GNSS gives current plate velocity in mm/cm per year.

en: Look up the Philippine Sea plate's published motion relative to the Sunda block, then apply that vector when predicting eastern Philippine positions.
verify_reason: Philippine Sea plate motion informs eastern side prediction.

en: The fingernail-speed metaphor is not a prediction method; replace it with a measured rate, a time span, and a drawn displacement.
verify_reason: Accurate method guidance for plate-motion prediction.

en: Draw an uncertainty band around the predicted islands, because errors in today's velocity grow when they are multiplied by 50 million years.
verify_reason: Velocity errors scale with time, so uncertainty grows.

en: Ask whether the trench itself will roll back or advance; that method step changes the future space available for the archipelago's shape.
verify_reason: Trench rollback or advance affects future plate space.

en: Label the product a scenario under stated assumptions, the scientific way to predict 50 million years without claiming a single certain map.
verify_reason: Scenario framing correctly avoids false certainty.

en: Put a scale bar on the predicted map so a reader can see how many kilometers the method moved the blocks, not only a pretty new outline.
verify_reason: Scale bars show real displacement distances.

en: One student gathers GNSS rates, one converts units, one draws arrows, and one writes uncertainties, a division of labor that matches the method.
verify_reason: Roles match the prediction method steps.

en: The competency is about position and shape of the crust, so the method should not wander into guessing 50-million-year rainfall or cities.
verify_reason: Correctly limits scope to crustal position and shape.

en: State that treating the Philippines as one rigid plate is an approximation; GNSS already shows internal deformation that a careful method includes.
verify_reason: Philippines has internal deformation; approximation is accurate.

en: Finish the prediction with because: the islands should sit farther along today's vectors because we multiplied measured velocity by geologic time.
verify_reason: Reasoning correctly links velocity, time, and displacement.

en: In one sentence: measure present plate velocity, multiply by 50 million years, draw the new block positions, and say which assumptions could be wrong.
verify_reason: Accurate one-sentence summary of the method.

en: Use dynamics carts on a track as a model: one cart hits another, then you measure speeds before and after to classify the collision.
verify_reason: Correct collision model for classifying by speed.

en: In a nearly elastic model, the carts bounce apart and the total kinetic energy stays almost the same, which you check with a calculator.
verify_reason: Nearly elastic collisions conserve kinetic energy approximately.

en: Press clay on the bumpers so the carts stick; that inelastic model shows kinetic energy dropping while momentum is still shared.
verify_reason: Inelastic sticking collision loses kinetic energy; momentum is conserved.

en: With two equal masses in a nearly elastic hit, the moving cart can almost stop while the other takes its speed, a model result to measure, not assume.
verify_reason: Equal-mass elastic collision can transfer speed nearly completely.

en: During the hit, each cart pushes the other with equal-and-opposite forces for the same short time, a Newton's-third description of the model.
verify_reason: Newton's third law gives equal opposite forces during contact.

en: In inelastic models the lasting effect is deformation or heat; look for a dent in clay or a warmer bumper after the carts join.
verify_reason: Inelastic collisions can leave deformation or heat.

en: Photogates or motion sensors give cleaner before-and-after speeds than a stopwatch, a measurement method that makes the model quantitative.
verify_reason: Photogates and motion sensors measure speeds more accurately.

en: A low-cost model is marbles in a ruler groove: vary mass by taping marbles together and describe bounce versus stick after each run.
verify_reason: Marbles in a groove model collisions cheaply.

en: Call a run elastic in the lab if the carts rebound and kinetic energy is nearly conserved, an operational definition you can apply to the model.
verify_reason: Elastic means rebound with nearly conserved kinetic energy.

en: Call a run inelastic if the objects deform or stay together and kinetic energy clearly falls, even if they do not perfectly glue.
verify_reason: Inelastic means deformation or sticking with kinetic energy loss.

en: Change only the bumper type or only the mass, keeping the release height the same, so the model test of collision type stays fair.
verify_reason: Changing one variable keeps the collision test fair.

en: Sketch force arrows only while the bumpers touch; before and after, those contact forces are gone, an effect of the short interaction.
verify_reason: Contact forces exist only while bumpers touch.

en: If the model carts latch and move as one mass, you have a perfectly inelastic case whose shared speed you can predict from momentum conservation.
verify_reason: Latched carts move together; momentum conservation predicts speed.

en: Drop a superball and a clay ball on the same tile as a qualitative model: one returns most kinetic energy, the other does not.
verify_reason: Superball bounces elastically; clay mostly doesn't.

topic: do not use people as models
en: Investigate with carts and marbles, not by crashing bikes or bodies; the competency is about models of collisions, not dangerous tests.
verify_reason: Carts and marbles safely model collisions.
