en: After an inelastic hit, some kinetic energy has become sound and heat; a microphone or a warm bumper is evidence of that effect in the model.
verify_reason: Inelastic collisions convert kinetic energy to sound and heat.

en: On a flat table, glancing marble hits let you investigate 2-D collisions, then describe how the forces acted along the line of contact.
verify_reason: Glancing collisions show 2-D forces along contact line.

en: Run at least three trials per bumper type so one lucky bounce does not decide whether the model looks elastic or inelastic.
verify_reason: Three trials reduce chance effects.

en: A complete lab sentence names the forces during contact and the effects after: bounce, stick, speed change, dent, or heat.
verify_reason: Lab sentences include contact forces and effects.

en: Say that the cart track is a model of a crash, not a highway crash itself, so the forces you describe are the model's contact pushes.
verify_reason: Cart track models crash contact forces.

en: Change mass ratio on purpose: a heavy cart hitting a light one should send the light cart off faster in the elastic model, a prediction to test.
verify_reason: Heavy-to-light elastic hit speeds light cart.

en: Video-analysis software can plot velocity dots before and after, a digital model record of the collision you can export to a table.
verify_reason: Video analysis records velocity data digitally.

en: In one sentence: build a bounce model and a stick model, measure speeds, then describe the contact forces and whether kinetic energy was kept.
verify_reason: Summary includes models, speeds, forces, energy kept.

en: Changing momentum always needs a force that lasts for some time; a force of zero duration does not change how much motion an object carries.
verify_reason: Impulse requires force over time.

en: The same change in momentum can come from a large force in a short time or a smaller force in a longer time, because both are force times time.
verify_reason: Impulse equals force times time.

en: If you push a stationary cart forward for two seconds, you have applied force over time, so the cart's momentum increases in that direction.
verify_reason: Force over time delivers impulse, increasing forward momentum.

en: To take momentum away you still apply a force over a period of time, which is why brakes need a stretch of road, not an instant halt.
verify_reason: Braking force over time reduces momentum; cannot stop instantly.

en: The force that changes momentum must have a component in the direction you want the momentum to change, acting across that interval of time.
verify_reason: Force component along desired direction changes momentum over time.

en: If the net force on an object stays zero, its momentum does not change, no matter how long you wait, because no impulse is delivered.
source: encyclopedia-stable; Newton's first law and momentum
verify_reason: Zero net force means no impulse, so momentum stays constant.

en: To identify crash-protection devices, gather crash-test reports from agencies such as NHTSA or your local transport office, then name seatbelts, airbags, and crumple zones.
verify_reason: NHTSA and local reports document seatbelts, airbags, crumple zones.

en: WHO road-safety pages list seatbelts as a proven way to reduce injury in collisions, a secondary source you can cite beside a local law.
verify_reason: WHO lists seatbelts as proven injury reducers.

en: Secondary safety sources also name head restraints that limit neck snap in a rear collision, another way to reduce impact effects besides the three famous devices.
verify_reason: Head restraints limit whiplash in rear collisions.

en: Car-safety papers describe side-impact beams in doors that spread a T-bone crash force, a sourced device that protects occupants from the side.
verify_reason: Side-impact beams spread side crash forces.

en: A collapsible steering column is designed to shorten in a frontal crash so the wheel does less harm to the driver's chest, a device named in engineering sources.
verify_reason: Collapsible steering columns reduce driver chest injury.

en: Child seats and booster seats, described in LTO and pediatric safety pages, reduce collision impact on small bodies that adult belts do not fit well.
verify_reason: Child seats fit small bodies better than adult belts.

en: Some vehicle standards require softer, more crumple-friendly fronts so a collision with a pedestrian delivers less peak force, a source-backed design choice.
verify_reason: Pedestrian-friendly fronts reduce peak collision force.

en: Compare a manufacturer's safety brochure with an independent crash-test page; if they disagree, prefer the independent test for how well a device reduces impact.
verify_reason: Independent tests are less biased than manufacturer brochures.

en: Laminated windshields that stay in one sheet are cited as reducing ejection and cutting injuries, another sourced way collisions do less harm.
verify_reason: Laminated glass holds together, reducing ejection and cuts.

topic: write the year of the test
en: Copy the year of the crash-test protocol, because airbag and crumple-zone rules have changed, and an old source may describe a weaker design.
verify_reason: Protocol years track changing safety standards.

en: WHO also documents motorcycle helmets as impact reducers for riders, a sourced example outside cars that still fits reducing collision harm.
verify_reason: WHO documents helmets reduce rider injuries.

en: Transport agencies publish that a belt only reduces impact if it is worn; reminder chimes in source specs exist because unused belts cannot help.
verify_reason: Belts must be worn to reduce impact.

en: Crash-test sources warn that airbags are designed to work with a seatbelt, so gathering 'ways' should present them as a pair, not as rivals.
verify_reason: Airbags supplement seatbelts, not replace them.

en: Engineering sources define a crumple zone as a designed crush space in front or rear, not random damage, so the cabin decelerates over a longer time.
verify_reason: Crumple zones increase impact time, lowering force.

en: Independent rating pages grade how well structures manage a collision; citing a rating is gathering evidence, not just naming the three devices.
verify_reason: Ratings are evidence of crash structure performance.

en: Local transport pages may discuss seatbelts on buses or jeepneys; gather whether those rules exist, because reducing impact is not only for private cars.
verify_reason: Seatbelt rules can apply beyond private cars.

en: If a source does not state a percent reduction, do not invent one; name the device and the agency, which is enough for the competency.
verify_reason: Don't fabricate percentages; cite device and agency.

en: Interior padding on dashboards, listed in safety standards, is another sourced way to lengthen contact time and lower peak force in a crash.
verify_reason: Padding lengthens contact time, reducing peak force.

en: Scientists often write a word equation first, naming reactants and products in words, then replace those names with formulas in a second line.
verify_reason: True; word equations often precede formula equations.

en: In both word and formula equations the arrow means yields or becomes, a method scientists use so the story of the reaction has a direction.
verify_reason: Arrow means yields or produces; correct.

en: Scientists add (s), (l), (g), or (aq) after formulas to show solid, liquid, gas, or dissolved, a detail word equations sometimes skip.
verify_reason: State symbols correctly show phases; (aq) means dissolved.

en: After formulas are written, scientists add coefficients so each element count matches on both sides, a step that word equations cannot show clearly.
verify_reason: Balancing with coefficients is correct.

en: A plus sign between formulas means 'and,' not addition in arithmetic; it is the method for listing more than one reactant or product.
verify_reason: Plus sign means 'and,' not arithmetic addition.

en: A classroom pair is the word equation methane plus oxygen yields carbon dioxide plus water, then the matching balanced formula equation.
verify_reason: Methane combustion word and balanced formula are correct.

en: Scientists may write a triangle or the word heat over the arrow to show that heating was needed, a method symbol used on formula equations.
verify_reason: Triangle over arrow indicates heat; correct.

en: A method for checking a formula equation is to tally each element on the left and right before you claim the reaction is correctly written.
verify_reason: Tallying atoms checks balance; correct.

en: Scientists describe reactions with equations: first in words, then in formulas with an arrow, plus signs, and coefficients that keep atoms counted.
verify_reason: Accurate description of chemical equations.

en: Green plants are called producers because they make their own food using sunlight, water, and air.
verify_reason: Correct: plants use sunlight, water, air.

en: A carnivore is an animal that eats only other animals, like the Philippine eagle hunting snakes and small birds.
verify_reason: Correct definition and example.

en: Most food chains have only about three or four steps because a lot of energy is lost at each step.
verify_reason: Energy loss limits chain length.

en: The first animal in a food chain, called a primary consumer, is always a herbivore because it eats the plant.
verify_reason: Primary consumers eat plants, so herbivores.

en: In a Philippine mangrove, leaves from bakawan trees are eaten by crabs, which are then eaten by herons.
verify_reason: Accurate mangrove food chain example.

en: Plants are food for herbivores, but they are also producers because they make their own food first.
verify_reason: Correct dual role of plants.

en: A food chain is really a path of energy, not just a list of who eats whom, because the energy from the Sun travels through it.
verify_reason: Correct: food chains transfer energy.

en: When a herbivore eats a plant, only about ten percent of the plant's energy becomes new animal body.
verify_reason: Ten percent rule is standard approximation.

en: In a drawn food chain, each animal is labeled with its name and whether it is a herbivore, carnivore, or omnivore.
verify_reason: Common labeling practice in food chain diagrams.

en: An omnivore can be a primary or secondary consumer in a food chain, depending on whether it eats the plant or the herbivore.
verify_reason: Omnivores eat plants and animals, so can occupy either level.

en: Scientists measure friction by pulling a wooden block with a spring scale, and the reading when the block just starts to move is the force of friction.
source: standard friction measurement procedure in school labs
verify_reason: Spring scale reading at start equals friction force.

en: To compare surfaces, a class tests the same block on sandpaper, carpet, wood, and tile, recording the spring scale reading for each one.
source: fair-test design with multiple surface conditions
verify_reason: Same block on different surfaces is a fair comparison.

en: Repeating the friction test several times on each surface and averaging the readings gives a more reliable result than a single trial.
source: experimental design: multiple trials improve reliability
verify_reason: Averaging repeated trials improves reliability.

en: A spring scale measures force in units called newtons, and a higher reading on a rough surface means that surface has more friction.
source: SI unit of force; spring scale calibration
verify_reason: Newtons measure force; rough surfaces show higher readings.

en: Before testing, a scientist writes a prediction about which surface will show the most friction, then checks the results against that prediction.
verify_reason: Predictions are checked against results.

en: The same person should push or pull the block each time, because different people may use different amounts of force and spoil the fair test.
verify_reason: Same person controls push/pull force variable.

en: A scientist records the distance the block slides on each surface using a meter stick, and a shorter slide means more friction stopped it sooner.
verify_reason: Shorter slide means friction stopped it sooner.

en: A data table for the friction experiment lists each surface in one column and the measured force or distance in the next column.
verify_reason: Data table lists surfaces and measurements.

en: A bar graph of the results shows each surface on the bottom and the friction reading on the side, so the tallest bar has the most friction.
source: bar graph for comparing categorical data
verify_reason: Tallest bar shows highest friction reading.

en: Keeping the starting point the same for every trial makes the test fair, because a different starting point would change the distance or speed.
verify_reason: Same starting point keeps distance measurement fair.

en: Scientists test one surface at a time and clean the block between trials so that dust or bits of the old surface do not change the result.
verify_reason: Cleaning prevents old surface debris affecting results.

en: To measure friction, scientists first find the force that starts the block moving, then the force that keeps it moving at a steady speed.
source: measurement of static and kinetic friction
verify_reason: Correctly distinguishes starting and steady-moving friction.

en: Scientists pull the block very slowly with the spring scale, because a fast pull gives a higher reading that is not the true friction.
source: measurement practice: slow pull for accurate friction
verify_reason: Slow steady pull avoids extra acceleration force.

en: To compare rough and smooth surfaces, a class can use sandpaper for rough and a glossy tile for smooth, keeping the block identical for both.
verify_reason: Sandpaper and glossy tile are suitable rough and smooth surfaces.

en: Scientists compare friction on wet and dry surfaces by testing the same block on each, because wet surfaces often have less friction than dry ones.
source: friction on wet vs dry surfaces
verify_reason: Wet surfaces often reduce friction; statement is generally accurate.

en: The ramp height must stay the same for every test, because a higher ramp gives the car more speed and would hide the effect of the surface.
verify_reason: Constant ramp height keeps speed from changing the results.

en: A good record of the experiment includes the date, the surfaces tested, the measurements, and a note about anything unusual that happened.
verify_reason: Good records include date, surfaces, measurements, and unusual events.

en: If the results show that the block moves farthest on sand, then sand has less friction than the other surfaces tested in the experiment.
verify_reason: Farther slide means less friction in that test.

en: A class can test friction with a rubber band: stretching the band to pull a block, and the longer the stretch, the bigger the friction force.
source: elastic band as simple force indicator
verify_reason: Rubber band stretch measures force; longer stretch means more force.

en: The conclusion of the experiment states which surface had the most friction and which had the least, using the recorded measurements as evidence.
source: scientific conclusion based on recorded data
verify_reason: Conclusion uses measurements to identify most and least friction.

en: A fair test of shape change keeps the pushing force the same and changes only the object being pressed, so the results really compare the objects.
source: fair-test design: one variable changed, the rest held constant
verify_reason: Keeping force same and changing only object is fair.

en: To measure how much a soft object squashes, place it on a flat table and use a ruler to record its height before and after pressing.
source: standard measurement practice with a ruler
verify_reason: Ruler before and after pressing correctly measures squash.

en: In a guided activity, learners first predict which objects will change shape, then test each one to check whether their prediction was right.
verify_reason: Predicting then testing is a valid guided activity.

en: A good record for a shape-change test is a table with columns for the object, its shape before, the force used, and its shape after.
verify_reason: Table records object, before/after shape, and force.

en: A spring scale lets a class apply the same measured force to different objects, so the shape-change test stays fair for every object.
source: spring scale use in force measurement
verify_reason: Spring scale measures equal force for fair testing.

en: To tell elastic from permanent change, press an object once, release it, and watch whether it springs back to its first shape.
verify_reason: Release and observe if shape springs back.

en: A hand lens helps learners see small dents or bends that appear on a soft object after a gentle push.
verify_reason: Hand lens magnifies small dents or bends.

en: Drawing a straight line on a soft object before bending it shows exactly where the shape changes when force is applied.
verify_reason: Line bends to reveal deformation location.

en: Before testing, learners sort objects into rigid and soft groups, then predict which group will change shape more easily.
source: classification as a first step in investigation
verify_reason: Sorting and predicting is a good test plan.

en: Drawing the object's outline before and after the push gives a clear picture of how its shape changed.
verify_reason: Outlines show shape change clearly.

en: Measuring a spring's length with a ruler when it is relaxed, stretched, and released shows whether it returns to its first length.
source: measurement with a ruler for elastic behavior
verify_reason: Ruler checks if spring returns to original length.

en: A bar chart of how much each object changed shape makes it easy to see which materials are soft and which are rigid.
verify_reason: Bar chart compares shape changes across materials.

topic: light and strong pushes on clay
en: To find how force affects shape, press the same clay ball with a light push and then a stronger push, measuring the height each time.
source: varying one variable while keeping the object the same
verify_reason: Controlled comparison of light and strong force on clay.

en: In a shape-change test, look at the object before pressing, press it once, then look again and describe any change you see.
verify_reason: Observing before and after pressing is correct.

en: Pushing a soft object with a stick instead of a hand lets learners see the shape change without their fingers blocking the view.
verify_reason: Stick allows clear view of deformation.

en: Testing a sponge and a stone with the same press shows that the sponge returns to its shape while the stone does not change at all.
source: comparative testing of elastic and rigid materials
verify_reason: Sponge is elastic; stone shows no visible change.

en: Continental crust is thicker but less dense than oceanic crust, so it floats higher on the mantle like a light block on water.
verify_reason: Continental crust is thicker, less dense, floats higher.

en: The mantle is about 2,900 kilometers thick, making it by far the thickest layer of the solid Earth.
verify_reason: Mantle is about 2,900 km thick, thickest layer.

en: The crust makes up less than one percent of Earth's total volume, like the thin skin of a huge fruit.
verify_reason: Crust is under one percent of Earth's volume.

en: A Croatian scientist named Andrija Mohorovičić discovered the Moho in 1909 by studying how earthquake waves travel.
verify_reason: Mohorovičić discovered Moho in 1909 via seismic waves.

en: Peridotite, the main rock of the upper mantle, is dark green and much denser than the granite and basalt of the crust.
verify_reason: Peridotite is dense, greenish upper-mantle rock.

en: In the upper crust, temperature rises about 25 to 30 degrees Celsius for every kilometer you dig deeper.
source: published geothermal gradient range in crustal rocks
verify_reason: Typical geothermal gradient is 25–30°C per km.

en: Earthquakes happen only in the rigid lithosphere, because the soft asthenosphere below cannot crack or break.
source: encyclopedia-stable; brittle vs ductile rock behavior
verify_reason: Earthquakes occur in brittle lithosphere, not ductile asthenosphere.

en: Mountain ranges have deep crustal roots, just like an iceberg has most of its mass hidden underwater.
verify_reason: Isostasy analogy with iceberg roots is accurate.

en: The lithosphere is broken into large plates that move in different directions, carrying continents and oceans with them.
verify_reason: Plates move and carry continents and ocean floor.

en: The Moho is shallower under the oceans and much deeper under tall mountain ranges, following the crust's thickness.
source: encyclopedia-stable; Moho depth variation by crust type
verify_reason: Moho depth follows crust thickness.

en: Continental crust is rich in silicon and aluminum, while the upper mantle holds more iron and magnesium, which is why it is denser.
source: encyclopedia-stable; elemental composition of crust vs mantle
verify_reason: Continental crust is Si/Al-rich; mantle is denser Fe/Mg-rich.

en: The asthenosphere is not fully liquid; it is solid rock with just a tiny bit of melted material between the crystals, which lets it flow.
source: encyclopedia-stable; partial melting in upper mantle
verify_reason: Mostly solid with slight melt, allowing flow.

en: As a population gets bigger, food and water become harder to find, so each new baby has less to live on.
source: ecological principle: resource limitation slows population growth
verify_reason: Limited resources slow population growth.

en: On a graph, this slowing growth makes an S-shaped curve that starts steep and then flattens out at the top.
source: standard logistic growth model in population ecology
verify_reason: S-shaped curve shows slowing then leveling growth.

en: If a population has unlimited food and no enemies, it can grow in a J-shaped curve, but that never lasts long in nature.
source: exponential vs logistic growth models in ecology
verify_reason: J-shaped growth is temporary in nature.

en: Storms, droughts, and fires can suddenly shrink a population even if it is not crowded at all.
source: density-independent limiting factors in population ecology
verify_reason: Weather and fire affect populations regardless of crowding.

en: A herd of deer on a small island grows fast at first, then slows down as the island's plants run out.
source: classic island population study example (e.g., deer on island)
verify_reason: Island resources limit deer population growth.

en: Bacteria in a closed dish multiply quickly, but soon their growth slows because the food in the dish is used up.
verify_reason: Closed dish food limits bacterial growth.

en: In a Philippine fish pond, the number of bangus that can grow depends on how much natural food the pond water makes.
source: aquaculture carrying capacity principle in Philippine fishponds
verify_reason: Pond food supply limits fish population.

en: When a population is below carrying capacity, births outnumber deaths; near it, births and deaths become almost equal.
source: population growth rate = births - deaths, standard ecology
verify_reason: Births and deaths balance near carrying capacity.

en: Carrying capacity is not a fixed number, because a good rainy season can raise it and a long drought can lower it.
source: carrying capacity varies with environmental conditions
verify_reason: Rainy and drought conditions change available resources.

en: Environmental resistance is the name for all the natural forces that stop a population from growing forever.
source: environmental resistance concept in population ecology
verify_reason: Natural limiting factors keep populations in check.

en: Carrying capacity is different for each species, so a field can hold thousands of grasshoppers but only a few eagles.
source: carrying capacity is specific to species and resource needs
verify_reason: Different species have different resource needs.

en: Pollution from factories can lower an ecosystem's carrying capacity by making the water and soil harmful to living things.
source: human pollution degrades habitat and reduces carrying capacity
verify_reason: Pollution harms water and soil, reducing supportable life.

en: Adding fertilizer to a rice field, or palay, can raise its carrying capacity so more rice plants can grow in the same space.
source: agricultural inputs increase carrying capacity for crops
verify_reason: Fertilizer adds nutrients, supporting more rice plants.

en: A watering hole in a dry area sets the carrying capacity for the animals that come to drink, because water is the limit.
source: water availability as a key limiting factor in dry ecosystems
verify_reason: Water scarcity limits animal numbers.

en: Animals need space to build nests and find food, so a limited territory naturally slows down how fast their numbers can grow.
source: space and territory as limiting factors in animal populations
verify_reason: Limited space and territory restrict population growth.

en: A forest can only support a certain number of birds because there are only so many nesting holes and seeds to go around.
source: habitat resources (nests, food) determine bird carrying capacity
verify_reason: Nesting holes and seeds limit bird numbers.

en: When sunlight hits the ground at a steep angle, it spreads over a smaller area and feels hotter than the same light hitting at a shallow angle.
source: encyclopedia-stable; solar intensity and incidence angle
verify_reason: Steep-angle sunlight is concentrated and heats more.

en: The poles receive sunlight at a very shallow angle, so the same amount of sunlight spreads over a huge area and warms the ground very little.
verify_reason: Shallow-angle sunlight spreads out, warming less.

en: In December, the Southern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun, so it is summer there while the Northern Hemisphere has winter.
verify_reason: Southern Hemisphere tilts toward Sun in December.

en: The Sun's direct rays never go beyond the tropics; they move between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn over a year.
verify_reason: Subsolar point stays between the tropics all year.

en: The Tropic of Cancer is the northernmost latitude where the Sun can be directly overhead, which happens around the June solstice.
verify_reason: Northernmost latitude for overhead Sun, near June solstice.

en: The length of daylight also changes with the tilt: summer days are longer and winter days are shorter, adding more hours of sunlight to warm the ground.
verify_reason: Tilt changes daylight length, affecting seasonal warming.

en: A common mistake is blaming seasons on Earth's distance from the Sun, but the real cause is the tilt that changes the angle of sunlight.
verify_reason: Seasons come from tilt, not distance.

en: The Sun's noon height in the sky changes through the year: it climbs higher in summer and sinks lower in winter because of the tilt.
verify_reason: Tilt changes the Sun's noon height seasonally.

en: The Philippines, being near the equator, gets strong sunlight all year, but the tilt still shifts the Sun's path and helps bring wet and dry seasons.
source: PAGASA; Philippine climate and solar path
verify_reason: Sun's shifting path influences Philippine wet and dry seasons.

en: When the Sun is high in the sky, its rays travel through less atmosphere, so more energy reaches the ground than when it is low.
verify_reason: High Sun passes through less atmosphere, delivering more energy.

en: The tilt makes the Northern and Southern Hemispheres have opposite seasons at the same time of year.
verify_reason: Tilt causes opposite seasons in each hemisphere.

en: The angle of sunlight is measured from the horizon: a high Sun means direct rays, and a low Sun means slanted rays that spread out.
verify_reason: High Sun is direct; low Sun spreads rays.

en: The Arctic Circle marks the latitude where the Sun can stay above or below the horizon for a full day at the solstices because of the tilt.
verify_reason: Arctic Circle has 24-hour light or dark at solstices.

en: Think of a flashlight shining straight down versus at a slant: the slanted beam covers more ground but each spot gets less light, just like sunlight on Earth.
verify_reason: Slanted beam spreads light over larger area.

en: The June and December solstices mark the times when one pole leans most toward the Sun and the other most away, giving the strongest seasonal contrast.
verify_reason: Solstices show maximum tilt toward and away from Sun.

en: The Tropic of Cancer passes north of the Philippines, while the equator lies south, so the Sun's direct rays cross the country twice a year.
source: encyclopedia-stable; Philippines latitude and solar declination
verify_reason: Philippines lies between equator and Tropic of Cancer; direct rays cross twice.

en: Both electric motors and generators have a coil of wire and a magnet, and the coil spins inside the magnetic field.
verify_reason: Both use coils and magnets with spinning coil in magnetic field.

en: Motors and generators both convert energy from one form to another, but neither creates or destroys energy.
source: encyclopedia-stable; law of conservation of energy
verify_reason: They convert energy; energy is conserved, not created or destroyed.

en: The electric motor in a ceiling fan uses electricity to spin the blades and cool the room.
verify_reason: Ceiling fan motor converts electricity to spinning motion.

en: Both motors and generators need a magnetic field, usually from a permanent magnet or an electromagnet, to work.
verify_reason: Motors and generators require magnetic fields from magnets or electromagnets.

en: In a motor, the coil turns because its own magnetic field pushes against the magnet's field, creating a spinning force.
source: encyclopedia-stable; interaction of magnetic fields in motor
verify_reason: Motor coil spins from interacting magnetic fields.

en: Both machines have a spinning part called a rotor and a fixed part called a stator that stay close together.
verify_reason: Rotor spins; stator stays fixed in motors and generators.

en: Electric jeepneys use motors to move, while the power plants that charge their batteries use generators, so both work together.
source: encyclopedia-stable; electric vehicles and charging infrastructure
verify_reason: Motors move jeepneys; power plant generators charge batteries.

en: A washing machine has a motor that spins the drum, and the electricity it uses comes from a generator somewhere else.
source: encyclopedia-stable; household appliance and power grid
verify_reason: Washing machine motor spins drum using electricity from generators.

en: Without magnetism, neither motors nor generators can work, because both depend on magnetic fields to function.
verify_reason: Both depend on magnetic fields to operate.

en: Power plants use huge generators that spin coils with steam, water, or wind to supply electricity to entire cities.
verify_reason: Large generators spun by steam, water, or wind supply cities.

en: Electric motors are everywhere: in fans, blenders, drills, and jeepneys, turning electricity into spinning motion.
verify_reason: Motors in appliances convert electricity into spinning motion.

en: In remote villages without power lines, small generators powered by diesel can supply electricity for lights and radios.
source: encyclopedia-stable; diesel generator use in off-grid areas
verify_reason: Diesel generators can supply electricity in off-grid areas.

en: Earthquake focuses are grouped by depth: shallow ones start about 70 kilometers down or less, while deep ones can start hundreds of kilometers underground.
verify_reason: Shallow foci are under 70 km; deep ones are hundreds.

en: Intensity describes how strongly people feel the shaking at a certain place, so it changes with distance from the epicenter and local soil.
verify_reason: Intensity varies with shaking, distance, and local soil.

en: In a reverse fault, rocks squeeze together and one block slides up over the other, which can push the seafloor upward during a quake.
verify_reason: Compression pushes one block up over the other.

en: In a normal fault, rocks pull apart and one block drops down, which can make the ground sink and sometimes change the shape of the land.
verify_reason: Tension makes one block drop down.

en: A tsunami has a very long wavelength, often hundreds of kilometers, so it acts like a moving wall of water rather than a single tall wave.
verify_reason: Tsunamis have very long wavelengths, like a water wall.

en: In a friction experiment, the surface is the independent variable that the scientist changes, and the friction force is the dependent variable that gets measured.
source: experimental design: independent and dependent variables
verify_reason: Surface is changed; friction force is measured.

en: The block, the pull speed, and the table stay the same in every trial so that only the surface changes and the test stays fair.
source: fair-test design: hold all variables constant except one
verify_reason: Keeping block, speed, and table same makes test fair.

en: Before measuring, the scientist checks that the spring scale reads zero when nothing pulls on it, so every measurement starts from the same point.
source: measurement practice: calibrate instrument before use
verify_reason: Zeroing ensures measurements start from same point.

en: The spring scale is held parallel to the table while pulling, because tilting it would add extra force and give a wrong friction reading.
source: measurement technique: keep force direction parallel to motion
verify_reason: Tilting adds extra force and distorts friction reading.

en: Testing at least three different surfaces, like sandpaper, carpet, and tile, gives enough data to compare friction fairly.
source: comparative experiment design: multiple conditions for meaningful comparison
verify_reason: Three surfaces give enough data for fair comparison.

en: A good hypothesis predicts which surface will have the most friction and gives a reason, such as roughness creating more rubbing.
source: scientific method: testable hypothesis with rationale
verify_reason: Predicting and giving a roughness reason is accurate.

en: Every friction reading is recorded with its unit, newtons, so the results are clear and can be compared correctly later.
source: measurement convention: SI unit for force is the newton
verify_reason: Recording units ensures clear, comparable results.

en: The same block is used for every surface because a heavier block would press down harder and increase the friction by itself.
source: fair-test design: normal force affects friction, so mass must stay constant
verify_reason: Heavier block increases friction; keeping block same is fair.

en: The average friction reading for each surface is compared, and the surface with the highest average has the most friction.
source: data analysis: compare means across conditions
verify_reason: Highest average friction reading shows most friction.

topic: one changing thing in fair test
en: A fair test has only one changing thing, the surface, so any difference in the friction reading must come from that surface.
source: fair-test principle: isolate the single variable being tested
verify_reason: Only surface changes, so differences come from surface.

en: Scientists check that the table is level with a small bubble level so the block does not slide on its own before pulling.
source: experimental setup: ensure no unintended motion from slope
verify_reason: Level table prevents unwanted sliding before pulling.

en: The scientist decides before starting how many trials to do on each surface, such as three, and does exactly that many.
source: experimental design: predetermined number of repetitions
verify_reason: Deciding trials ahead ensures consistent repeated testing.

en: Writing down the steps in order before starting helps the scientist follow the same method for every surface tested.
source: scientific method: written procedure ensures consistency
verify_reason: Ordered steps help repeat the same method.

en: The measurement is written down right after each pull, because waiting and writing from memory can make the data wrong.
source: data collection practice: record immediately to avoid error
verify_reason: Immediate recording avoids memory errors.

en: If the results do not match the prediction, the scientist still records them honestly and explains what might have caused the difference.
source: scientific integrity: report actual data even when unexpected
verify_reason: Honest recording and explaining differences is correct.

en: The same spring scale is used for all the measurements because different scales may be calibrated differently and give different readings.
source: measurement consistency: same instrument avoids calibration differences
verify_reason: Same scale avoids calibration differences between tools.

en: A labeled diagram of the setup shows the block, spring scale, and surface, so someone else can repeat the same experiment.
source: scientific communication: labeled diagram aids reproducibility
verify_reason: Correct; labeled diagrams support replication.

en: After the block is moving, the scientist reads the spring scale again to get the kinetic friction, which is usually smaller than static friction.
source: physics of friction: kinetic friction is less than static friction
verify_reason: Correct; kinetic friction is usually less than static.

en: The conclusion states which surface had the most friction using the recorded numbers, not just what the scientist expected to happen.
source: scientific method: conclusions must be supported by evidence
verify_reason: Correct; conclusions should use recorded data.

en: A fair comparison of longitudinal and transverse waves uses the same spring, the same stretch length, and the same push strength, changing only the direction of the hand.
source: fair-test design: one variable changed, the rest held constant
verify_reason: Correct; only wave type direction changes.

en: Wave speed in a slinky is measured by marking start and end points, timing the wave with a stopwatch, and dividing distance by time.
verify_reason: Correct; speed is distance divided by time.

en: A light paper ball at the far end of a stretched slinky moves when the wave arrives, showing the wave carried energy to it.
source: standard demonstration: wave transfers energy to an object
verify_reason: Correct; moving paper ball shows energy transfer.

en: A good record of a wave demonstration includes a drawing with arrows showing the wave's direction and the material's direction, plus the measured distances.
source: science notebook practice: labeled diagram with directions
verify_reason: Correct; arrows and measurements record wave details.

en: The wavelength of a transverse wave on a rope is measured with a meter stick as the distance between two neighboring crests.
verify_reason: Correct; wavelength is crest-to-crest distance.

en: A graph of a wave's motion shows time on the horizontal axis and the position of one point on the medium on the vertical axis.
source: standard graphing convention: time on x-axis
verify_reason: Correct; displacement-time graph for a point.

en: Placing three paper markers along a slinky shows that wave energy weakens with distance, because the farthest marker moves the least.
source: standard observation: amplitude decreases with distance
verify_reason: Correct; damping reduces amplitude with distance.

en: A clear transverse wave needs a tight rope and a steady rhythm at the free end so the crests stay even and easy to measure.
source: standard demonstration technique: steady driving motion
verify_reason: Correct; tension and steady rhythm make clear waves.

en: PHIVOLCS scientists read the time gap between the longitudinal and transverse waves on a seismograph to estimate how far an earthquake is.
verify_reason: Correct; P and S wave time gap estimates distance.

en: Comparing wave speeds uses the same long spring for both wave types, timing each over the same distance.
source: fair comparison: same medium, same distance
verify_reason: Same spring and distance controls variables for fair comparison.

en: A floating cork on water bobs up and down as a wave passes but stays in place, showing the wave moves energy, not water.
source: standard demonstration: wave transfers energy, not matter
verify_reason: Cork bobs in place; wave transfers energy, not water.

en: Testing how push strength affects wave energy keeps the same spring and stretch, changing only how far the end is pulled back.
source: fair-test design: change only the independent variable
verify_reason: Same spring and stretch; only pull-back distance changes.

en: A results table for wave experiments lists wave type, push strength, distance traveled, and how far a marker moved, so patterns are easy to see.
source: science notebook practice: organized data table
verify_reason: Table lists variables and results for clear patterns.

en: A reliable wave speed comes from timing the wave three times with the same spring and push, then taking the average of the times.
source: standard measurement practice: repeated trials and averaging
verify_reason: Repeated trials and averaging improve reliability.

en: A wave sent along a rope tied to a fixed post bounces back upside down, showing reflection at a fixed end.
source: standard demonstration: reflection of a wave at a fixed boundary
verify_reason: Fixed-end reflection inverts the wave.

en: A slinky laid on a smooth, flat floor and stretched to the same length each time lets the wave travel in a straight, even path.
source: standard demonstration technique: controlled setup on flat surface
verify_reason: Smooth floor and same stretch ensure straight path.

en: A food chain with only two living things is possible, such as a plant and the animal that eats it, but most chains have more steps.
verify_reason: Producer-to-herbivore chain is possible.

en: A food chain is a straight line of arrows, not a circle, because energy moves in one direction from the Sun to the top animal.
verify_reason: Energy flows one way, so chain is linear.

en: A mango tree is a producer, and a fruit bat that eats its fruit is a herbivore, starting a food chain in a backyard.
verify_reason: Mango tree produces; fruit bat is herbivore.

en: In a freshwater river, tiny algae are eaten by small fish, and a Philippine crocodile eats the fish, forming a food chain.
verify_reason: Algae, small fish, and crocodile form a valid river chain.

en: Decomposers like fungi and bacteria are not usually drawn in a simple food chain, but they break down dead plants and animals.
verify_reason: Decomposers break down dead matter; often omitted from simple chains.

topic: food chain does not show size
en: A food chain shows the feeding order, but it does not show how big the animals are or how strong they are.
verify_reason: Food chains show feeding order, not size or strength.

en: A food chain can be found in a garden, a pond, a forest, or a rice field, because every habitat has living things that eat each other.
verify_reason: Habitats have feeding relationships, so food chains occur there.

en: The Philippine tarsier is a carnivore that eats insects, so it is a secondary consumer when the insects eat plants.
verify_reason: Tarsier eats insects; insects eating plants makes it secondary consumer.

en: A food chain shows interdependence: each living thing depends on the one before it for energy.
verify_reason: Each organism depends on previous one for energy.

en: A food chain is a model that simplifies real feeding relationships, which are often more complex.
verify_reason: Food chains simplify complex real feeding relationships.

en: A food chain can be drawn with labels for each organism's role, like producer, herbivore, carnivore, to show its job.
verify_reason: Labels can show producer, herbivore, carnivore roles.

en: A food chain is a straight line, but a food web is a tangle of lines, showing that real feeding is more connected.
verify_reason: Food chain linear; food web shows interconnected feeding.

en: The Philippine archipelago sits where the Philippine Sea Plate meets the Eurasian Plate, so both plates control where the islands go.
verify_reason: Archipelago sits between two plates; both influence motion.

en: A plate's velocity is its speed and its direction together, so predicting the future needs both, not just how fast the plate moves.
verify_reason: Velocity includes speed and direction; both needed for prediction.

en: On the western side, the Manila Trench swallows the other plate, so the whole archipelago is squeezed between two converging plates.
verify_reason: Manila Trench subducts west side; archipelago squeezed between converging plates.

en: The same plate motion that builds mountains and feeds volcanoes today is the motion that will carry the archipelago to a new position.
source: encyclopedia-stable; plate motion and landform formation
verify_reason: Same tectonic motion builds volcanoes and moves islands.

en: Satellites send signals to ground stations on the islands, and the tiny yearly shifts in those signals reveal the plate's true velocity.
verify_reason: GPS measures tiny station movements to reveal plate velocity.

en: Fifty million years is far longer than all of human history, so even a slow crawl of centimeters per year adds up to an enormous distance.
source: geologic time vs human history; encyclopedia-stable
verify_reason: Fifty million years dwarfs human history; slow motion adds up.

en: New volcanoes may rise and old islands may sink, so the 50-million-year archipelago will likely have a different lineup of islands than today.
verify_reason: Volcanic and erosional processes will change island lineup.

en: If a car keeps driving at a steady speed, you can predict where it will be later; the same math predicts where the Philippine Plate will be in 50 million years.
verify_reason: Constant-velocity math predicts future position; analogy is sound.

en: The 50-million-year map is called a model because it uses today's measurements and stated assumptions, not a guaranteed future.
verify_reason: Model uses assumptions, not a guaranteed future.

en: To measure how far a soft object moves, a class marks its starting spot on the floor and uses a tape measure after a gentle push.
source: method for measuring displacement in fair tests
verify_reason: Marks start and measures final distance; appropriate.

en: A class uses a spring scale to pull a rubber band and reads the force when it stretches to a certain length, showing how force changes shape.
source: method for measuring force with spring scale
verify_reason: Spring scale measures pull force; shows stretch.

en: To compare hardness, a class drops a small ball from the same height onto each object and records how much the object dents.
source: method for comparing hardness by impact
verify_reason: Same height drop; dent depth indicates hardness.

en: A class takes a photo of a soft object before and after pressing it, then compares the two photos side by side to see the change.
source: method for recording observations with camera
verify_reason: Photos show before/after change.

en: To test movement, a class gives the same push to a rigid box and a soft box, then measures how far each slides on the floor.
verify_reason: Same push; distance shows movement difference.

en: A class uses a spring scale to apply a measured force to a sponge and records its thickness with a ruler at each force level.
verify_reason: Measured force and thickness show deformation.

en: A class wraps a piece of string around a ball before and after squeezing it to measure its circumference and see if size changed.
verify_reason: String measures circumference change.

en: A class uses a ramp to roll a toy car into different objects and measures how far each object moves from the impact.
source: method for testing force from moving object
verify_reason: Ramp impact distance shows force effect.

en: To see how force stretches a spring, a class hangs different weights on it and measures its length with a ruler for each weight.
verify_reason: Hanging weights stretch spring; length measured.

en: A class uses a stopwatch to time how long different soft materials take to return to their original shape after being pressed.
verify_reason: Timing return compares material recovery.

en: Before testing, a class feels each object and ranks them from softest to hardest to predict which will change shape most.
source: method for predicting based on texture
verify_reason: Softness ranking reasonably predicts shape change.

en: A class draws small dots on a soft object, presses it, then watches how the dots move apart or together to see the shape change.
verify_reason: Dots show movement and deformation when pressed.

en: A class uses a spring scale to press a soft object and reads the force at which a dent appears, then measures the dent with a ruler.
source: method for finding force needed to deform
verify_reason: Spring scale measures force; ruler measures dent.

en: A class uses a marker to draw a grid on a soft object, then bends it and sees how the grid lines curve to show where the shape changed.
verify_reason: Grid lines curve to reveal bending deformation.

en: A class uses a pencil to poke a soft object and sees if it leaves a mark, which shows how easily the material is changed.
verify_reason: Poke mark indicates material changed easily.

en: A class uses a protractor to measure the angle of a bent object before and after pressing, showing how much the shape changed.
verify_reason: Protractor measures bend angle before and after.

en: Before testing, learners make a prediction about which objects will change shape, then they test each object to check their guess.
verify_reason: Prediction then testing is valid scientific practice.

en: A class presses the same soft object on a hard table and on a soft cloth to see how the surface changes the object's shape.
source: fair-test design: changing surface, holding object constant
verify_reason: Surface support affects how object deforms.

en: To see how much force is needed, a class pushes a rigid box harder and harder until it starts to move, then notes that force.
source: observation practice: threshold force for movement
verify_reason: Pushing until movement shows force threshold.

en: A class records the steps of a shape-change test in order: look at the object, press it, then look again and write down the change.
verify_reason: Ordered observation before and after pressing is correct.

en: Using a ruler to measure an object's height before and after pressing gives a clear number that shows how much the shape changed.
verify_reason: Height change is a clear measure of deformation.

en: Oxygen and silicon make up about three-quarters of the crust's mass, mostly combined as silicate minerals.
verify_reason: Oxygen and silicon total about 74% of crust mass.

en: The crust is the coldest layer of Earth, with temperatures starting at the surface and rising gradually with depth.
verify_reason: Crust is coolest; temperature rises with depth.

en: Weathering and erosion constantly break down crust rocks into soil and carry the pieces to the sea.
verify_reason: Weathering and erosion do transport sediment to sea.

en: Oceanic crust also has layers: a thin sediment cover, then basalt, and below that gabbro.
verify_reason: Oceanic crust layers are sediment, basalt, gabbro.

en: The crust provides most of the minerals we use, like copper, gold, and iron, which are mined from its rocks.
verify_reason: Crust rocks supply mined minerals.

en: The crust is the thinnest layer of Earth relative to its size, but it is the only one we can see and walk on.
verify_reason: Crust is thinnest and accessible surface layer.

en: The crust is the boundary where the solid Earth meets the oceans and atmosphere, shaping coastlines and weather.
verify_reason: Crust surface meets oceans/atmosphere; influences coastlines/weather.

en: The crust breaks into faults, and when the rocks slip along a fault, the energy causes an earthquake.
verify_reason: Fault slip releases energy as earthquakes.

en: The crust is recycled at plate boundaries: new crust forms at mid-ocean ridges and old crust sinks at subduction zones.
verify_reason: Crust forms at ridges and recycles at subduction zones.

en: The crust is the least dense layer of Earth, so it floats on the denser mantle below.
verify_reason: Crust is least dense and floats on mantle.

en: The crust is the most varied layer, with different rock types, ages, and structures in different regions.
verify_reason: Crust has diverse rocks, ages, and structures.

en: Mines and drill cores give scientists direct samples of the crust, making it the most accessible layer to study.
verify_reason: Mines and drill cores directly sample crust.

en: Most volcanoes on Earth occur where magma from the mantle rises through cracks in the crust.
verify_reason: Most volcanoes occur where mantle magma rises through crust.

en: The crust under the Philippines is a patchwork of continental and oceanic fragments, making it geologically active.
verify_reason: Philippines has complex crustal fragments and active tectonics.

en: The subsolar point is the one place on Earth where the Sun is directly overhead at noon, and it receives the most intense sunlight because the rays hit at 90 degrees.
verify_reason: Subsolar point gets direct 90-degree sunlight.

en: The tilt makes the Sun rise and set at different points on the horizon, so in the Philippines the Sun rises more toward the north in summer and more toward the south in winter.
source: observational astronomy; seasonal sunrise azimuth shift
verify_reason: Northern Hemisphere sunrise shifts north in summer, south in winter.

en: The intensity of sunlight depends on the Sun's angle above the horizon, so a Sun at 90 degrees gives full intensity and a Sun at 30 degrees gives about half.
source: sine of solar altitude; trigonometry of insolation
verify_reason: Intensity follows sine of sun angle; sin 30° is half.

en: The tilt causes the Sun's path across the sky to be a higher arc in summer and a lower arc in winter, so the Sun climbs higher at noon.
verify_reason: Summer sun path is higher; winter lower.

en: In the Philippines, the Sun is directly overhead at noon twice a year, and on those days a vertical stick casts almost no shadow.
source: geography of tropics; PAGASA-consistent solar position
verify_reason: Philippines lies in tropics; overhead sun twice yearly.

en: The tilt causes seasons to be more extreme at high latitudes and milder near the equator, because the angle of sunlight changes more at high latitudes.
source: climatology; seasonal insolation variation with latitude
verify_reason: High latitudes have greater seasonal sunlight angle changes.

en: The angle of incidence is the angle between the Sun's rays and a line pointing straight up from the ground, and it is zero when the Sun is overhead.
verify_reason: Angle from vertical; zero when Sun is directly overhead.

en: The total solar energy a place receives in a day depends on both the angle of sunlight and the number of daylight hours.
verify_reason: Sun angle and daylight hours both affect total energy.

en: The tilt is about 23.5 degrees, which is the same as the latitude of the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn.
source: axial tilt equals tropical latitudes; encyclopedia-stable
verify_reason: Earth's tilt and tropics latitude are both about 23.5 degrees.

en: The Sun's rays are more slanted in the early morning and late afternoon, so the ground warms less then even though the Sun is shining.
verify_reason: Slanted rays spread energy, so ground warms less.

en: The tilt is the reason the shadow of a stick at noon changes length through the year, getting shorter in summer and longer in winter.
verify_reason: Tilt changes noon Sun height, making shadows shorter in summer.

en: The angle of sunlight can be estimated from shadow length, because a longer shadow means a lower Sun and less intense rays.
source: trigonometry of shadows; simple measurement method
verify_reason: Longer shadow means lower Sun and less intense rays.

en: At the North Pole, the Sun stays above the horizon for about six months of daylight and below for six months of night because of the tilt.
source: polar day and polar night; encyclopedia-stable
verify_reason: Tilt causes about six months of daylight and darkness.

en: Because of the tilt, the summer hemisphere gets sunlight at a steeper angle and the winter hemisphere at a shallower angle, so the two hemispheres receive different amounts of energy.
verify_reason: Tilt gives steeper rays in summer, shallower in winter.

en: The tilt causes the Sun's rays to be more concentrated in the summer, which is why the ground warms up more even though the Sun's output stays the same.
source: solar constant vs. incidence angle; encyclopedia-stable
verify_reason: Tilt concentrates rays in summer; Sun's output is unchanged.

en: As a population grows, its own waste builds up in the water or soil, which can poison the environment and slow down further growth.
source: encyclopedia-stable; density-dependent limiting factors include waste accumulation
verify_reason: Waste buildup can poison environment and slow population growth.

en: Near carrying capacity, animals must travel farther to find food, using up energy that could have gone to raising young.
source: encyclopedia-stable; resource limitation affects reproductive energy
verify_reason: Resource scarcity near carrying capacity forces energy tradeoffs.

en: When all the good nesting spots or hiding places are taken, many young animals cannot survive, so the population stops growing as fast.
source: encyclopedia-stable; limited shelter as a limiting factor
verify_reason: Limited nesting sites reduce survival and slow growth.

en: A population far below its limit might grow by ten percent a year, but near the limit it grows by only one or two percent a year.
source: logistic growth model; rate decreases as N approaches K
verify_reason: Illustrative rates show slower growth near limit.

en: As a population approaches carrying capacity, the number of new individuals added each year gets smaller and smaller.
source: logistic growth; absolute growth rate decreases near K
verify_reason: Additions decline as population nears carrying capacity.

en: When a population is small, each individual has plenty of resources, but as it grows, the same amount must be split among many, so growth slows.
verify_reason: Resource sharing slows growth as population rises.

en: In a small Philippine pond, tilapia growth slows down as they eat up the algae, leaving less for each new fish to eat.
verify_reason: Algae depletion leaves less food, slowing tilapia growth.

en: In a Philippine bakawan, or mangrove forest, the crab population slows down as they use up the fallen leaves that are their main food.
verify_reason: Fallen leaf depletion slows mangrove crab population growth.

en: A population's growth slows down when it runs low on the single resource it needs most, like water during a dry spell.
verify_reason: Scarcest resource limits growth, e.g., water.

en: Overcrowding itself can stress animals, making them produce fewer young and slowing the population's growth.
source: encyclopedia-stable; physiological stress in dense populations
verify_reason: Crowding stress lowers reproduction and slows growth.

en: Near carrying capacity, the population size does not stay perfectly still but wobbles up and down slightly as births and deaths balance out.
verify_reason: Populations fluctuate slightly around carrying capacity.

en: The growth of a population slows down because the death rate rises as resources become scarce, not just because the birth rate falls.
source: population ecology; death rate response to scarcity
verify_reason: Death rate rises with scarcity, slowing growth.

en: Growth starts to slow down before the population reaches the absolute limit, because resources get harder to find as it gets closer.
verify_reason: Growth slows before limit as resources become scarce.

en: Weeds in a field grow quickly at first, but their growth slows down as they crowd each other out for sunlight and water.
verify_reason: Competition for resources slows growth.

en: In a forest, the number of squirrels slows down as the acorn supply runs out, because each squirrel needs a certain number of acorns to survive the winter.
source: encyclopedia-stable; seed/food limitation in animal populations
verify_reason: Food shortage limits population growth.

en: If a lake has only a certain amount of oxygen, the fish population slows down as that oxygen gets used up by more fish.
source: aquatic ecology; dissolved oxygen as a limiting factor
verify_reason: Limited oxygen slows fish population growth.

en: The birth rate falls as food gets scarce, because mothers have less energy to make healthy babies, so growth slows down.
verify_reason: Food scarcity can lower birth rates.

en: In a rice field, the number of frogs slows down as the insects they eat become harder to find, so fewer tadpoles survive.
verify_reason: Less food reduces tadpole survival.

en: A population that is far below its carrying capacity grows quickly, but one that is near it grows very slowly, because every extra mouth makes the shortage worse.
verify_reason: Logistic growth near carrying capacity slows.

en: Earth's lithospheric plates are not just crust; each one includes the crust and the rigid top layer of the mantle, moving as a single slab.
verify_reason: Plates include crust and rigid upper mantle.

en: Tectonic plates drift about 2 to 5 centimeters per year, roughly the length of a paperclip, so their movement is too slow to feel.
verify_reason: Plate speeds match paperclip-length scale.

en: Continental crust is made mostly of light granite, while oceanic crust is made of dark, dense basalt from cooled lava.
verify_reason: Granite and basalt crust types are correct.

en: Some continental crust is over 3 billion years old, yet the oldest oceanic crust is only about 200 million years because it gets recycled.
verify_reason: Continental crust older; oceanic crust recycled.

en: When an oceanic plate collides with a continental plate, the ocean floor sinks and the land edge crumples into mountains and volcanoes.
verify_reason: Oceanic plate subducts; continental edge forms mountains and volcanoes.

en: When a continent pulls apart at a divergent boundary, the crack can widen into a new ocean, leaving the two halves on different plates.
verify_reason: Continental rifting can form new ocean basins.

en: Because continental crust is thick and light, it floats high and does not sink into the mantle, so it survives for billions of years.
verify_reason: Continental crust is buoyant and long-lived.

en: At a subduction zone, the sinking edge of a plate pulls the rest of the plate behind it, like a heavy tablecloth tugging downward.
verify_reason: Slab pull is a real plate-driving force.

en: Old oceanic crust is swallowed back into the mantle at subduction zones, which is why the ocean floor is always much younger than the continents.
verify_reason: Oceanic crust recycles, so ocean floor is younger.

en: Focal depth is the straight-line distance from an earthquake's focus underground to the epicenter on the surface above it.
source: encyclopedia-stable; earthquake focus and epicenter geometry
verify_reason: Focal depth is vertical distance from focus to epicenter.

en: Intensity is measured by collecting reports from many places about how people felt the shaking and what damage they saw.
source: encyclopedia-stable; intensity from felt reports and damage surveys
verify_reason: Intensity uses felt shaking and damage reports.

en: A simple fault model uses two blocks of wood with sandpaper between them that slide to show how rocks move.
source: classroom model of fault motion; DepEd MATATAG activity
verify_reason: Common classroom fault model uses blocks and friction.

en: In a classroom model, the focus is a point deep inside a box of clay, and the epicenter is the mark on the top surface.
source: classroom model of focus and epicenter; DepEd MATATAG activity
verify_reason: Clay model correctly shows focus and epicenter.

en: A seismograph draws its wiggly lines on paper or a screen, and that record is called a seismogram.
verify_reason: Seismogram is the record from a seismograph.

en: A very deep earthquake under the ocean may not create a tsunami because the seafloor barely moves at the surface.
source: encyclopedia-stable; deep quakes produce little seafloor displacement
verify_reason: Deep quakes may not move seafloor enough.

en: News reports usually name an earthquake by its epicenter, such as a quake near a town, even though the focus is underground.
source: encyclopedia-stable; epicenter used for locating earthquakes in reports
verify_reason: News uses epicenter location, not focus.

en: A tsunami's height at the shore depends partly on the shape of the seafloor, so some coastal areas get bigger waves than others.
verify_reason: Seafloor shape affects tsunami wave height at shore.

en: Many countries use the Modified Mercalli scale from I to XII, while PHIVOLCS's Philippine scale goes from I to X.
source: encyclopedia-stable; Modified Mercalli and PHIVOLCS intensity scales
verify_reason: MMI uses I-XII; PHIVOLCS uses I-X.

en: A scientific investigation begins with a clear question, like which surface makes the block hardest to pull, before any measuring is done.
source: scientific method: question first, then plan
verify_reason: Investigations start with a clear testable question.

en: Scientists pick surfaces that look very different, such as rough sandpaper and smooth glass, so the friction readings are easy to compare.
source: fair-test design: choose contrasting levels of the variable
verify_reason: Contrasting surfaces make friction comparisons clearer.

en: A scientist first pulls the block on a plain table to get a baseline reading, then compares every other surface with that starting value.
source: experimental design: baseline measurement for comparison
verify_reason: Baseline reading gives a comparison starting value.

en: The scientist reads the spring scale only when the needle stops swinging, so the number is steady and not too high or too low.
source: measurement practice: read instruments when stable
verify_reason: Wait for steady needle to read accurately.

en: Along with the numbers, the scientist writes how each surface feels or looks, like rough or shiny, to help explain the results later.
source: science inquiry: qualitative and quantitative observations
verify_reason: Qualitative notes help explain numerical results.

en: The written method is clear enough that another person could follow the same steps and check whether the results come out the same.
verify_reason: Clear methods allow others to repeat and check.

en: Scientists test the surfaces in a mixed order, not always the same sequence, so practice with one surface does not change the later readings.
verify_reason: Mixed order reduces practice-order bias.

en: A flat wooden block is used instead of a rolling toy because the spring scale measures sliding friction between the block and the surface.
source: friction measurement: sliding vs rolling friction
verify_reason: Block measures sliding friction, not rolling friction.

en: After making the bar graph, the scientist looks for a pattern, like rougher surfaces having taller bars, before writing the conclusion.
source: data analysis: look for patterns before concluding
verify_reason: Graph patterns inform conclusions.

en: The scientist clears the table of extra objects so nothing bumps the block or the spring scale while the measurement is taken.
verify_reason: Clear table prevents bumps during measurement.

en: If one trial gives a reading that is very different from the others on the same surface, the scientist repeats that trial to check it.
verify_reason: Repeating unusual trials is standard scientific practice.

en: In a motor, electricity makes the coil spin, but in a generator, an outside force like water or wind makes the coil spin, so the cause of the spin is opposite.
verify_reason: Motor uses electricity; generator uses outside motion.

en: A motor gets its energy from a battery or a wall outlet, while a generator gets its energy from a crank, a turbine, or an engine, so their energy sources are opposite.
verify_reason: Motor input is electrical; generator input is mechanical.

en: In the energy chain, a generator changes mechanical energy into electrical energy, and a motor changes it back, so they are opposite steps in the same cycle.
verify_reason: Generator and motor convert energy in opposite directions.

en: A common mistake is thinking a generator creates electricity from nothing, but it only changes motion into electricity, so it must be kept spinning by an outside force.
verify_reason: Generators convert motion, not create energy from nothing.

en: A generator only makes electricity while its coil is spinning, so if you stop turning the crank, the light goes out.
verify_reason: No spin means no electricity in simple generator.

en: In a hydroelectric dam, falling water turns a turbine that spins a generator, and the electricity then runs motors in homes, showing how the two work together.
verify_reason: Falling water spins turbine, generator, then powers motors.

en: In some continental regions, seismic waves reveal a boundary called the Conrad discontinuity that separates the upper and lower crust.
verify_reason: Conrad discontinuity separates upper and lower crust in some regions.

en: The upper crust holds most of the world's groundwater in porous rocks like sandstone and limestone, which form aquifers that supply wells.
verify_reason: Aquifers in porous upper crust rocks hold groundwater.

en: The oldest rocks on Earth, about 4 billion years old, are found in the upper crust of ancient continents called cratons.
verify_reason: Oldest rocks about 4 billion years old occur in cratons.

en: The upper crust is cold and brittle, so it breaks during earthquakes, while the lower crust is hot and can bend without breaking.
verify_reason: Upper crust brittle; lower crust hot and ductile.

en: The upper crust contains most of the world's coal, oil, and natural gas, trapped in layers of sedimentary rock.
source: fossil fuel reservoirs in sedimentary basins
verify_reason: Correct; fossil fuels occur in sedimentary rock layers.

en: The upper crust is the only part of the crust that is directly exposed at the surface, while the lower crust lies hidden beneath.
verify_reason: Correct; surface exposures are upper crust.

en: The upper crust is less dense than the lower crust because it is richer in silica and lighter minerals like quartz and feldspar.
source: compositional difference between upper and lower crust
verify_reason: Correct; upper crust is more silica-rich and less dense.

en: The upper crust is the layer most shaped by weathering and erosion, creating soil, valleys, and plains on the land surface.
verify_reason: Correct; weathering and erosion shape the upper crust.

en: The upper crust holds fossils because sedimentary rocks form on top of it and preserve the remains of ancient organisms.
verify_reason: Correct; fossils are preserved in upper crust sedimentary rocks.

en: A class uses a spring scale to push a toy car with a measured force, then uses a ruler to measure how far the car slides.
source: standard method for measuring force and distance
verify_reason: Correct; spring scale measures force, ruler measures distance.

en: A class uses a stopwatch to time how many seconds a pushed toy car takes to stop, showing which surface slows it down more.
source: standard stopwatch timing for comparing motion
verify_reason: Correct; stopwatch times stopping on different surfaces.

en: A class draws two dots on a clay cylinder and measures the distance between them with a ruler before and after stretching to see how much it lengthened.
verify_reason: Correct; ruler measures stretch between dots.

en: A class makes a data table with a column for each object's predicted change and a column for the actual change, then compares the two.
verify_reason: Correct; table compares predictions and actual results.

en: The labels herbivore, carnivore, and omnivore are used only for animals, not for plants, because plants are producers that make their own food.
verify_reason: Correct; these consumer labels apply to animals, plants are producers.

en: An animal's label in a food chain is based on its usual diet, so a pig that eats both plants and scraps is an omnivore even if it sometimes eats only plants.
verify_reason: Pigs are omnivores; label based on usual diet.

en: In a simple food chain, you typically draw one producer, one herbivore, and one carnivore, but you can replace the herbivore or carnivore with an omnivore.
verify_reason: Omnivores can occupy herbivore or carnivore roles in chains.

en: The Sun is not a living thing, so it is never labeled as a herbivore, carnivore, or omnivore; it is only the source of energy.
verify_reason: Sun is energy source, not a consumer.

en: To draw a correct food chain, you must choose a plant that a herbivore really eats and a herbivore that a carnivore really eats, so the chain is realistic.
verify_reason: Real food chains need actual predator-prey links.

en: A food chain diagram can be drawn with the producer on the left and the top consumer on the right, but the order is determined by who eats whom.
verify_reason: Order follows energy flow, often left to right.

en: In this investigation, the raw material that is changed is the independent variable, and the starch the leaf makes is the dependent variable that is measured.
verify_reason: Independent variable changed; starch production measured.

en: Before testing, a plant is kept in a dark cupboard for about 24 hours so all stored starch is used up.
verify_reason: Darkness destarches plant by using stored starch.

en: One setup keeps the raw material present as a control, while the other setup removes it, so the two results can be compared.
verify_reason: Control and experimental setups allow comparison.

en: To remove carbon dioxide from the air, a scientist puts soda lime or a sodium hydroxide solution inside the sealed jar with the plant.
source: standard CO2-absorption method in photosynthesis labs
verify_reason: Soda lime or NaOH absorbs carbon dioxide.

en: To test water, two similar potted plants are used, one watered and one kept dry, while both get the same light.
source: standard controlled comparison for water as a reactant
verify_reason: Watered vs. dry plants with same light tests water.

en: A leaf partially covered with black paper tests light needs, because the covered and uncovered halves share the same leaf.
source: classic partial-cover experiment for light requirement
verify_reason: Covered and uncovered halves compare light effect.

en: The leaf is first boiled in water to kill it and make its cells soft enough for the next steps.
verify_reason: Boiling kills leaf and softens cells for testing.

en: The soft leaf is then boiled in alcohol over a water bath to remove the green chlorophyll that would hide the iodine color.
source: standard decolorization step in starch testing
verify_reason: Alcohol removes chlorophyll so iodine color is visible.

en: After rinsing the pale leaf in water, iodine solution is dropped on it to reveal any starch that was made.
verify_reason: Iodine reveals starch as blue-black after rinsing.

en: The result is recorded by drawing the leaf and coloring the blue-black patches that show where starch formed.
source: standard data recording for starch distribution
verify_reason: Drawing and shading blue-black patches records starch locations.

en: The whole setup is repeated with several leaves or plants so the finding is not due to chance.
verify_reason: Repeating trials reduces chance findings.

en: A testable hypothesis states that if carbon dioxide is missing, then the leaf will show no blue-black color with iodine.
verify_reason: No CO2 means no starch, so no blue-black.

topic: soil is not a raw material
en: The investigation compares plants with and without each suspected raw material, which can show that soil is not among them.
source: consensus: soil is not a photosynthesis reactant
verify_reason: Soil is not a photosynthesis raw material.

topic: BTB to show carbon dioxide use
en: To verify carbon dioxide is used, a plant is sealed in a jar with BTB, and the liquid turning blue shows the gas was consumed.
source: BTB color change as CO2 uptake indicator
verify_reason: BTB turns blue as CO2 is consumed.

en: Limewater turns milky when carbon dioxide is present, so it can check that the jar truly has no carbon dioxide.
source: standard limewater test for carbon dioxide
verify_reason: Limewater turns milky with CO2.

en: The plant is left in the setup for several hours under bright light so photosynthesis has time to make starch.
verify_reason: Bright light gives time to make starch.

en: Keeping both setups at the same temperature matters because heat changes how fast photosynthesis happens.
source: controlled variable: temperature in fair tests
verify_reason: Temperature affects photosynthesis rate.

en: If only the setup without carbon dioxide shows no starch, the result supports that carbon dioxide is a raw material.
verify_reason: No CO2 leads to no starch; supports CO2 as raw material.

en: To identify a compression, look for the crowded coils of a slinky, and to identify a rarefaction, look for the spread-out coils.
source: classroom observation of longitudinal wave parts
verify_reason: Compressions are crowded coils; rarefactions are spread out.

en: To find the crest of a transverse wave, look for the highest point above the rest line, and the trough is the lowest point.
source: classroom observation of transverse wave parts
verify_reason: Crest is highest point; trough is lowest point.

en: To tell the wave types apart, watch the direction of vibration: transverse moves at a right angle, longitudinal moves along the wave path.
source: comparison of wave types by vibration direction
verify_reason: Transverse vibrates perpendicular; longitudinal vibrates parallel.

en: To calculate wave speed without timing a wave, multiply the measured wavelength by the frequency, and the product is the speed.
verify_reason: Wave speed equals wavelength times frequency.

en: To compare the energy of two waves, measure their amplitudes and remember that doubling the amplitude gives about four times the energy.
source: wave energy proportional to amplitude squared
verify_reason: Energy scales with amplitude squared; doubling gives four times.

en: To demonstrate reflection of a longitudinal wave, clap near a large wall and listen for the echo that returns.
verify_reason: Echo is reflected sound, a longitudinal wave.

en: To measure how mangroves reduce wave energy, compare wave height in front of and behind a mangrove stand.
source: coastal ecology; wave attenuation by mangroves
verify_reason: Comparing wave height before and after mangroves shows energy loss.

en: PAGASA uses floating buoys in the ocean to measure wave height, which tells how much energy the waves carry.
verify_reason: Wave buoys measure wave height, indicating wave energy.
