source: plant science: soil aeration and root growth
verify_reason: Clay's tiny pores limit air and root growth.

en: Dark soil often has more humus, so it tends to hold more water than light-colored sandy soil.
source: soil observation: color as indicator of organic matter
verify_reason: Humus darkens soil and boosts water holding.

en: Plants like cactus and some beach grasses grow well in sandy soil because it drains fast and doesn't stay wet.
source: ecology: adaptations to dry, well-drained soils
verify_reason: These plants tolerate fast-draining, dry sandy soil.

en: The size of soil particles determines how much space is between them, and that space controls water flow.
source: soil physics: relationship between particle size and porosity
verify_reason: Particle size affects pore space and water flow.

en: The amount of water a soil can hold depends on how much organic matter it has, not just particle size.
source: soil science: organic matter influence on water retention
verify_reason: Organic matter also strongly affects water retention.

en: Fungi and bacteria are both microorganisms, but fungi have a nucleus (the cell's control center) while bacteria do not.
source: encyclopedia-stable; cell structure of fungi and bacteria
verify_reason: Fungi are eukaryotic; bacteria lack nuclei.

en: A flying airplane has mechanical energy from both its forward motion and its height above the ground, so its total mechanical energy is the sum of its kinetic and potential energies.
source: encyclopedia-stable; physics of mechanical energy as a sum
verify_reason: Mechanical energy sums kinetic and potential energy.

en: Mechanical energy is a single number, so you simply add the kinetic and potential energy values, ignoring direction, to get the total.
source: encyclopedia-stable; mechanical energy is a scalar quantity
verify_reason: Energy is scalar; directions don't affect sum.

en: When sea animals with shells die, their shells can slowly turn into limestone rock, storing carbon in the earth for millions of years.
source: geological carbon cycle, limestone formation from marine organisms
verify_reason: Shells lithify into limestone, storing carbon long-term.

en: In cold places, water can freeze into glaciers that hold water for a long time, and when they melt, the water keeps moving through the water cycle.
source: water cycle includes storage in glaciers and ice caps
verify_reason: Glaciers store water; melting returns it to cycle.

en: When leaves and roots die, some of their carbon stays in the soil as humus, so soil stores carbon for many years.
source: soil organic matter and carbon storage in terrestrial ecosystems
verify_reason: Dead plant matter forms humus, storing carbon long-term.

en: Plants need water from the water cycle to combine with carbon dioxide and make food, so the water and carbon cycles work together in every leaf.
source: photosynthesis requires water and carbon dioxide, linking the two cycles
verify_reason: Photosynthesis uses water and CO2, linking cycles in leaves.

en: Earth's shadow does not cause moon phases; it only creates lunar eclipses when Earth blocks the Sun's light from the Moon.
verify_reason: Earth's shadow causes lunar eclipses, not phases.

en: The Moon's phase changes gradually, so each night it looks slightly different from the night before.
verify_reason: Phases change gradually night to night.

en: The Moon's distance from Earth changes slightly, but this does not change the phase; only the angle between Sun, Earth, and Moon matters.
verify_reason: Distance affects size, not phase; angle does.

en: The Moon's phases are not caused by Earth's rotation; they come from the Moon's own movement around Earth.
verify_reason: Phases come from Moon's orbit, not Earth's rotation.

en: The Moon's phase cycle is used in many calendars, such as the Islamic lunar calendar, to mark months.
verify_reason: Islamic calendar uses lunar phase cycle for months.

en: In a model of the solar system, the Sun is the light source, Earth moves around the Sun, and the Moon circles Earth, showing how phases depend on the Moon's position.
verify_reason: Model correctly shows Sun, Earth, Moon positions causing phases.

en: The Moon's phase at any time is determined by the angle between the Sun and the Moon as seen from Earth.
verify_reason: Phase depends on Sun-Moon angle from Earth.

en: The Moon's phases repeat in a cycle, so if you know today's phase, you can predict the phase for any future date.
verify_reason: Cycle repeats, allowing future phase prediction.

en: The word 'month' comes from 'moon' because the Moon's phase cycle takes about a month.
verify_reason: Month derives from moon; cycle about a month.

en: To draw moon phases, place the Sun on one side, Earth in the middle, and show the Moon in different positions around Earth.
verify_reason: Standard top-down diagram for moon phases.

en: The Moon's phase can be used to estimate the time of night, but it is not a precise clock.
verify_reason: Phase gives approximate rise/set times, not precise.

en: The Moon's phase cycle is used in many cultures for religious festivals, such as Eid al-Fitr.
verify_reason: Eid al-Fitr follows the lunar calendar.

en: Everyone on Earth sees the same moon phase on a given day, but the time it rises and sets changes with your location.
verify_reason: Phase is global; rise/set time varies by location.

en: Before planting, write a hypothesis that predicts which soil type will grow the tallest plant.
verify_reason: Testable prediction before experiment is correct.

en: Use a pH strip to test the acidity of each soil type before planting, and record the color change.
verify_reason: pH strips indicate soil acidity or alkalinity.

en: Use a measuring cup to collect and measure the water that drains from each pot after watering.
verify_reason: Measuring drained water is a valid method.

en: Use a ruler to measure the width of the largest leaf on each plant to compare leaf size.
verify_reason: Ruler measurement compares leaf size.

en: Use a stopwatch to time how long it takes for water to soak into each soil type.
verify_reason: Stopwatch times water infiltration.

en: Use a magnifying glass to look for tiny root hairs that help the plant take up water.
verify_reason: Magnifier can show root hairs.

en: Blood from the intestines goes straight to the liver first, so the liver can process nutrients and catch harmful substances before they reach the rest of the body.
source: hepatic portal circulation; liver first-pass metabolism
verify_reason: Intestinal blood goes to liver via portal vein.

en: Your kidneys keep the right amount of water in your blood, which your digestive system needs to make saliva and stomach juices.
source: kidney water balance; digestive secretions require water
verify_reason: Kidneys regulate blood water; digestive juices need water.

en: A meal can take about one to three days to travel through your digestive tract, while your kidneys filter your blood continuously.
source: gastrointestinal transit time ~1-3 days; continuous renal filtration
verify_reason: Digestive transit time and continuous kidney filtration are accurate.

en: To make the results fair and unbiased, ask someone else to measure the plants without knowing which soil each pot holds.
source: scientific method: blinding to reduce observer bias
verify_reason: Blinding the measurer reduces bias.

en: A cell is the smallest unit of a living thing that can carry out life processes like getting energy and making copies of itself.
verify_reason: Accurate basic cell definition.

en: A tissue is a group of similar cells that work together to do one job, like muscle tissue that helps you move.
verify_reason: Accurate tissue definition.

en: An organ is made of two or more different tissues that work together, such as the heart pumping blood using muscle and nerve tissue.
verify_reason: Accurate organ definition.

en: An organism is any living thing that can carry out all life processes on its own, from a single bacterium to a human being.
verify_reason: Accurate organism definition.

en: An ecosystem includes a community of living things plus the non-living parts of their environment, like water, soil, and sunlight.
verify_reason: Accurate ecosystem definition.

en: Each level of biological organization contains the level below it, so a tissue is made of cells and an organ is made of tissues.
verify_reason: Accurate levels-of-organization statement.

en: In the human body, muscle cells form muscle tissue, which makes up the heart organ, which is part of the circulatory system.
verify_reason: Correct hierarchy from muscle cells to circulatory system.

en: A leaf is an organ made of different tissues, such as the outer skin tissue and the inner food-making tissue.
verify_reason: Leaf is an organ with multiple tissues.

en: A human body contains about 37 trillion cells, and they are organized into tissues, organs, and systems to keep you alive.
verify_reason: 37 trillion cells is a common accurate estimate.

en: A population is just one species, but a community includes many species; for example, all the tilapia in a lake are a population, while the tilapia, snails, and algae together are a community.
verify_reason: Correctly distinguishes population and community with example.

en: An ecosystem is not only living things; it also includes the non-living parts like rocks, water, and air that living things depend on.
verify_reason: Ecosystems include living and non-living parts.

en: The tropical rainforest biome in the Philippines contains many different ecosystems, from mountain forests to lowland swamps.
verify_reason: Rainforest biome contains varied ecosystems.

en: In a labelled diagram, arrows from cell to biosphere show that each higher level is made up of the levels below it.
verify_reason: Arrows show levels built from lower levels.

en: Cells become specialized for different jobs, and this specialization allows tissues, organs, and systems to perform complex tasks.
verify_reason: Specialized cells enable complex tissue and organ functions.

en: An organ is not just a bigger cell; it is a structure made of many different tissues, each with its own role.
verify_reason: Correctly clarifies organs are made of tissues.

en: In a rice field, a single palay plant is an organism, all the palay plants are a population, and the field with frogs and insects is a community.
verify_reason: Correct organism, population, and community example.

en: When shaken with water, soil particles settle in layers with the largest sand at the bottom, silt in the middle, and the smallest clay at the top.
source: standard classroom demonstration: particle size affects settling rate in water
verify_reason: Sand settles bottom, silt middle, clay top.

en: Farmers water sandy soil more often because it drains quickly, while clay soil stays wet longer and needs less watering.
source: agricultural practice: irrigation scheduling based on soil texture and water retention
verify_reason: Sandy soil drains fast; clay retains water.

topic: outer core vs inner core thickness
en: The outer core is about 2,200 km thick, which is nearly twice the inner core's radius of about 1,200 km, so it appears as a thicker ring in a scale drawing.
source: rounded values from Earth structure models
verify_reason: Outer core thickness is nearly twice inner core radius.

en: The mantle is about 2,900 km thick, which is nearly half of Earth's radius of about 6,400 km, so it takes up the largest portion of a scale drawing.
source: rounded values of mantle thickness and Earth's radius
verify_reason: Mantle is about 45% of Earth's radius, largest layer.

en: The asthenosphere lies roughly between 100 and 350 kilometers deep, so it is a soft zone within the upper mantle that appears as a thin band in a scale drawing.
source: commonly cited depth range for asthenosphere
verify_reason: Depth range and thin upper-mantle band are accurate.

en: Using a scale of 1 cm = 100 km, the 2,900 km mantle becomes 29 cm on paper, which is about the length of a long ruler.
source: scale conversion example with 1 cm = 100 km
verify_reason: 2900 km at 1 cm per 100 km equals 29 cm.

en: The geologic time scale is built from the order of rock layers and the fossils inside them, so it tells the sequence of Earth's past events.
verify_reason: Rock layers and fossils give relative sequence.

en: In undisturbed rock layers, the oldest layer lies at the bottom and the youngest at the top, giving a natural order to Earth's history.
verify_reason: Oldest bottom, youngest top in undisturbed layers.

en: The geologic time scale combines the relative order of rock layers with absolute ages from radiometric dating to give a complete timeline.
source: combination of relative and absolute dating
verify_reason: Relative order plus radiometric dating gives timeline.

en: The boundaries between divisions of the geologic time scale often mark major changes in life, such as a sudden appearance or extinction of many species.
source: geologic time scale boundaries and biotic events
verify_reason: Boundaries often mark extinctions or new life.

en: The Cambrian explosion, about 541 million years ago, marks a time when many major animal groups first appear in the fossil record.
verify_reason: About 541 million years ago, many animal groups appeared.

en: The Phanerozoic eon, meaning "visible life," covers the last 541 million years, when abundant fossils make Earth's history easier to read.
verify_reason: Visible life eon covers last 541 million years.

en: The geologic time scale shows Earth is about 4.5 billion years old, far older than any written human record, which only goes back a few thousand years.
verify_reason: Earth is billions of years old; written records recent.

en: By reading the geologic time scale, scientists can see that life evolved from simple single-celled organisms to complex multicellular animals over billions of years.
verify_reason: Fossil record shows this progression over billions of years.

en: The geologic time scale lets scientists match rock layers of the same age on different continents, showing that they formed at the same time.
verify_reason: Same-age rock layers can be correlated across continents.

en: Many geologic period names come from places where their rocks were first studied, like the Jurassic period from the Jura Mountains in Europe.
verify_reason: Jurassic is named after Jura Mountains.

en: The geologic time scale helps geologists find coal and oil because these resources are trapped in rocks of specific ages.
verify_reason: Coal and oil occur in rocks of particular ages.

en: The geologic time scale acts like a giant calendar, allowing scientists to place events such as volcanic eruptions and asteroid impacts in order.
source: geologic time scale as chronological framework
verify_reason: It orders major Earth events chronologically.

en: The geologic time scale reveals that mass extinctions, like the one that killed off the dinosaurs, have punctuated Earth's history.
source: mass extinction events in geologic record
verify_reason: Mass extinctions mark boundaries in Earth's history.

en: Matching rock ages and fossils across continents using the geologic time scale supports the idea that continents have moved over time.
source: evidence for plate tectonics from rock correlation
verify_reason: Matching rocks and fossils supports continental drift.

en: The geologic time scale records past climate changes, including ice ages and warm periods, helping scientists understand today's climate.
verify_reason: Rock records reveal past climates and ice ages.

en: In the Philippines, scientists use the geologic time scale to date rocks and fossils found in areas like Palawan and Cebu.
verify_reason: Scientists date Philippine rocks and fossils using it.

en: The geologic time scale is not fixed; scientists keep refining it as new fossils and dating techniques provide better evidence.
source: dynamic nature of geologic time scale
verify_reason: New evidence leads to refinements.

en: The geologic time scale works like the chapters of a book, each division telling a part of Earth's story from its birth to now.
verify_reason: Divisions tell Earth's history like book chapters.

en: For a box sliding at constant speed on a flat floor, the push arrow and the friction arrow are drawn equal in length because the forces are balanced.
source: balanced forces: constant velocity means net force is zero
verify_reason: Constant speed means balanced forces, equal arrows.

en: To find the net force from a free-body diagram, subtract the shorter arrow's length from the longer arrow's length when they point in opposite directions.
source: net force = vector sum; opposite forces subtract
verify_reason: Opposite forces subtract to find net force.

en: When drawing a free-body diagram for an object on a ramp, tilt the coordinate axes so one axis runs along the ramp surface and the other is perpendicular to it.
source: inclined plane analysis: axes along and normal to surface
verify_reason: Tilted axes match ramp surface and perpendicular direction.

en: When a rope pulls an object at an angle, draw the tension arrow from the object's point at that exact angle, not along the horizontal or vertical.
source: force direction follows the rope's actual orientation
verify_reason: Tension acts along the rope's angle.

en: When two forces act on an object in the same direction, draw both arrows from the same point pointing the same way, with the longer one showing the larger force.
source: multiple forces: each drawn separately from the point
verify_reason: Same-direction forces add; longer arrow shows larger force.

en: Draw the arrow for gravity first in a free-body diagram because it always points straight down and gives a reference for the other forces.
source: gravity direction is fixed downward; serves as reference
verify_reason: Gravity points straight down, giving a reference.

en: When drawing a free-body diagram for an object hanging from two ropes, draw each tension arrow along its own rope, pointing away from the object toward the ceiling.
source: tension acts along each rope away from the object
verify_reason: Tension pulls away from object along each rope.

en: A free-body diagram of an object moving at constant velocity shows balanced forces, so opposite arrows are equal even though the object is moving.
source: Newton's first law: constant velocity means zero net force
verify_reason: Constant velocity means balanced forces.

en: When a force acts at an angle, use a protractor to measure the angle from the horizontal or vertical axis before drawing the arrow.
verify_reason: Protractor measures force angle before drawing.

en: For an object being pushed but not moving, the push arrow and the friction arrow are equal in length, showing the forces are balanced.
source: static friction balances applied force until motion starts
verify_reason: Equal push and friction show balanced forces.

en: Draw the arrow for the applied force in the direction the hand or machine pushes, and the friction arrow in the opposite direction along the surface.
source: applied force direction matches push; friction opposes motion
verify_reason: Applied force and friction oppose along surface.

en: For an object with three forces, draw all three arrows from the same point, then check if any two opposite arrows are equal to spot balanced pairs.
source: systematic check of force pairs in a diagram
verify_reason: Arrows from same point; equal opposite arrows form balanced pair.

en: To draw a free-body diagram for an object on a table being pulled to the right, draw the pull arrow to the right, friction to the left, gravity down, and normal force up.
source: complete set of forces for a pulled object on a surface
verify_reason: Correct free-body directions for pull, friction, gravity, normal.

en: For a person walking forward, draw the friction arrow pointing forward, because friction from the ground pushes the person in the direction of motion.
source: friction as the driving force for walking
verify_reason: Ground friction pushes forward on walking person.

en: When drawing a free-body diagram for an object in an elevator accelerating upward, draw the normal force arrow longer than the gravity arrow.
source: apparent weight: normal force exceeds gravity during upward acceleration
verify_reason: Upward acceleration requires normal force greater than gravity.

en: A free-body diagram for a ball kicked into the air shows the gravity arrow pointing down and a shorter air resistance arrow pointing opposite to the ball's motion.
source: projectile with air resistance: two forces acting
verify_reason: Correct for rising ball; air resistance opposes motion.

en: For an object floating in water, draw the buoyancy arrow upward and the gravity arrow downward at equal lengths because the object is not sinking or rising.
source: buoyancy balances gravity for a floating object
verify_reason: Floating at rest means buoyancy equals gravity.

en: Draw a free-body diagram before solving a force problem so the balanced and unbalanced forces are visible and the net force direction is clear.
source: free-body diagram as first step in force analysis
verify_reason: Free-body diagrams reveal balanced forces and net force direction.

en: A clear aim names the one thing you want to find out, such as whether more water makes seeds sprout faster.
source: scientific investigation steps: aim defines the question
verify_reason: Clear aim states what you want to find out.

en: The materials list tells what you need and how much, like 100 grams of soil, so another person can prepare the same setup.
source: scientific investigation: materials and equipment step
verify_reason: Materials list includes quantities for repeatable setup.

en: Choose the measuring tool that matches what you measure, such as a ruler for length, a graduated cylinder for liquid, and a balance for mass.
source: measurement instruments match the property measured
verify_reason: Use ruler, graduated cylinder, balance for length, liquid, mass.

en: Number each step in the method so the experimenter knows the exact order, from preparing the setup to recording the final reading.
source: scientific investigation: method or procedures step
verify_reason: Numbered steps ensure correct order.

en: The conditions you keep the same, like temperature and amount of light, are called controlled variables and they make the test fair.
source: experimental design: controlled variables held constant
verify_reason: Controlled variables kept same ensure fair test.

en: Doing the experiment three or more times and averaging the results helps you spot mistakes and makes the data more dependable.
source: repeated trials improve reliability of data
verify_reason: Repeated trials and averaging improve reliability.

en: Use a bar graph to compare different groups and a line graph to show how one measurement changes as another value increases.
source: graph choice: bar for categories, line for trends
verify_reason: Bar graphs compare groups; line graphs show change.

en: Read measuring instruments at eye level and read liquid volume at the bottom of the curved surface to get an accurate value.
source: accurate instrument reading: eye level and meniscus
verify_reason: Eye level and meniscus bottom give accurate readings.

en: Results can be quantitative, like 40 degrees Celsius, or qualitative, like describing the liquid as clear and slippery.
source: types of data: quantitative numbers vs qualitative descriptions
verify_reason: Quantitative uses numbers; qualitative uses descriptions.

en: In the conclusion, you compare your actual results with your aim and say plainly what the data show, even if it is not what you wanted.
source: scientific investigation: conclusion answers the aim
verify_reason: Conclusions compare results to the aim.

en: Write down observations during the experiment, not later from memory, because details like color changes fade quickly.
verify_reason: Immediate notes prevent forgetting details.

en: Safety items such as goggles, gloves, or an apron are listed as materials when the procedure uses heat, chemicals, or sharp tools.
source: safety equipment part of materials list
verify_reason: Safety gear belongs in materials for risky procedures.

en: Every graph has labeled axes with units and a title, so a reader knows what each bar or line represents.
source: graph conventions: labeled axes, units, title
verify_reason: Labels, units, and titles make graphs clear.

en: A weather scientist at PAGASA records rainfall amounts in a table each day, then looks for patterns across the wet season.
verify_reason: Recording daily rainfall and finding patterns is accurate.

en: The aim guides your choice of materials and steps, because what you want to find out decides what you measure and how.
verify_reason: The aim determines what to measure and how.

en: The method is written clearly enough that another scientist can follow it and get similar results, which makes the investigation reliable.
verify_reason: Clear methods allow replication and reliability.

en: An oxygen atom needs two more electrons to fill its outer shell, and each hydrogen atom needs one, so they share to form water.
source: encyclopedia-stable; valence electron counts for H and O
verify_reason: Correct electron needs and sharing in water.

en: A carbon atom needs four more electrons, and each oxygen atom needs two, so carbon shares two pairs with each oxygen in CO2.
source: encyclopedia-stable; valence electron counts for C and O
verify_reason: Correct electron sharing in CO2 double bonds.

en: When two atoms share only one pair of electrons, the bond is called a single bond, like each hydrogen-oxygen link in water.
verify_reason: Single bond definition and water example correct.

en: Forming a covalent bond releases energy, which is why atoms bond willingly and why molecules stay together instead of falling apart.
verify_reason: Bond formation releases energy; stable molecules.

en: Because oxygen has two lone pairs of electrons, a water molecule is bent like a V, not a straight line.
verify_reason: Lone pairs repel, giving water bent shape.

en: Carbon dioxide is a straight molecule because carbon has no lone pairs, so the two oxygen atoms line up on opposite sides.
verify_reason: CO2 linear; central carbon has no lone pairs.

en: In water, oxygen pulls the shared electrons more strongly than hydrogen, so one end of the molecule is slightly negative and the other slightly positive.
verify_reason: Oxygen's higher electronegativity makes water polar.

en: Water is a liquid at room temperature but carbon dioxide is a gas, because of the weak forces between molecules, not the covalent bonds inside them.
source: encyclopedia-stable; physical states of molecular compounds
verify_reason: Phase depends on intermolecular forces, not covalent bonds.

en: A Lewis dot structure shows a covalent bond as a pair of dots or a line placed between the symbols of the two atoms.
verify_reason: Lewis structures show bonds as dot pairs or lines.

topic: bonding pairs and lone pairs in water
en: In water, oxygen has two bonding pairs shared with hydrogen and two lone pairs that are not shared with any other atom.
verify_reason: Oxygen in water has two bonding and two lone pairs.

en: The carbon dioxide that people breathe out and that jeepneys release is a covalent molecule made of one carbon and two oxygen atoms.
verify_reason: Correct: CO2 has one carbon and two oxygen atoms.

en: Table salt melts at about 800°C because its ions are locked in a strong crystal lattice, while sugar melts at a much lower temperature.
verify_reason: Salt melts near 800°C; sugar melts much lower.

en: Tapping an ionic crystal like salt shatters it into smaller cubes because pushing layers brings same-charged ions together, which repel.
source: ionic crystal brittleness due to ion repulsion
verify_reason: Same-charge repulsion explains ionic crystal shattering.

en: The formula NaCl means one sodium ion for every chloride ion in the entire crystal, not a single molecule like H2O.
source: ionic formula unit vs molecular formula
verify_reason: NaCl is a formula ratio, not a molecule.

en: Carbon dioxide is a covalent compound where each CO2 molecule is separate, so it is a gas at room temperature.
verify_reason: CO2 is separate molecules and gas at room temperature.

en: Most ionic compounds are solid at room temperature because their ions are held tightly in a rigid lattice, unlike many covalent compounds that are gases or liquids.
source: states of matter for ionic vs covalent compounds
verify_reason: Ionic lattices are rigid; many covalent compounds are not.

en: Covalent compounds like methane have individual molecules that move freely as a gas, with no repeating crystal structure at all.
verify_reason: Methane gas has free molecules, no crystal structure.

en: Ionic crystals are hard because strong ionic bonds hold the lattice, but covalent solids like wax are soft because their molecules are only weakly attracted.
source: physical properties of ionic and molecular solids
verify_reason: Ionic bonds are strong; wax has weak attractions.

en: Sugar is a covalent compound that forms separate molecules, while salt is ionic and forms a giant repeating lattice of ions.
source: comparison of sucrose and NaCl structures
verify_reason: Sugar is molecular; salt is an ionic lattice.

en: When melted, ionic compounds also conduct electricity because the ions can move; covalent liquids like oil do not.
verify_reason: Melted ions move and conduct; oil does not.

en: Some think salt is made of molecules, but it is actually a huge repeating pattern of ions, so each grain is one big crystal.
verify_reason: Salt is a repeating ion crystal, not molecules.

en: Even solid covalent compounds like ice are made of separate water molecules held by weak forces, not a lattice of charged ions.

verify_reason: Heterozygote shows dominant trait under complete dominance.

en: Recessive traits are not always harmful; they are simply hidden when a dominant allele is present.

en: Predicting ratios means using the parents' genotypes to list the possible genotypes and phenotypes of their offspring before they are born.

en: If a trait skips a generation, it is often recessive, because carriers can pass it on without showing it themselves.

en: The three-domain system is newer than the six-kingdom system, and it places kingdoms inside larger domains based on DNA evidence.

en: Classification helps scientists trace how different species evolved from common ancestors over millions of years.

en: After an earthquake, do not use matches or lighters because a gas leak could cause a fire.

topic: stay away from beach after quake

en: At the assembly area, teachers do a headcount to make sure every student is safe and no one is missing.

en: When you evacuate, bring your emergency go-bag so you have water, food, and a flashlight while you wait.

en: Wear closed shoes and long sleeves when you evacuate, because broken glass and debris can hurt your feet and skin.

en: During evacuation, the plan says to help younger children or classmates who are scared, so everyone moves together safely.

en: Use your phone only for emergencies after an earthquake, because too many calls can block the network for people who need help.

en: Follow the marked evacuation route even if it looks longer, because it is the path that avoids the most dangers.
verify_reason: Marked routes are designed to avoid known dangers.

topic: check walls for cracks before reentry

verify_reason: Cracks can signal structural damage after a quake.

en: Keep a small copy of your family disaster plan inside your school bag, so you can remember what to do even if you are away from home.
verify_reason: A copy helps you remember the plan away from home.

en: To see a rock's true color, break it open or look at a fresh chip, because the outside surface is often stained by weather or soil.
source: observation method: fresh surface vs weathered surface
verify_reason: Fresh surfaces show true color; outer surfaces weather and stain.

en: To see grain crystal size, hold a hand lens close to your eye and bring the rock toward it until the grains look sharp.
verify_reason: Correct hand lens technique for sharp viewing.

en: To describe texture, run a finger across the rock's fresh surface and note if it feels smooth, rough, gritty, or glassy.
verify_reason: Feeling fresh surface helps describe rock texture.

en: A good rock record lists each sample's color, texture, grain size, and hardness in a table so comparisons are easy to see.
verify_reason: Tables organize color, texture, grain size, and hardness.

en: When collecting rocks, wrap each sample in paper, label it with the date and place, and keep the label with the rock.
verify_reason: Wrapping and labeling samples preserves key information.

en: To compare colors fairly, look at all rock samples under the same bright light, because shadows can make colors look darker.
verify_reason: Same lighting makes color comparisons fair.

en: To describe luster, hold the rock so light bounces off it and decide if the shine looks metallic, glassy, pearly, or dull.
verify_reason: Luster terms metallic, glassy, pearly, dull are standard.

en: To describe grain shape, look at the edges of the crystals and note whether they are sharp and angular or smooth and rounded.
verify_reason: Angular versus rounded grain edges is correct.

en: To check for layering, turn the rock sideways and look for flat bands or stripes that run in one direction across the sample.
verify_reason: Layering appears as flat bands or stripes.

en: When comparing two rocks, choose chips of similar size, because a big piece can look rougher or darker than a small one.
verify_reason: Similar size helps fair comparison.

en: To compare density, hold one rock in each hand and feel which is heavier for its size, or use a balance scale.
verify_reason: Hefting or balance with similar size compares density.

en: To record where a rock was found, draw a simple map of the school grounds and mark each collection spot with a number.
verify_reason: Simple map with numbered spots records locations.

en: A weathered rock surface is often brown or gray from rain and air, so scientists always check the fresh break for true color.
verify_reason: Fresh breaks reveal true rock color.

en: A magnifying glass helps count tiny grains, and scientists record whether they can see grains without it or only with it.
verify_reason: Hand lens helps see tiny grains.

en: A battery has two ends, positive and negative, and it pushes electrical energy through the wires when the circuit path is complete.
verify_reason: Battery drives current in complete circuit.

en: Metals like copper, iron, and aluminum conduct electricity because their outer electrons are loose and free to move from atom to atom.
source: encyclopedia-stable; free electron model of metals
verify_reason: Metals have free-moving outer electrons.

en: The bulb lights only when the circuit is complete, meaning there is one unbroken path from one battery end, through the wires and bulb, back to the other end.
verify_reason: Complete circuit needed for bulb to light.

en: Even a tiny gap anywhere in the loop stops the electricity, because electrons need a continuous path from the battery through the bulb and back.
verify_reason: Continuous path needed; gap stops current.

en: Coins, paper clips, aluminum foil, metal spoons, and keys are everyday conductors that can complete a simple circuit and light a bulb.
verify_reason: Metals conduct and complete circuit.

en: Insulators act like a broken bridge in a circuit: electrons cannot cross them, so the current stops at that point.
verify_reason: Insulators block electron flow like broken bridge.

en: The wires in a circuit are like pipes for electricity; they guide the electrons from the battery to the bulb and back again.
verify_reason: Wires guide electrons like pipes.

en: Dry wood is an insulator, but wet wood can conduct a little electricity because the water in it carries dissolved minerals.
verify_reason: Dissolved minerals in moisture allow slight conduction.

en: Electric current is the flow of electrons through a wire, and it only happens when the circuit is closed and unbroken.
verify_reason: Current is electron flow in closed circuit.

en: A conductor is like an open door that lets electricity pass through, while an insulator is like a wall that blocks it.
verify_reason: Conductor open door; insulator wall analogy.

en: A complete circuit needs four parts: a source like a battery, wires to carry current, a load like a bulb, and a closed path.
verify_reason: Source, wires, load, closed path are needed.

en: Electric current is measured in amperes, but in a school circuit you can just watch the bulb to know that current is flowing.
source: encyclopedia-stable; ampere as unit of current
verify_reason: Amperes measure current; bulb shows flow.

en: Before testing, name the lever class by finding the fulcrum, load, and effort positions, because each class changes the force differently.

verify_reason: Lever class depends on fulcrum, load, effort positions.

en: Hold the spring scale at a right angle to the lever when pulling, so the reading shows only the lifting force and not a sideways pull.

en: Use a balance to check that the load weighs the same before every trial, so the weight is not a hidden variable.
source: fair-test design: verify constants before trials
verify_reason: Checking weight controls a hidden variable.

en: Start each trial with the lever horizontal and the load resting on the table, so every trial begins from the same position.

en: To test a second-class lever, place the load between the fulcrum and your hand, and move the load to see how the force changes.
source: lever classes: second-class lever (load between fulcrum and effort)
verify_reason: Load sits between fulcrum and effort in second-class levers.

en: Use a protractor to keep the pull angle the same in every trial, so only the lever arm distance changes.
source: fair-test design: hold angle constant as a control
verify_reason: Keeping angle constant isolates lever arm distance.

en: Mark the hand position on the lever with chalk or tape, so you push at the exact same spot in every trial.
source: fair-test design: mark positions for reproducibility
verify_reason: Marking ensures same push spot each trial.

en: Read the spring scale at eye level so the pointer lines up with the numbers, because looking from above or below changes the reading.
source: measurement practice: read at eye level to avoid parallax
verify_reason: Eye-level reading avoids parallax error.

en: Have the same person pull the spring scale in all trials, so the speed and smoothness of the pull stay consistent.
source: fair-test design: keep operator consistent across trials
verify_reason: Same person helps keep pulling style consistent.

en: Pull the spring scale slowly and steadily, because a fast jerk makes the reading jump higher than the true force.
source: measurement practice: slow steady pull avoids dynamic overshoot
verify_reason: Jerking adds extra force and false high reading.

en: In a lever fair test, multiplying the effort force by the effort distance gives the same number as multiplying the load force by the load distance.

en: A vector is a quantity that has both a size and a direction, so velocity is a vector because it includes which way something moves.

en: A scalar is a quantity that has only a size, so speed is a scalar because it just tells how fast without any direction.
verify_reason: Speed has magnitude only; scalar definition is correct.

en: To draw velocity, you use an arrow whose length shows the speed and whose direction points where the object is going.
verify_reason: Arrow length shows magnitude, direction shows velocity direction.

en: When a jeepney turns a corner at the same speed, its velocity changes because the direction of its motion changes.
verify_reason: Direction change means velocity changes even if speed constant.

en: A common mistake is thinking velocity is just a larger speed, but velocity is a different idea because it always has a direction.
verify_reason: Velocity includes direction, not just larger speed.

en: If a runner keeps a steady speed on a straight path, their velocity stays the same because both speed and direction are unchanged.
verify_reason: Constant speed and straight path mean constant velocity.

en: To measure velocity, you need a speedometer for the size and a compass or map to know the direction.
verify_reason: Speedometer gives magnitude; compass/map gives direction.

en: Two velocities can cancel out, like a boat moving forward while the river current pushes it backward at the same speed.
verify_reason: Equal opposite velocities can cancel to zero.

en: Velocity uses displacement, which is the straight-line change in position, while speed uses the total distance traveled.
verify_reason: Velocity uses displacement; speed uses total distance.

en: A ball thrown straight up has a velocity that points up first, then down, even though its speed just gets smaller and bigger.
verify_reason: Direction changes at top; speed decreases then increases.

en: A bus moving north on EDSA has a velocity of 40 km/h north, but the same bus moving south has a different velocity.
verify_reason: Same speed opposite directions are different velocities.

en: The unit for velocity is the same as speed, like meters per second or kilometers per hour, but it must include a direction.
source: SI units for velocity and speed
verify_reason: Velocity units match speed units plus direction.

en: A boat crossing a river has a velocity that combines its own engine speed and the river's current speed and direction.
verify_reason: Vector addition of engine and current velocities.

en: A runner sprinting 100 meters has a velocity pointing toward the finish line, while a runner sprinting back has a velocity pointing the opposite way.
verify_reason: Velocity direction matches motion; opposite for return.

en: Velocity can be split into parts, like a car moving northeast having a northward part and an eastward part.
verify_reason: Vector components split into perpendicular parts.

en: A car moving straight at a constant speed has a velocity that is constant, but if it brakes, its velocity changes because speed changes.
verify_reason: Braking reduces speed, so velocity changes.

en: To estimate grain crystal size, scientists compare the grains to everyday objects like sugar, rice, or peas on a printed chart.

en: A field sketch records the rock's outline, visible grains, and any bands, so the shape and details are kept even after leaving the site.

en: Before picking up a rock, scientists note whether it lies loose on the ground or is part of a larger layer or outcrop.

en: Comparing granite from two different provinces shows that the same rock type can vary in color and grain size from place to place.

en: A football kicked high into the air stays above the ground longer than one kicked low and flat, even if both travel the same forward distance.

en: In the Filipino game sipa, each kick sends the washer or ball on a projectile path, and a higher kick gives the player more time to prepare the next hit.

en: Rocks and ash thrown out of a volcano like Mayon follow projectile paths, and their range depends on the speed and angle of the eruption.

en: Range is the horizontal distance a projectile travels from its launch point to where it lands on the ground.

en: A projectile launched at a very steep angle, like 80 degrees, goes almost straight up and lands very close to the launch point.

en: Doubling the launch speed of a projectile makes it travel about four times farther, because range grows with the square of the speed.

en: A common mistake is thinking a heavier ball thrown the same way travels farther, but in ideal projectile motion, weight does not change the path at all.

en: A ball launched straight up at 20 meters per second takes about 2 seconds to reach its peak and about 4 seconds to return to the ground.

en: Water fountains shoot streams that curve like projectiles, and the nozzle angle controls how high and how far each stream sprays.

en: When you test a material, it becomes part of the circuit loop, so a conductor completes the path and lights the bulb, while an insulator breaks it.

en: Early scientists like Lavoisier defined an element as a pure substance that cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical means.
