en: Today's periodic table is ordered by increasing atomic number, which is the exact count of protons in an atom's nucleus.
source: Modern periodic table ordering by atomic number
verify_reason: Correct; atomic number equals proton count.

en: The periodic law states that element properties repeat in a regular pattern when elements are arranged by increasing atomic number.
verify_reason: Correct periodic law statement.

en: Jöns Jacob Berzelius introduced the one- or two-letter chemical symbols we still use, like O for oxygen and Fe for iron.
verify_reason: Correct historical symbol system.

en: Before Berzelius, scientists used different names and pictures for elements, so a shared symbol system made communication much easier.
verify_reason: True; shared symbols aided communication.

en: Mendeleev's table was powerful because it placed elements with similar chemical reactions in the same vertical column.
verify_reason: Correct; Mendeleev grouped by similar properties.

en: Early lists had fewer than 40 known elements, while the modern periodic table contains about 118 confirmed elements.
verify_reason: Correct; early lists under 40, now about 118.

en: Moseley used X-rays to show that atomic number, not atomic mass, is the true basis for ordering the elements.
verify_reason: Correct; Moseley established atomic number ordering.

en: The periodic table lets scientists predict how an unknown element will react based on its position among known neighbors.
verify_reason: Correct; position predicts chemical behavior.

en: The periodic table grew through the work of many scientists over more than a century, each building on the last person's findings.
verify_reason: Correct; many scientists contributed over time.

en: Classifying the Philippine crocodile as a separate species helps conservationists protect it, because it is found only in the Philippines and is endangered.
source: IUCN Red List; Philippine crocodile (Crocodylus mindorensis) endemic and endangered
verify_reason: Endemic and endangered; separate species aids targeted protection.

en: A common mistake is thinking all microbes are germs, but classification shows many bacteria and protists help break down waste and make food.
source: encyclopedia-stable; beneficial roles of microbes in decomposition and food production
verify_reason: Many microbes are beneficial decomposers and food producers.

en: Farmers use classification to choose crop varieties that share resistance to pests, because related plants often have similar defenses.
source: agriculture science; related crop varieties share genetic traits
verify_reason: Related plants can share pest resistance traits.

en: When doctors find a new microbe, they compare its DNA to known groups to predict how it spreads and what medicine might work.
source: medical microbiology; DNA comparison for pathogen identification
verify_reason: DNA comparison predicts traits and treatments.

en: The word 'bayawak' can mean different lizards in different provinces, so scientific names from classification prevent confusion.
source: encyclopedia-stable; common names vary by region, scientific names are universal
verify_reason: Common names vary; scientific names avoid confusion.

en: Classification helps scientists compare organisms from different regions, so a Filipino frog and an African frog can be checked if they are the same species.
source: biogeography; classification enables cross-regional species identification
verify_reason: Classification checks if distant populations are same species.

en: Classification helps scientists estimate how many species are still unknown by comparing new finds with already grouped organisms.
source: taxonomy; extrapolation from known groups to estimate biodiversity
verify_reason: Taxonomy estimates unknown species by comparing known groups.

en: All living things share the same genetic code for building proteins, so the three-domain system shows they all came from one common ancestor.
source: molecular biology; universal genetic code indicates common ancestry
verify_reason: Shared genetic code supports common ancestry.

en: Before building a road, scientists classify the plants and animals in the area to know which rare species need protection.
source: conservation biology; environmental impact assessments require species inventories
verify_reason: Surveys identify rare species needing protection.

en: Many archaea live in extreme conditions like hot springs, so scientists study them to understand how the first life on Earth survived.
source: astrobiology and evolutionary biology; extremophiles as models for early life
verify_reason: Extremophiles model early Earth life.

en: Field guides use classification to organize species into groups, so a hiker can identify a bird by matching it to its family.
source: natural history; field guides arranged by taxonomic groups
verify_reason: Field guides group species for identification.

en: If a scientist finds a new fungus, classification tells them it likely lives in damp places because fungi need moisture to grow.
source: ecology; kingdom-level traits predict habitat requirements
verify_reason: Fungi generally need moisture, so damp habitat is likely.

en: DNA-based classification can show that two look-alike organisms, like some desert plants, are actually from different families.
source: molecular phylogenetics; convergent evolution can mislead morphology
verify_reason: DNA evidence can reveal convergent look-alikes are unrelated.

en: Learning the six kingdoms helps Filipino students see the variety of life, from bakawan in the sea to eagles in the sky.
source: educational science; six-kingdom framework introduces biodiversity
verify_reason: Shows plant and animal variety; bakawan and eagles are examples.

en: Meiosis is a two-step division that reduces the chromosome number by half, turning one diploid cell with paired chromosomes into four haploid cells with single chromosomes.
verify_reason: Accurate description of meiosis reducing chromosome number.

en: Having genes from two parents creates more variety in a population, which helps the species survive changes in the environment.
source: biology: genetic variation and natural selection
verify_reason: Genetic variation aids survival in changing environments.

en: A corn kernel gets one set of genes from the pollen parent and one from the seed parent, so kernels on one cob can have different colors.
verify_reason: Each kernel results from separate pollen, so colors vary.

en: Some people think a child gets more traits from the parent they resemble, but meiosis gives an equal number of chromosomes from each parent.
verify_reason: Meiosis gives equal chromosomes from each parent.

en: Plant breeders in the Philippines pollinate one rice plant with another so the resulting seeds get DNA from both, a direct use of meiosis and fertilization.
source: agriculture: rice breeding in the Philippines (IRRI)
verify_reason: Pollination combines DNA from two plants via fertilization.

en: The first division of meiosis separates matched chromosome pairs, so each sex cell ends up with just one chromosome from each pair.
source: biology: meiosis stages (Prophase I to Telophase II)
verify_reason: First division separates pairs; final sex cells have one.

en: In flowering plants, meiosis makes pollen and egg cells inside the flower, and fertilization joins them to form a seed.
source: botany: plant life cycle and alternation of generations
verify_reason: Meiosis makes gametes in flower; fertilization forms seed.

en: A child's traits come from the specific genes they inherit, not from a blending of parents' blood, because meiosis sorts genes into separate sex cells.
verify_reason: Traits come from genes, not blended blood.

en: A person walking forward on a moving bus has a velocity that is the sum of the bus's velocity and their own walking velocity.
source: relative velocity concept in moving frames
verify_reason: Correct relative to ground.

en: The speed of a car is just the size of its velocity vector, so a car moving 60 km/h north has a speed of 60 km/h.
verify_reason: Speed is velocity magnitude.

en: A car reversing out of a driveway has a velocity pointing backward, while its speedometer still shows a positive speed.
source: direction of velocity vs speedometer reading
verify_reason: Velocity direction backward, speed positive.

en: A car driving up a steep hill has a velocity pointing up the slope, and if it turns around to go down, its velocity points down.
verify_reason: Velocity points along slope direction.

en: A pendulum swinging has a velocity that changes direction every swing, but its speed is highest at the bottom and zero at the ends.
source: pendulum motion: changing direction, varying speed
verify_reason: Speed highest at bottom, zero at ends.

en: Two cars moving at the same speed in opposite directions have velocities that are exact opposites, so one is positive and the other is negative.
verify_reason: Opposite directions give opposite signs.

en: When a car slows down on a straight road, its velocity gets smaller but still points the same way, so only the size changes.
source: velocity magnitude changes with speed while direction constant
verify_reason: Magnitude decreases, direction unchanged.

en: When a car speeds up on a straight road, its velocity gets bigger but still points the same way, so the arrow gets longer.
source: velocity magnitude increases with speed while direction constant
verify_reason: Magnitude increases, direction unchanged.

en: A ball thrown straight up at 20 meters per second reaches about 20 meters high, because gravity slows it down at about 10 meters per second each second.
source: kinematic equation h = v²/(2g) for vertical launch
verify_reason: Correct ideal physics; v²=2gh gives 20 m.

en: Air resistance also lowers the peak of a projectile, so a real baseball does not fly as high as the ideal calculation predicts.
source: real-world projectile motion; air drag reduces maximum height
verify_reason: Air resistance reduces height.

en: When a basketball player shoots from above the rim, the ball can be released at a flatter angle and still reach the hoop, because it starts higher.
source: projectile motion with different initial heights; higher start allows flatter trajectory
verify_reason: Higher release allows flatter angle.

en: Throwing a ball faster at the same angle makes it stay in the air longer, because it rises higher before gravity pulls it back down.
source: vertical motion independence; greater initial vertical speed increases time of flight
verify_reason: Greater speed increases height and time.

en: At the highest point of its flight, a projectile has already traveled half of its total horizontal range.
source: symmetry of projectile path on level ground
verify_reason: True for ideal level-ground projectile.

en: A football kicked straight up at 30 meters per second slows to about 20 meters per second after one second, because gravity reduces its speed by about 10 meters per second each second.
source: constant acceleration due to gravity, 9.8 m/s² rounded to 10
verify_reason: Correct; gravity slows it 10 m/s each second.

en: For a basketball free throw, players often aim for a release angle of about 50 degrees, which gives the ball a high arc and a better chance of dropping in.
source: common coaching advice and biomechanics studies; rounded value
verify_reason: About 50 degrees is common for free throws.

en: Gravity changes a projectile's vertical speed by about 10 meters per second every second, no matter how heavy the object is.
source: Galileo's principle; gravitational acceleration independent of mass
verify_reason: Gravity acceleration is mass-independent.

en: Fishing boats that scoop up fish faster than they can reproduce empty the ocean of certain species, leaving too few adults to make the next generation.
verify_reason: Overfishing can deplete species.

en: Chemical pollution from factories and farms can poison rivers and lakes, killing fish and the insects that other animals depend on for food.
verify_reason: Chemical pollution can poison aquatic life.

en: As the planet warms, some animals cannot find the cooler places they need to live, so their populations shrink and may die out.
verify_reason: Accurate and clear for grade 5.

en: When seawater gets too warm, corals lose the colorful algae that feed them, turn white, and can die—destroying homes for thousands of fish species.
verify_reason: Correctly explains coral bleaching and reef habitat loss.

en: A species with only a few dozen members left is in danger because a single storm, disease, or hunting event can wipe out the whole group at once.
verify_reason: Correctly describes extinction risk for tiny populations.

en: When a species has very few members left, they must breed with close relatives, and the loss of genetic variety makes them weaker against new diseases.
verify_reason: Accurate about inbreeding and reduced disease resistance.

en: Scientists estimate species are disappearing about 1,000 times faster than the natural rate before humans appeared on Earth.
verify_reason: Common scientific estimate, appropriately qualified.

en: Some birds and butterflies migrate to cooler places each year, but climate change shifts the seasons so they arrive when their food is already gone.
verify_reason: Correctly describes climate-driven timing mismatch.

en: Protected areas like national parks give endangered species a safe place to live, but they work only if the animals' needs for food and space are met.
verify_reason: Accurate and balanced about protected areas.

en: When a species goes extinct, the ecosystem services it provided—like pollination or pest control—are lost, and people lose food and medicine sources.
verify_reason: Correctly links extinction to lost ecosystem benefits.

en: Distance and displacement are both measured from a reference point, the fixed place you choose as the starting line for describing motion.
source: encyclopedia-stable; definition of reference point in kinematics
verify_reason: Acceptable for grade-level motion description.

en: Displacement always includes a direction, like north or east, while distance is just a number with no direction attached to it.
verify_reason: Correctly contrasts vector displacement and scalar distance.

en: Distance can never be negative because it only counts how much ground you covered, and you cannot cover less than zero ground.
source: encyclopedia-stable; scalar quantities are always non-negative
verify_reason: Correct, distance is a nonnegative scalar.

en: Displacement can be negative if you choose one direction as positive, so moving the opposite way gives a negative displacement value.
verify_reason: Correct, displacement sign depends on chosen direction.

en: Displacement is always the straight-line distance from start to finish, so it is never longer than the distance you actually traveled.
source: encyclopedia-stable; definition of displacement as shortest path
verify_reason: Straight-line displacement magnitude never exceeds path distance.

en: A jeepney that winds through narrow streets to reach the plaza covers a long distance, but its displacement is just the short line from terminal to plaza.
verify_reason: Correct: winding path distance exceeds straight displacement.

en: A basketball player dribbling from one hoop to the other and back has a large distance, but zero displacement because he returns to the same hoop.
verify_reason: Returns to start, so displacement is zero.

en: To find displacement on a map, draw a straight arrow from start to finish and measure it, while distance requires tracing the whole path.
verify_reason: Correct method: straight arrow for displacement, trace path for distance.

en: Whenever a trip ends exactly where it began, the displacement is zero, no matter how long or winding the journey was.
verify_reason: Closed trip has zero displacement regardless of path.

en: Walking from school to home through a market adds extra distance, but displacement is just the straight-line gap between the school gate and your front door.
verify_reason: Correct: extra path distance, straight-line displacement.

en: Distance and displacement are equal only when you travel in a perfectly straight line without turning or changing direction.
verify_reason: Only straight one-way motion makes them equal.

en: An airplane flying from Manila to Cebu follows a curved route in the sky, so its distance is longer than the straight displacement between the two cities.
verify_reason: Curved route distance exceeds straight displacement.

en: Because distance has no direction, speed is just how fast you go, while velocity uses displacement and direction to tell where you are heading.
verify_reason: Speed is scalar; velocity is vector from displacement.

en: In a diverse ecosystem, some species can handle heat, others handle cold, so when the climate shifts, at least some survive.
verify_reason: Diverse species improve survival when climate shifts.

en: The Philippines grows many rice varieties, so if a new disease attacks one type, the other types still produce grain for harvest.
verify_reason: Different rice varieties can resist disease differently.

en: Many kinds of decomposers, like different fungi and bacteria, break down dead leaves, so if one dies out, the others keep the soil rich.
verify_reason: Multiple decomposers provide backup for soil health.

en: One hectare of tropical rainforest can hold about 300 tree species, while a plantation has just one, so a single disease can wipe out the plantation.
source: published estimate: ~300 tree species per hectare in tropical rainforest
verify_reason: Rainforests have many tree species; plantations are vulnerable monocultures.

en: Mangroves along Philippine coasts shelter many species, and if one mangrove type dies, the others still hold the soil during storms.
verify_reason: Mangrove diversity helps maintain coastal protection.

en: Ecosystems with few species are easier for invaders to take over, because there are fewer native competitors to stop them.
verify_reason: Fewer native competitors make invasion easier.

en: In a diverse animal community, a disease spreads less because the germ has fewer suitable hosts, so more animals stay healthy.
verify_reason: Diverse hosts can slow disease spread.

en: A coral reef with many coral species recovers faster after bleaching, because some corals can survive warmer water and regrow the reef.
verify_reason: Some corals tolerate heat and help reef regrow.

en: When many bird species spread seeds, a forest can regrow after a typhoon, because some birds survive and carry seeds from other trees.
verify_reason: Birds disperse seeds, aiding forest regrowth after disturbance.

en: As the climate changes, a diverse ecosystem can rearrange itself, with new species taking over roles that others can no longer fill.
verify_reason: Ecosystems can shift species roles as climate changes.

en: High biodiversity is not just for saving rare animals; it also keeps our farms, water, and air working for people every day.
verify_reason: Biodiversity provides ecosystem services for farms, water, air.

en: During a typhoon, a diverse forest loses some trees but keeps its soil, while a single-species plantation may fall down completely.
verify_reason: Diverse forests resist wind and soil loss better than monocultures.

en: In a diverse farm, natural enemies like spiders and birds control pests, so a pest outbreak does not destroy the whole crop.
verify_reason: Natural enemies help reduce pest outbreaks in diverse farms.

en: A diverse ocean with many fish species keeps the food chain stable, so a drop in one fish population does not empty the sea for fishers.
verify_reason: Species diversity stabilizes food webs and fisheries.

en: Earthquakes in the Philippines come from two main sources: fault movements like the Philippine Fault, and subduction at trenches like the Manila Trench.
verify_reason: Philippine earthquakes come from faults and subduction zones.

en: The Philippine Sea Plate moves northwest at about 7 centimeters per year, slowly pushing against the Eurasian Plate to build the islands.
verify_reason: Plate moves northwest about 7 cm/year, building islands.

en: Deep earthquakes near trenches occur at increasing depths farther from the trench, tracing the path of the subducting plate into the mantle.
verify_reason: Earthquake depths trace subducting plate path.

en: The Pacific Ring of Fire also includes Japan and Indonesia, so those islands share the same pattern of trenches, volcanoes, and earthquakes as the Philippines.
verify_reason: Japan and Indonesia share Ring of Fire tectonic patterns.

en: On a map, large mountain ranges on land often sit next to deep ocean trenches, because both are formed by the same plate collision.
verify_reason: Convergent plate collisions often form mountains and trenches together.

en: A deadly skin fungus called chytrid has wiped out many frog species around the world, because it blocks their skin from absorbing water.
verify_reason: Fungus damages skin, disrupting water and salt balance.

en: Fishing nets meant for tuna often trap sea turtles and dolphins, which drown because they cannot reach the surface to breathe.
verify_reason: Turtles and dolphins are air-breathers and drown.

en: People dig up rare orchids from Philippine forests to sell, and when too many are taken, the wild plants can no longer make seeds.
source: encyclopedia-stable; orchid trade in the Philippines
verify_reason: Overharvest can leave too few plants to reproduce.

en: When crocodiles or eagles attack livestock, farmers sometimes kill them to protect their animals, reducing the wild predator population.
verify_reason: Retaliatory killing reduces predator numbers.

en: Dams built across rivers stop salmon and other migratory fish from swimming upstream to lay eggs, so their numbers drop sharply.
verify_reason: Dams block spawning routes, lowering fish populations.

en: Warmer sand from climate change makes sea turtle eggs hatch mostly females, so too few males remain to fertilize future eggs.
verify_reason: Warmer nests produce mostly female hatchlings.

en: Bright lights on beaches make baby sea turtles crawl toward the road instead of the ocean, where they often die from cars or heat.
verify_reason: Artificial lights misdirect hatchlings away from ocean.

en: Too many livestock on dry grassland eat every plant, leaving native animals like prairie dogs with no food or cover to survive.
verify_reason: Overgrazing removes food and shelter for native animals.

en: Plant cells have tiny connecting pores called plasmodesmata, but animal cells do not have these bridges between cells.
verify_reason: Only plant cells have plasmodesmata.

topic: cell membrane position in plant and animal cells
en: In a plant cell, the cell membrane sits just inside the stiff cell wall, but in an animal cell, the membrane is the outer boundary.
verify_reason: Plant membrane is inside wall; animal membrane is outer.

en: Animal cells have lysosomes that break down waste, while plant cells usually use their vacuoles for storage and breakdown instead.
verify_reason: Animal lysosomes and plant vacuoles handle waste breakdown.

en: Plant cells have plastids like chloroplasts to make and store food, but animal cells have no plastids at all.
verify_reason: Plastids occur in plant cells, not animal cells.

en: Both cells use mitochondria to release energy, but only plant cells also use chloroplasts to capture energy from sunlight.
verify_reason: Mitochondria release energy; chloroplasts capture sunlight in plants.

en: A plant cell's large vacuole often pushes the nucleus to the side, while an animal cell's nucleus stays near the center.
verify_reason: Large vacuole often shifts plant nucleus; animal nucleus usually central.

en: Animal cells can change shape to move through tiny spaces, but plant cells stay fixed because of their rigid cell wall.
verify_reason: Animal cells can change shape; plant cell walls limit movement.

topic: plant cell size due to vacuole
en: Plant cells are often larger than animal cells because the big central vacuole takes up so much room.
verify_reason: Central vacuole makes many plant cells larger.

en: Plant cells store extra sugar as starch, while animal cells store it as glycogen, a different type of stored food.
verify_reason: Plants store starch; animals store glycogen.

en: The cell wall gives plant cells a strong frame, so plants can stand tall, while animal cells rely on other tissues for support.
verify_reason: Cell walls support plants; animal tissues provide support.

en: Because plant cells have chloroplasts, they can make their own food, but animal cells must eat other organisms to get energy.
verify_reason: Chloroplasts allow photosynthesis; animals must consume food.

en: Plant cells divide without centrioles, but animal cells use these tiny structures to help pull chromosomes apart.
verify_reason: Plant cells lack centrioles; animal cells use them.

en: A thermometer works by letting its liquid expand or contract until it matches the object's temperature, so it shows temperature, not heat.
verify_reason: Liquid expansion shows temperature, not heat.

en: Heat is measured in joules, while temperature is measured in degrees Celsius, so they are different quantities with different units.
source: SI units: joule for heat, Celsius for temperature
verify_reason: Joules measure heat; Celsius measures temperature.

en: Cold is not a separate thing; it is simply the lack of heat, so heat always moves from warmer to cooler places.
source: concept: heat is energy, cold is lack of heat
verify_reason: Heat flows warmer to cooler; cold is lack of heat.

en: Heat is not a substance that can be stored; it is energy in motion, so it only exists while it is being transferred.
source: definition of heat as energy transfer
verify_reason: Heat is energy transfer, not stored substance.

en: Water needs more heat to raise its temperature than sand does, so a beach's sand heats up faster than the sea during the day.
source: specific heat of water vs sand
verify_reason: Water's higher specific heat makes sand warm faster.

en: A forest with many tree species has roots at different depths, so a drought that dries the topsoil still lets deep-rooted trees find water.
source: plant ecology: root stratification in mixed forests
verify_reason: Deep roots access water when topsoil is dry.

en: In a diverse meadow, different flowers bloom at different times, so pollinators always find nectar even if one plant fails to flower.
source: plant-pollinator phenology in diverse plant communities
verify_reason: Different bloom times provide continuous nectar.

en: A species with many genetic variations has a better chance that some individuals resist a new disease, so the whole population does not die out.
source: population genetics: genetic diversity buffers disease
verify_reason: Genetic variation improves disease resistance chances.

en: Tree holes, logs, and leaf litter create small shelters, so many species survive storms or droughts even if the main habitat is damaged.
verify_reason: Microhabitats shelter species during disturbances.

en: A wetland with many plant species filters different pollutants, so the water stays clean even if one plant dies.
source: ecosystem services: phytoremediation in diverse wetlands
verify_reason: Diverse plants filter pollutants, maintaining water quality.

en: In a diverse forest, trees with different leaf shapes catch sunlight at different heights, so even if some trees fall, others still get light.
verify_reason: Different heights and leaf shapes capture light; true.

en: In a diverse grassland, different grasses grow in different seasons, so the soil is covered all year and erosion is prevented.
verify_reason: Different seasonal growth keeps soil covered, reducing erosion.

en: A diverse forest has many tree species that drop leaves at different times, so the soil gets a steady supply of nutrients.
verify_reason: Staggered leaf drop supplies nutrients steadily.

en: For the main groups, the group number tells you how many valence electrons an atom has, like group 2 means two.
source: periodic table group number = valence electrons for main-group elements
verify_reason: Main group number indicates valence electrons; accurate.

en: Magnesium and calcium are in group 2, so both have two valence electrons and react in similar ways.
verify_reason: Both group 2, two valence electrons, similar reactions.

en: Carbon and silicon are in group 14, each having four valence electrons, which lets them form four bonds.
verify_reason: Group 14 elements have four valence electrons, form four bonds.

en: Nitrogen and phosphorus are in group 15, each with five valence electrons, so they often make three bonds.
verify_reason: Group 15 elements have five valence electrons, often form three bonds.

en: Elements in group 1 have one valence electron, while group 2 elements have two, so group 1 metals react more easily.
source: comparison of group 1 and group 2 reactivity
verify_reason: Group 1 metals lose one electron, react more easily.

en: Moving across a period changes the number of valence electrons, but moving down a group keeps that number the same.
source: periodic table trends across periods and down groups
verify_reason: Valence electrons change across periods, same down groups.

en: Elements in the same group do not have the same number of electron shells; they have the same number of valence electrons.
source: common misconception about electron shells vs valence electrons
verify_reason: Same group shares valence electrons, not shell number.

en: Sodium and potassium are both group 1 elements, and both form salts, like table salt and a salt substitute.
source: sodium and potassium compounds in daily life
verify_reason: Both group 1; form chloride salts.

en: Calcium and magnesium are group 2 elements, and both are important for strong bones and healthy plants.
source: calcium and magnesium in biology and agriculture
verify_reason: Both support bones and plant health.

en: The outermost electrons are the ones that touch other atoms, so having the same number of them makes elements act alike.
source: chemical reactivity determined by outer electrons
verify_reason: Outer electrons determine bonding; 'touch' is simplified but okay.

en: Transition metals in the middle columns do not follow the simple group-number rule for valence electrons, so we focus on main groups.
source: transition metals exception to group number rule
verify_reason: Transition metals have variable valence electrons; main groups are simpler.

en: Helium has two valence electrons, while other noble gases have eight, and this complete set makes them very stable.
verify_reason: Helium has full shell with two; other noble gases have eight.

en: Because group 1 elements have just one valence electron, they easily lose it to become a positive ion with a +1 charge.
verify_reason: Group 1 has one valence electron, forms +1 ions.

en: Because group 17 elements have seven valence electrons, they easily gain one to become a negative ion with a -1 charge.
verify_reason: Group 17 has seven valence electrons, gains one for -1.

en: Knowing an element's group lets you predict its valence electrons and therefore how it will react with other elements.
source: predicting chemical properties from group number
verify_reason: Group gives valence electrons, helping predict reactions.

en: Oxygen and sulfur are both in group 16, so each has six valence electrons and typically needs two more to fill its outer shell.
source: periodic table group 16 valence electron configuration
verify_reason: Group 16 has six valence electrons; needs two more.

en: Lithium, sodium, and potassium are group 1 metals with one valence electron, so they are stored under oil to keep them from reacting with air.
source: standard laboratory safety for alkali metals
verify_reason: Group 1 metals react with air/moisture; oil prevents this.

en: A common mistake is thinking elements in a group have the same total number of electrons, but they actually share the same number of outer electrons only.
verify_reason: Correct: same group shares valence electrons, not total electrons.

en: Bromine and iodine are in group 17, so they each have seven valence electrons and easily gain one to form salts like potassium bromide.
source: group 17 halogens reactivity and ion formation
verify_reason: Halogens have seven valence electrons and gain one electron.

en: Strontium and calcium are in group 2, so both have two valence electrons, and they give fireworks their red and orange colors when burned.
source: flame test colors of alkaline earth metals
verify_reason: Group 2 elements have two valence electrons; flame colors correct.

en: Seismic waves are vibrations that spread out from an earthquake, and the way they travel tells scientists what the ground is made of.
verify_reason: Seismic waves reveal Earth's interior materials.

en: When a seismic wave crosses from one layer to another, it bends, just like a straw looks bent in a glass of water.
source: encyclopedia-stable; wave refraction at layer boundaries
verify_reason: Waves bend when entering different layers, like light refraction.

en: The Earth's core is about half the size of the whole planet's radius, making it a huge central sphere.
source: rounded value; core radius ~3500 km vs Earth radius ~6371 km
verify_reason: Core radius is about half Earth's radius.

en: The crust is the thinnest layer, like the skin of an apple compared to the whole fruit.
verify_reason: Crust is thinnest, like apple skin.

en: The inner core is a solid ball of iron and nickel, kept solid by the crushing pressure around it.
source: encyclopedia-stable; inner core composition and state
verify_reason: Inner core is solid iron-nickel due to pressure.

en: The pressure at the center of the Earth is millions of times stronger than the air pressure at the surface.
verify_reason: Center pressure is millions of times surface pressure.

en: The Earth's average density is about 5.5 times that of water, but surface rocks are lighter, so the deep interior must be very dense.
source: rounded value; Earth's average density vs surface rocks
verify_reason: Average density implies dense deep interior.

en: By comparing wave arrival times at different stations, scientists build a 3D picture of the inside of the Earth.
source: encyclopedia-stable; seismic tomography and model building
verify_reason: Wave arrival times help map Earth's interior.

topic: P-wave speed drop in outer core
en: The speed of P-waves suddenly drops when they enter the outer core, which tells scientists that this layer is liquid.
source: encyclopedia-stable; P-wave velocity drop in liquid
verify_reason: P-wave velocity drops at liquid outer core.

topic: P-wave speed increase in inner core
en: The speed of P-waves speeds up again when they reach the inner core, showing that this deepest layer is solid.
source: encyclopedia-stable; P-wave velocity increase in solid inner core
verify_reason: P-wave speed increases at solid inner core.

en: The Lehmann discontinuity is the boundary between the liquid outer core and the solid inner core, discovered by studying P-wave behavior.
verify_reason: Boundary discovered via P-wave data.

en: The Earth is layered like an onion, with a thin crust, a thick mantle, a liquid outer core, and a solid inner core.
verify_reason: Earth's main layers are correctly described.

en: The model of Earth's layers was built from thousands of earthquakes recorded all over the world, not just one event.
source: encyclopedia-stable; global seismic network and model development
verify_reason: Seismic model uses global earthquake records.

en: The Philippine archipelago is made of several island arcs, each with its own trenches and volcanoes, so different regions have different features.
source: plate tectonics theory on island arcs
verify_reason: Philippines has multiple island arcs and trenches.

en: Not all mountains in the Philippines are volcanoes; some ranges were pushed up by plate collisions without volcanic activity.

en: Mendeleev placed tellurium before iodine even though tellurium is heavier, because their chemical properties matched better that way.

en: The lanthanide elements were so similar to each other that scientists placed them in a separate row below the main periodic table.
source: Placement of lanthanides in the periodic table

en: By Mendeleev's time, about 60 elements were known, and his table organized them all into a single chart.
source: Historical count of known elements by 1869

en: Mendeleev's table was not the first attempt, but it was the first to be widely accepted because it predicted new elements.

en: Humphry Davy used electricity to break down compounds and discover new elements like sodium and potassium.
source: Davy's use of electrolysis to discover elements

en: Narrow valleys between mountains can squeeze typhoon winds, making them blow faster in those gaps, just like air speeding through a narrow pipe.

en: A typhoon gets more fuel when the warm ocean layer is deep, because even after stirring the sea, there is still warm water to keep it going.
verify_reason: Deep warm layer sustains typhoon after mixing.

en: As a typhoon churns the sea, it pulls up cooler water from below, which can weaken the storm by taking away its warmth.
verify_reason: Upwelling cooler water reduces storm heat source.

en: The Philippines' many islands act like a series of brakes, so a typhoon that crosses several islands becomes much weaker than one that stays over the ocean.
verify_reason: Multiple landfalls increase friction and cut ocean fuel.

en: Tall mountains like the Cordillera weaken typhoons more than low hills because they force air to rise higher, causing more rain and wind disruption.

en: A gently sloping seafloor lets storm surge push farther inland, while a steep underwater drop-off keeps the surge closer to the shore.

en: A typhoon weakens more over a large island like Luzon than over a small island, because there is more land to create friction and cut off the ocean fuel.

en: Typhoons need a large area of warm ocean water to form and grow, not just a small warm patch, so they typically start in the open Pacific.

en: A mountain range that runs across a typhoon's path blocks and weakens the wind, but a range that runs parallel lets the wind slide along it.

en: When a typhoon passes over land, its calm eye often becomes cloudy and ragged because the storm loses its organized structure.

en: A typhoon weakens faster when it hits a mountainous coast than a flat one, because the mountains cause more friction and disrupt the wind flow.
verify_reason: Mountains increase friction, weakening winds faster.

en: The western Pacific Ocean has the warmest water on Earth, which is why most strong typhoons form and grow there.
verify_reason: Western Pacific warm pool fuels strong typhoons.

en: If a typhoon crosses a small island and then returns to warm ocean, it can regain strength, because the sea provides the energy it lost on land.
verify_reason: Warm ocean can restore energy after land.

en: The periodic table's rows and columns are a direct map of an atom's electron shells and outer electrons.
source: periodic table structure: rows = shells, columns = outer electrons
verify_reason: Rows show shells; columns show outer electrons.

en: The electron structure of an atom acts like a code, so reading its position on the table reveals its electron arrangement.
source: periodic table as a code for electron configuration
verify_reason: Position reveals electron arrangement for main groups.

en: The outermost shell of an atom is called the valence shell, and its electrons are the ones that join in chemical bonds.
verify_reason: Valence shell electrons form chemical bonds.

en: The electron structure decides if an element is a metal or nonmetal, because metals have few outer electrons while nonmetals have many.
source: metal/nonmetal classification based on outer electrons
verify_reason: Metals tend to have fewer outer electrons than nonmetals.

en: The electron structure explains the staircase line on the table that separates metals from nonmetals, based on their outer electron counts.
source: periodic table staircase line, metal/nonmetal boundary
verify_reason: Staircase line reflects outer-electron trends.

en: The electron structure explains why the first period has only two elements, because the first shell can hold only two electrons.
verify_reason: First shell holds two electrons, so two elements.

en: The electron structure explains why the table has a short first row and longer rows below, because each shell can hold more electrons.
source: periodic table row lengths based on shell capacity
verify_reason: Higher shells hold more electrons, making longer rows.

en: Magnesium's 12 electrons are arranged 2-8-2, so it sits in period 3, group 2, just below beryllium.
verify_reason: Magnesium 2-8-2 is period 3, group 2.

en: Carbon's 6 electrons are arranged 2-4, placing it in period 2, group 14, where it can form four bonds.
verify_reason: Correct electron arrangement and bonding capacity.

en: Phosphorus's 15 electrons are arranged 2-8-5, placing it in period 3, group 15, just below nitrogen.
verify_reason: Correct electron arrangement and periodic position.

en: Aluminum's 13 electrons are arranged 2-8-3, placing it in period 3, group 13, just below boron.
verify_reason: Correct electron arrangement and periodic position.

en: The electron structure of an atom determines its position on the table, which is why carbon's position tells us it can form many different molecules.
source: carbon's position and its ability to form diverse molecules
verify_reason: Correct; four valence electrons allow diverse bonding.

en: The electron structure determines the charge an atom will form when it becomes an ion, like calcium losing two electrons to become +2.
source: ion formation, calcium loses 2 electrons to form +2 ion
verify_reason: Correct; calcium loses two valence electrons.

en: The electron structure explains why the table is divided into blocks, like the s-block on the left and the p-block on the right.
source: periodic table blocks (s, p, d, f) based on subshell filling
verify_reason: Correct; s- and p-blocks reflect electron subshells.

en: The electron structure explains why the periodic table is a tool for predicting an element's behavior without memorizing its properties.
verify_reason: Correct; periodic table predicts behavior from electron structure.

en: The electron structure explains why some elements are very reactive and others are not, based on how close they are to a full outer shell.
source: reactivity based on distance to full outer shell
verify_reason: Correct; reactivity relates to outer shell fullness.

en: The electron structure explains why the table is called 'periodic,' because the pattern of outer electrons repeats every row, causing properties to repeat too.
source: periodic law: repeating properties based on electron configuration
verify_reason: Correct; outer electron pattern repeats periodically.

en: The electron structure of an atom determines its position on the table, which is why the table is a universal tool for chemists everywhere.
source: periodic table universal use in chemistry
verify_reason: Correct; electron structure determines table position.

en: The mantle is solid because S-waves pass through it, but it can flow very slowly over millions of years, like thick honey.
source: S-wave transmission indicates solid mantle; mantle convection
verify_reason: Correct; S-waves indicate solid, slow flow possible.

en: The crust is thicker under mountains and thinner under oceans, a difference that seismic wave travel times reveal clearly.
source: seismic refraction studies of crustal thickness
verify_reason: Seismic travel times show crust is thicker under mountains, thinner under oceans.

en: The inner core was discovered when a faint P-wave appeared in the shadow zone, showing that a solid inner core reflects waves.
source: Lehmann's observation of P-wave arrivals in shadow zone
verify_reason: Faint P-waves in shadow zone revealed solid inner core.

en: By measuring how long seismic waves take to reach stations around the world, scientists calculate the depth of each boundary inside Earth.
verify_reason: Travel-time measurements locate internal boundaries.

en: Seismic waves curve as they travel deeper because their speed gradually increases, so they follow curved paths, not straight lines.
source: seismic refraction in a layered Earth
verify_reason: Speed increases with depth, bending seismic waves.

en: Earth's land is split into separate continents, while the ocean is one connected body of water covering most of the surface.

en: The Pacific Ocean alone spreads over a larger area than all of Earth's land put together.
source: encyclopedia-stable; Pacific Ocean area vs total land area
verify_reason: Pacific area exceeds all land area.

en: Earth's water fills the low ocean basins, so the higher land sticks out as continents and islands.
source: encyclopedia-stable; formation of ocean basins and continents
verify_reason: Water fills low basins; land rises above.

en: Because people live on land, it is easy to think land is bigger, but water actually covers most of Earth's surface.
source: common misconception corrected by Earth surface data
verify_reason: Water covers most of Earth's surface.

en: Looking down from a high airplane, you would see far more blue ocean than brown or green land.
source: observational fact; aerial view of Earth's surface
verify_reason: Ocean dominates Earth's surface view.

en: On any world map, the blue of oceans takes up more space than all the other colors of land put together.
verify_reason: Ocean area exceeds land on world maps.

topic: total area of oceans and land
en: Earth's oceans cover about 361 million square kilometers, while all land covers about 149 million square kilometers.
source: rounded values from Earth fact sheets
verify_reason: Areas match known ocean and land totals.

en: The amount of silica in magma controls its stickiness: more silica means thicker, stickier lava that forms steep cones.
source: encyclopedia-stable; silica content determines magma viscosity
verify_reason: Correct; more silica increases viscosity and steepness.

en: Runny lava spreads far from the vent before hardening, widening the base, while sticky lava hardens close by, building height.
source: encyclopedia-stable; lava flow distance vs viscosity
verify_reason: Correct; runny lava widens base, sticky builds height.

en: Runny lava lets gas bubbles escape easily, so eruptions are quiet and the lava flows out to form a wide, gently sloping shield.
verify_reason: Correct; gas escapes easily from runny lava.

en: Cinder cones are built from loose rock fragments that settle at a steep angle of about 30 degrees, giving them straight, steep sides.
source: encyclopedia-stable; angle of repose for granular materials
verify_reason: Correct; cinder slopes near angle of repose.

en: Basaltic lava is very hot, about 1100 degrees Celsius, so it stays thin and runny, while cooler lava is thicker and builds steeper shapes.
verify_reason: Correct for grade 5; temperature affects viscosity.

en: A tall, steep volcano does not mean it is more powerful; it simply means its lava is stickier and piles up closer to the vent.
verify_reason: Correct; shape does not equal power.

en: Imagine pouring syrup on a plate: thin syrup spreads flat like a shield volcano, while thick syrup piles up like a steep stratovolcano.
verify_reason: Correct analogy for lava viscosity and shape.

en: The lava that builds Mayon and other Philippine stratovolcanoes is andesitic, meaning it has enough silica to be sticky and explosive.
verify_reason: Correct; Mayon is andesitic and sticky.

en: A plate boundary is the meeting line where two of Earth's moving crust pieces touch, and most earthquakes and volcanoes happen along these lines.
verify_reason: Correct; most quakes and volcanoes occur there.

en: At the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, new crust is born as magma fills the gap, pushing the plates apart at about 2 to 5 centimeters a year.
verify_reason: Correct; spreading rate about 2-5 cm/year.

en: Earth's outer shell is broken into about seven large plates and several smaller ones that all move at different speeds.
verify_reason: About seven major plates plus smaller ones is accurate.

en: Divergent boundaries create new crust while convergent boundaries destroy it, so Earth's surface stays about the same size.
source: encyclopedia-stable; conservation of Earth's surface area
verify_reason: Divergent creates, convergent destroys; surface area stays balanced.

en: Earthquakes happen at all three types of plate boundaries, not just transform faults, because all moving plates build up stress.
source: encyclopedia-stable; earthquakes occur at all boundary types
verify_reason: All boundary types can produce earthquakes from built-up stress.

en: At subduction zones, the sinking plate carries water down, which helps the mantle melt and rise to feed volcanoes above.
source: encyclopedia-stable; flux melting at subduction zones
verify_reason: Water from sinking plate lowers mantle melting point.

en: Decomposition reactions need an energy input like heat, light, or electricity to break a compound apart into simpler substances.
verify_reason: Heat, light, or electricity often drive decomposition.

en: A metal can only replace another metal in a single replacement reaction if it is more reactive, a ranking shown in the activity series.
verify_reason: More reactive metals replace less reactive ones.

en: Double replacement reactions often happen because they form a solid precipitate, a gas, or water, which removes ions from the solution.
source: encyclopedia-stable; driving forces of double replacement
verify_reason: Precipitate, gas, or water formation drives double replacement.

en: Combination and decomposition are opposite processes: combination builds a bigger compound from smaller parts, while decomposition breaks a compound into smaller parts.
verify_reason: Opposite processes: building versus breaking compounds.

en: When a metal reacts with an acid, it is a single replacement reaction where the metal replaces hydrogen, producing hydrogen gas and a salt.
verify_reason: Metal replaces hydrogen in acid, producing salt and hydrogen gas.

en: Mixing vinegar and baking soda causes a double replacement reaction that forms carbonic acid, which quickly decomposes into water and carbon dioxide gas.
verify_reason: Vinegar and baking soda form carbonic acid, then water and CO2.

en: Rust forms through a combination reaction where iron, oxygen, and water join together to create a new reddish-brown compound.
verify_reason: Iron, oxygen, and water combine into hydrated rust.

en: Electrolysis is a decomposition reaction where electricity forces a compound like water to break apart into its elements.
verify_reason: Electricity decomposes water into hydrogen and oxygen.

en: A more reactive metal like zinc can replace copper in a blue copper sulfate solution, turning it colorless as zinc sulfate forms.
verify_reason: Zinc replaces copper, fading blue copper sulfate solution.

en: Mixing two clear solutions can produce a solid precipitate in a double replacement reaction, like silver chloride forming from silver nitrate and sodium chloride.
verify_reason: Silver nitrate and sodium chloride form solid silver chloride.

en: When a new substance forms from two simpler ones, like sodium and chlorine making table salt, it is a combination reaction.
verify_reason: Sodium and chlorine combine to form table salt.

en: An acid-base neutralization is a special double replacement reaction where an acid and a base swap partners to form water and a salt.
verify_reason: Acid and base exchange partners forming water and salt.

en: Combination reactions are common in daily life, such as when iron combines with sulfur to make iron sulfide, or when hydrogen burns with oxygen to make water.
verify_reason: Iron with sulfur and hydrogen with oxygen form compounds.

en: When limestone (calcium carbonate) is heated strongly, it decomposes into calcium oxide (quicklime) and carbon dioxide gas, a reaction used in making cement.

topic: food gives energy to living things

en: A stone stays the same size for many years, but a small seedling grows into a tall tree.

en: A plant slowly bends toward the sunny window, showing it responds to light, while a plastic plant never moves.

en: A hen lays eggs that can hatch into chicks, so chickens can make new chickens, but a glass of water cannot make more water.

en: The sun gives light and heat, but it is not alive because it does not grow, eat, or reproduce.

en: Water is not alive, yet every living thing from a carabao to a rice plant needs it to survive.

en: A carabao eating grass in the field is living, but the wooden cart it pulls is non-living because it cannot eat or grow.

en: A mango tree is living: it grows from a small seed into a tall tree that bears fruit year after year.

en: A wooden chair was once part of a living tree, but after cutting and drying, it no longer grows or breathes.

en: A spider's web is not alive, but a living spider made it to catch its food.

en: A plant with a broken stem can heal and grow new parts, but a broken plastic toy stays broken forever.

en: A cat walks, runs, and jumps by itself, while a toy cat moves only when someone pushes or winds it.

en: Living things live for a time and then die, while stones just wear away and do not die.

en: Fish need water to live, and worms need soil, but a rock can stay anywhere because it is not alive.

en: Momentum is conserved because during a collision, the forces two objects exert on each other are equal and opposite, so their momentum changes cancel out.
verify_reason: Equal and opposite forces cause equal and opposite momentum changes.

en: When two ice skaters push away from each other on ice, their total momentum stays zero, so they glide apart with equal and opposite momenta.

verify_reason: Initially at rest, total momentum remains zero.

en: A slow, heavy truck and a fast, light bicycle can have the same momentum, because momentum equals mass times velocity.
verify_reason: Momentum equals mass times velocity.

en: When a ball stops rolling on the ground, its momentum is not destroyed; it passes to the Earth, which moves a tiny, unmeasurable amount.
source: conservation of momentum with the Earth as part of the system
verify_reason: Friction transfers momentum to Earth.

en: In a crash test, a car hits a heavy wall; the wall barely moves, but the car's momentum change is balanced by the wall's tiny momentum change.
source: conservation of momentum with a massive object
verify_reason: Wall/Earth gains equal but tiny momentum.

en: During a jeepney-tricycle collision, the lighter tricycle changes speed more than the heavier jeepney, but their total momentum stays conserved.
source: conservation of momentum applied to unequal masses

en: Two identical carts, one moving at 2 meters per second and one at rest, move together at 1 meter per second after a sticky collision.
verify_reason: Momentum before equals after: 2m = 2m×1.

en: Conservation of momentum applies to the whole system of colliding objects, not to each object on its own.
source: conservation law for a closed system
verify_reason: Momentum conservation applies to whole system.

en: Momentum has direction, so two objects moving toward each other can have momenta that cancel out to zero.
verify_reason: Momentum is a vector; opposite directions can cancel.

en: When a firecracker explodes, its pieces fly in all directions, but the total momentum of all the pieces together stays zero.

en: A bowling ball slows down when it hits a pin, but the total momentum of the ball and pin together is the same before and after.
source: conservation of momentum in an elastic collision
verify_reason: Total momentum is conserved without outside forces.

en: In any collision, the momentum one object gains is exactly equal to the momentum the other object loses, keeping the total unchanged.
source: Newton's third law and momentum transfer
verify_reason: Momentum changes are equal and opposite in collisions.

en: Investigators use conservation of momentum to estimate how fast vehicles were moving before a crash by studying their damage and final positions.

en: An explosion is like a collision played backward: pieces fly apart, yet the total momentum before and after stays the same.

en: Conservation of momentum holds true for every collision, from tiny atoms bumping into each other to entire galaxies interacting.

en: Fossils give the relative age of a rock—whether it is older or younger than another—but not the exact number of years.

en: Fossil types appear in a fixed order through time, so scientists can tell a rock's age by which fossils are inside it.

en: Each fossil species appears in the rock record at one time and disappears later, so its presence marks a specific span of time.

en: A group of different fossils found together in a rock layer gives a more accurate age than just one fossil type.

en: Trilobites, extinct sea animals with three-part shells, are index fossils that date rocks from the Paleozoic era.

en: Pollen grains from ancient plants, found in lake mud, are fossils that help date the age of the sediment.

en: Solar panels are tilted to face the Sun because a surface facing the rays directly captures more energy than one lying flat.

en: The equator gets about 12 hours of daylight every day all year, while higher latitudes swing between long summer days and short winter days.

en: The tilt makes the Sun's angle change gradually through the year, so seasons flow smoothly instead of switching suddenly from hot to cold.

en: Because the tilt stays at about 23.5 degrees, the seasons repeat at the same time every year.

en: The tropics are the warmest region on Earth because the tilt keeps the Sun's rays arriving steeply there all year.

en: In summer, the ground absorbs more heat from the direct Sun, and the air above it becomes warmer.

en: Herbivores like carabao and grasshoppers eat plants directly, so they occupy the second trophic level just above the producers.

en: Carnivores that eat herbivores, like a frog eating a grasshopper, sit on the third trophic level, and those that eat other carnivores sit even higher.

en: Fungi and bacteria break down dead bodies and animal waste, returning nutrients to the soil, but they are not drawn as a level in an energy pyramid.

en: A pyramid of numbers counts individual organisms at each level, while an energy pyramid measures stored energy, so the two can have different shapes.

en: In a bakawan mangrove, young fish and crabs eat fallen leaves and algae, then bigger fish eat them, moving energy upward through the pyramid.

en: People usually sit near the top of a food pyramid because we eat both plants and animals that have already eaten plants.

en: Both plant and animal cells use mitochondria to break down food, but only plant cells have chloroplasts to make that food in the first place.

en: The energy released in mitochondria is stored in ATP, which acts like a rechargeable battery for moving, building, and repairing cells.

en: Uniform velocity is motion with a constant speed and a constant direction, so the object never speeds up, slows down, or turns.

en: An object with uniform velocity covers the same distance in each equal time interval, like 5 meters every second.

en: A car cruising at a steady 60 km/h on a straight highway is an example of uniform velocity, so its distance-time graph is a straight line.

en: A jeepney moving at a constant speed on a straight road shows uniform velocity, and its distance-time graph is a straight line.

en: A train traveling at a steady 80 km/h on a straight track has uniform velocity, so its graph is a straight line.

en: A ball rolling on a smooth, flat floor at a steady speed has uniform velocity, and its distance-time graph is a straight line.

en: On a uniform velocity graph, the slope calculated from any two points gives the same speed, proving the speed never changes.

en: Uniform velocity differs from uniform speed because uniform velocity also requires a constant direction, though both look like straight lines on distance-time graphs.

en: A distance-time graph of uniform velocity that does not pass through the origin means the object started at a distance away from the reference point.

en: You can predict where a uniformly moving object will be later by extending the straight line on its distance-time graph.

en: In uniform velocity, the speedometer reading stays the same, so the line on a distance-time graph has the same steepness all along.

en: To draw a distance-time graph of uniform velocity, plot equal distance increases for equal time steps and connect the points with a straight line.

en: In uniform velocity, distance increases linearly with time, meaning the graph is a straight line and the ratio of distance to time is constant.

en: A distance-time graph of uniform velocity has no curves, because a curve would mean the speed is changing.

en: The y-intercept of a uniform velocity graph shows the object's starting distance from the reference point.

en: Uniform velocity is also called constant velocity, and it means the object's velocity vector does not change.
verify_reason: Correct definition of constant velocity.

en: If a uniform velocity graph passes through the origin, the object started at the reference point at time zero.

en: Uniform velocity is the simplest motion to graph because its distance-time graph is always a straight line.

en: On a distance-time graph, the horizontal axis measures time in seconds and the vertical axis measures distance in meters, so the slope's unit is meters per second.

en: A mature plant makes flowers, and each flower can turn into a fruit that holds seeds for new plants to grow.

en: A mango tree grows from a seed into a seedling, then a tall tree that bears fruit with seeds inside for new trees.

en: Unlike mammals, birds do not nurse their babies with milk; they bring insects, seeds, or worms to feed their chicks.

en: Some mammals, like dogs, become adults in about a year, while elephants take many years to reach adulthood.

en: A bird's egg has a hard shell that protects the growing chick inside from harm until it is ready to hatch.

en: A seed sprouts into a seedling, which grows leaves and roots, then becomes a mature plant that can flower and make seeds.

en: Speeding up and slowing down are both acceleration, but slowing down is sometimes called deceleration.

en: The nucleus is the atom's central core, and it is packed tightly with protons and neutrons.

en: When drawing an atom, put the nucleus in the middle and draw the shells as circles around it.

en: The first electron shell, which is closest to the nucleus, can hold up to two electrons.

en: The second electron shell can hold up to eight electrons, but only after the first shell is full.
verify_reason: Second shell holds up to eight after first fills.

en: Electrons fill the shell nearest the nucleus first before they move to the outer shells.

en: When drawing shells, each one is a complete circle around the nucleus, and the circles never cross each other.

en: A sodium atom has eleven electrons: two in the first shell, eight in the second, and one in the third.

en: Electrons are negatively charged, so they are pulled toward the positive nucleus at the center.

en: To draw an atom, count its electrons, then place them shell by shell starting from the inside.

en: Helium has just two electrons, both fitting in the first shell, so its drawing shows only one shell.

en: In the Bohr model, each shell sits at a fixed distance from the nucleus, like floors in a building.

en: Relative dating arranges events from oldest to youngest, while absolute dating measures actual years, and together they build the geologic time scale.

en: Sediments usually settle in flat, horizontal layers, so if scientists see tilted rock layers, they know something moved them after they formed.
verify_reason: Original horizontality explains tilted layers.

en: Fossils appear in a consistent order in rock layers, so a fossil found in one place can help match the age of layers in another place.
verify_reason: Fossil succession correlates rock layers.

en: Scientists choose the dating isotope by the rock's age: carbon-14 suits young remains, while potassium-argon and uranium-lead measure much older rocks.
verify_reason: Carbon-14 dates young remains; K-Ar and U-Pb date older rocks.

en: Potassium-argon dating measures the decay of potassium into argon in volcanic rocks, giving ages from about 100,000 years to billions of years.
verify_reason: K-Ar dates volcanic rocks from 100,000 to billions of years.

en: Uranium-lead dating uses the decay of uranium into lead inside zircon crystals, and it can date rocks that are billions of years old.
verify_reason: U-Pb dates zircon crystals billions of years old.

en: After one half-life, half the parent atoms remain; after two, one-quarter remain, so counting parent and daughter atoms reveals the rock's age.
verify_reason: Half-life decay ratios reveal age.

en: Absolute dating adds real numbers to the relative order of rock layers, turning a simple sequence into a time scale measured in millions of years.

en: By matching the same fossil or ash layer in different places, scientists connect rock layers and build one timeline for a whole region.

en: When the same index fossil appears in two distant rock layers, scientists conclude those layers formed at about the same time.
