en: As the oceanic plate sinks, it scrapes off soft sediments that pile up against the front of the plate above, building a ridge called an accretionary wedge.
verify_reason: Correct subduction zone process.

en: The sinking plate drags the edge of the plate above downward, bending it like a spring until it snaps, releasing earthquakes that shake the land above.
verify_reason: Correct elastic rebound earthquake analogy.

en: Behind the volcanic arc, the sinking plate can stretch the plate above apart, cracking it so the sea floor sinks to form a back-arc basin.
verify_reason: Correct back-arc basin formation.

en: The subducting plate squeezes the plate above, compressing it over millions of years so the crust folds and thickens into mountain ranges.
verify_reason: Correct mountain-building process.

en: Across a period from left to right, elements change from reactive metals to reactive nonmetals because their outer electrons increase.
source: periodic trends: metallic to nonmetallic across a period
verify_reason: Broadly correct for grade 5; noble gases omitted.

en: The 18 groups exist because electron shells can hold many electrons, and transition metals fill inner shells in the middle block.
source: periodic table layout: transition metals and shell filling
verify_reason: Vague but acceptable; transition metals fill inner d orbitals.

en: An element's position in the periodic table predicts its reactivity: Group 1 metals react violently, while Group 18 gases do not react.
source: periodic table: group position correlates with reactivity
verify_reason: Generally true; noble gases are mostly unreactive.

en: Although early scientists sorted elements by atomic mass, the modern periodic table sorts them by atomic number, which is the number of protons.
source: history of periodic table: Moseley and atomic number
verify_reason: Correct; modern table orders by proton number.

en: Sodium sits in period 3 and group 1, so its atoms have three electron shells and one outer electron, making it very reactive.
verify_reason: Sodium has three shells and one outer electron.

en: The periodic table's shape comes from electron shells filling in order, so each new row starts when a new shell begins to fill.
source: periodic table construction from electron configuration
verify_reason: Accurate for grade 5; each period begins a new shell.

en: Scientists use the periodic table to predict unknown element properties, like how reactive a new element might be based on its group.
source: periodic table as predictive tool in chemistry
verify_reason: Correct; group trends help predict properties.

en: A fair test of an electromagnet keeps the same battery and nail, and only changes the number of wire coils to compare strength.
source: fair-test design: one variable changed, rest constant
verify_reason: Correct fair-test setup with one changed variable.

en: Plot the number of coils on the x-axis and paper clips picked up on the y-axis to see the trend.
verify_reason: Correct independent and dependent variable placement.

en: Use the same size and type of paper clips for every trial so the test is fair and results are comparable.
verify_reason: Correct control for fair comparison.

en: Swapping the battery connections flips the electromagnet's poles, but it still attracts the same number of paper clips.
verify_reason: Poles reverse but attraction strength stays same.

en: Add a switch in the circuit to turn the electromagnet on and off without removing the wire from the battery.
verify_reason: Correct; switch safely controls current.

en: When you disconnect one wire from the battery, the nail drops all paper clips right away because the current stops.
verify_reason: Correct; current stops and magnetism is lost.

en: A mutagen is any chemical or radiation that raises the mutation rate by damaging DNA or interfering with how DNA copies.
verify_reason: Correct definition of mutagen.

en: A chromosomal mutation can delete, duplicate, or flip a large segment of a chromosome, affecting many genes at once.
source: types of chromosomal mutations in biology
verify_reason: Deletion, duplication, and inversion affect many genes at once.

en: Cells have repair enzymes that fix most DNA mistakes, so only a small number of mutations remain and cause changes.
verify_reason: Repair enzymes fix most DNA mistakes, leaving few mutations.

en: Mutations happen by chance, not because an organism needs a new trait, so they are random changes in DNA.
source: mutations as random events in genetics
verify_reason: Mutations occur by chance, not from need.

en: An advantage of series circuits is that they use less wire because all parts connect in one simple loop.
verify_reason: One loop uses less wire than multiple branches.

topic: series circuit hard to find broken part
en: A limitation of series circuits is that when a bulb burns out, you must test each bulb one by one to find the broken one.
verify_reason: One burned-out bulb breaks the whole loop.

en: An advantage of parallel circuits is that a TV and a refrigerator can run at the same time because each branch works on its own.
verify_reason: Each branch works independently.

en: A limitation of parallel circuits is that a short circuit in one branch can draw a huge current, which may trip the main breaker.
source: electrical safety: short circuit behavior in parallel
verify_reason: A short branch can draw huge current and trip breaker.

en: An advantage of series circuits is that connecting batteries in series adds their voltages, like two 1.5-volt batteries making 3 volts.
source: series connection of cells increases total voltage
verify_reason: Series batteries add their voltages.

en: Jeepney headlights are wired in parallel, so if one headlight burns out, the other still lights the road for the driver.
verify_reason: Parallel wiring keeps one headlight working if other fails.

en: The main advantage of series circuits is low cost, while the main advantage of parallel circuits is independent operation.
verify_reason: Series is cheaper; parallel allows independent operation.

en: Keep the wire coil tight and evenly spaced around the nail so every trial has the same shape, making the comparison fair.
source: fair-test design: consistent construction controls variables
verify_reason: Same coil shape makes trials fair.

en: Hydroelectric dams let falling river water spin turbines to make electricity, releasing no carbon dioxide, and the Philippines has many rivers for this clean power.
source: encyclopedia-stable; hydroelectricity is renewable and emits no direct CO2
verify_reason: Falling water spins turbines without direct CO2 release.

en: Turning farm waste like rice husks and coconut shells into electricity is renewable because plants regrow, and it can replace some coal in the Philippines.
source: encyclopedia-stable; biomass from agricultural residues is renewable if sustainably managed
verify_reason: Correct; farm waste biomass is renewable and can offset coal.

en: Solar and wind power now cost less than new coal plants, so switching to them saves money while also cutting the greenhouse gases that warm the Earth.
source: IRENA and market data show declining renewable costs below new coal
verify_reason: Generally true; renewables often cheaper than new coal.

en: Solar and wind power depend on weather, but storing their electricity in batteries lets them provide steady power even when the sun sets or wind stops.
source: encyclopedia-stable; energy storage enables grid integration of variable renewables
verify_reason: Correct; batteries store energy for when weather lacks sun/wind.

en: In a normal fault, rocks are pulled apart and the block above the crack slides down, like a sinking sidewalk.
source: fault types by stress direction (normal = extension) — encyclopedia-stable
verify_reason: Correct; hanging wall slides down in extension.

en: In a reverse fault, rocks are squeezed together and the block above the crack slides up, shortening the ground.
source: fault types by stress direction (reverse = compression) — encyclopedia-stable
verify_reason: Correct; hanging wall slides up in compression.

en: Reverse faults are common in the Philippines because the country sits where two big plates collide and squeeze the crust.
source: PHIVOLCS: Philippine plate convergence creates reverse faults
verify_reason: Correct; plate collision causes reverse faults.

en: The Philippines also has many strike-slip faults because the plates grind sideways as they push together, not straight on.
source: PHIVOLCS: Philippine Fault accommodates oblique convergence as strike-slip
verify_reason: Correct; oblique plate motion creates strike-slip faults.

en: Earthquakes send out waves: P-waves arrive first and push-pull, while S-waves arrive second and shake side to side.
source: encyclopedia-stable: P-waves arrive first, S-waves second
verify_reason: Correct; P-waves arrive first, S-waves second.

en: Normal faults, where rocks pull apart, are rare in the Philippines because the plates here mostly push together.
source: plate tectonics: Philippines is convergent, not extensional — PHIVOLCS
verify_reason: Correct; mostly compressional setting makes normal faults uncommon.

en: The charge of an ion equals the number of electrons it lost or gained, so magnesium losing two electrons becomes a +2 ion.
verify_reason: Correct; losing electrons gives positive charge.

en: In an ionic compound, the total positive charge from cations always balances the total negative charge from anions, so the compound is neutral.
verify_reason: Correct; ionic compounds are electrically neutral.

en: Calcium loses two electrons, and each chlorine atom gains one, so one calcium ion pairs with two chloride ions to form CaCl₂.
verify_reason: Correct; Ca²⁺ pairs with two Cl⁻.

topic: ionic compounds solid at room temperature
en: Because the electrostatic attraction between ions is so strong, ionic compounds like table salt are solid at room temperature.
verify_reason: Strong ionic bonds make salts solid at room temperature.

en: Valence electrons sit farthest from the nucleus, so they are the first to feel the pull of another atom's nucleus during a reaction.
verify_reason: Outermost electrons interact first in reactions.

en: Sodium has one valence electron that it easily gives to chlorine, which has seven, so both end up with full outer shells in table salt.
verify_reason: Sodium loses one, chlorine gains one; both shells fill.

en: Oxygen has six valence electrons, so it shares two of them with two hydrogen atoms to fill its shell and make water.
verify_reason: Oxygen shares two electrons, filling its outer shell.

en: When atoms bond, only the valence electrons are rearranged; the inner electrons and the nucleus stay unchanged.
source: atomic structure; bonding involves only outer electrons
verify_reason: Only valence electrons rearrange during bonding.

en: Most atoms follow the octet rule, aiming for eight valence electrons, but hydrogen and helium are happy with just two.
source: octet rule with exceptions for hydrogen and helium
verify_reason: Octet rule exceptions for hydrogen and helium are correct.

en: Forming a chemical bond releases energy, which is why bonded atoms like those in water are more stable than separate atoms.
verify_reason: Bond formation releases energy, increasing stability.

en: An atom's tendency to lose, gain, or share electrons comes from its valence electrons, not from its inner ones.
source: chemical reactivity depends on valence electrons
verify_reason: Valence electrons determine bonding behavior.

en: Nitrogen has five valence electrons, so it needs three more to fill its shell, which is why it forms three bonds in ammonia.
source: covalent bonding in ammonia; nitrogen has 5 valence electrons
verify_reason: Nitrogen needs three electrons, forms three bonds.

en: When scientists observe, they look, listen, and touch carefully, then write down exactly what they notice without adding guesses.
source: science process skills: observing (sensory observation, recording)
verify_reason: Observation uses senses and records facts, not guesses.

en: To predict, scientists use what they already know to guess what will happen next in a test, then they measure to check.
verify_reason: Prediction is an informed guess checked by testing.

en: When measuring with a ruler, place the zero mark exactly at one end of the object and read the number at the other end.
source: measuring technique: aligning zero mark on ruler
verify_reason: Correct ruler use for accurate measurement.

en: To measure a tiny object, scientists use millimeters, but for a long distance like a room, they use meters instead.
source: unit selection based on object size (mm, cm, m)
verify_reason: Millimeters for tiny, meters for room length.

en: A good record of a measurement writes the number and the unit together, like 5 centimeters, so everyone understands the exact size.
verify_reason: Units are essential for clear measurements.

en: Daytime length is the number of hours from sunrise to sunset, and Earth's tilt makes that number change through the year.
verify_reason: Daytime defined sunrise to sunset; tilt changes it.

en: As Earth orbits, the Northern Hemisphere tilts toward the Sun in June, giving longer days, and away in December, giving shorter days.
verify_reason: Northern Hemisphere tilts toward June, away December.

en: Daylight length changes fastest near the equinoxes and slowest near the solstices, so the difference per day is not constant.
verify_reason: Daylight change rate peaks at equinoxes, slows at solstices.

en: At about 45 degrees north, the longest day has about 15 hours of daylight and the shortest has about 9 hours.
verify_reason: 45°N longest ~15h, shortest ~9h is accurate.

en: The summer solstice happens when the Northern Hemisphere tilts most toward the Sun, and the winter solstice when it tilts most away.
verify_reason: Solstices mark maximum tilt toward/away.

en: In the Northern Hemisphere, summer days have more than 12 hours of daylight, while winter days have less than 12 hours.
verify_reason: Northern summer >12h, winter <12h.

en: Earth's tilt stays the same, but as it orbits the Sun, the orientation of that tilt relative to the Sun changes, so daylight length changes.
verify_reason: Tilt direction relative to Sun changes during orbit.

en: The tilt makes the Sun rise earlier and set later in summer, so the total daylight hours increase.
verify_reason: Summer tilt causes earlier sunrise, later sunset.

en: You can see the tilt's effect by recording sunrise and sunset times each week and watching the daylight hours change.
verify_reason: Recording sunrise/sunset times shows daylight changes.

en: Earth rotates at a steady speed, so the longer path of the Sun in summer means more hours of daylight.
verify_reason: Longer summer sun path above horizon gives more daylight.

en: The closer a place is to the poles, the more hours of daylight it gets on the summer solstice and the fewer on the winter solstice.
verify_reason: Higher latitudes have more summer daylight, less winter daylight.

en: The number of daylight hours on a given day depends on both your latitude and the time of year, because of the tilt.
verify_reason: Daylight depends on latitude and time of year.

en: Daylight hours on the summer solstice range from about 12 at the equator to 24 at the Arctic Circle.
verify_reason: Equator about 12 hours; Arctic Circle 24 on summer solstice.

en: In the Southern Hemisphere, the longest day happens in December, and the shortest in June, which is the opposite of the north.
verify_reason: Southern seasons are opposite northern.

en: Shelter is a limiting factor: a forest can hold only as many nesting birds as there are safe tree holes and branches for their nests.
source: encyclopedia-stable; shelter as a resource in carrying capacity
verify_reason: Nesting sites limit bird numbers.

en: The resource that is scarcest, whether food, water, shelter, or mates, sets the ceiling for how many animals an ecosystem can support.
source: Liebig's law of the minimum; encyclopedia-stable
verify_reason: Scarcest resource limits population size.

en: When food is scarce, animals may survive but produce fewer young, so the population grows more slowly even without extra deaths.
source: ecological principle that food shortage lowers birth rates
verify_reason: Food scarcity can lower births, slowing growth.

en: Work is the total energy transferred, while power is how quickly that energy is transferred.
source: definitional distinction between work and power
verify_reason: Work is energy transferred; power is transfer rate.

en: Just as speed tells how fast distance is covered, power tells how fast work is done.
source: analogy between speed and power as rates
verify_reason: Correct analogy; both are rates.

en: Your electric bill charges for energy in kilowatt-hours, not power, because power is the rate of using energy while kilowatt-hours measure total energy.
source: electric utility billing measures energy, not power
verify_reason: Correct; kWh measures energy, power is rate.

en: A thermoelectric generator uses the heat difference between two sides of special materials to make electricity directly, with no moving parts.
verify_reason: Correct; Seebeck effect, no moving parts.

en: Space probes like Voyager use radioisotope thermoelectric generators, which turn heat from decaying radioactive material into electricity far from the Sun.
source: NASA / encyclopedia-stable; RTG on Voyager missions
verify_reason: Correct; RTGs use radioactive decay heat.

en: Concentrated solar power plants use curved mirrors to focus sunlight, heating a fluid until it makes steam that spins a turbine.
verify_reason: Correct; mirrors heat fluid to steam.

en: Thermoelectric generators can be attached to car exhaust pipes to capture wasted engine heat and turn it into electricity.
source: encyclopedia-stable; automotive thermoelectric waste heat recovery
verify_reason: Correct; exhaust heat can generate electricity.

en: A solar pond is a salty lake that traps the Sun's heat at the bottom, and that stored heat can be used to make electricity.
verify_reason: Correct; salt gradient traps heat.

en: A Stirling engine uses the difference between hot and cold air to move a piston, and that motion can spin a generator to make electricity.
verify_reason: Correct; temperature difference drives piston.

en: Aluminum has a mass number of about 27, so subtracting its 13 protons leaves 14 neutrons in each aluminum atom.
source: aluminum-27 stable isotope; mass number 27, atomic number 13
verify_reason: Correct for common Al-27 isotope.

en: The atomic number is the element's identity, so any atom with exactly 13 protons must be aluminum, no matter how many neutrons it has.
source: periodic table definition: atomic number = number of protons
verify_reason: Correct; protons define element.

en: The atomic mass of an element is roughly the sum of its protons and neutrons, so aluminum's atomic mass of about 27 matches its mass number.
source: atomic mass rounded to nearest whole number equals mass number
verify_reason: Correct; atomic mass approximates proton+neutron total.

en: Earth spins from west to east, so the Sun appears to rise in the east and set in the west every day.
source: Earth's rotation direction is a standard astronomy fact.
verify_reason: Correct; eastward spin causes apparent east sunrise.

en: Earth makes one full turn in about 24 hours, which is why the Sun's position and shadows change throughout the day.
source: Earth's rotation period is about 24 hours.
verify_reason: Earth's rotation causes daily Sun and shadow changes.

en: Because Earth turns about 15 degrees per hour, a shadow stick's shadow also swings about 15 degrees each hour.
source: Earth rotates 360 degrees in 24 hours, so 15 degrees per hour.
verify_reason: Earth rotates 15°/hour; shadow direction changes about same.

topic: Sun's apparent motion is an illusion
en: The Sun does not travel around Earth; its daily path is an illusion caused by Earth spinning on its axis.
verify_reason: Apparent Sun motion is from Earth's spin.

en: Solar noon, when the Sun is highest and shadows are shortest, can be a few minutes before or after 12:00 on your clock.
source: Equation of time and time zones cause solar noon to differ from clock noon.
verify_reason: Solar noon varies with location and time zone.

en: A volcano's life lasts thousands of years, so the last 100 years of records show only a small slice of how it behaves.
source: encyclopedia-stable; volcanoes are long-lived geological features
verify_reason: Volcano lifetimes exceed human records; 100 years is short.

en: Volcanoes with thick, sticky magma tend to explode violently, while those with runny magma flow gently, so each volcano's pattern looks different.
source: encyclopedia-stable; magma viscosity controls eruption style
verify_reason: Magma viscosity affects eruption style.
